en: The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter One: Requesting the Buddha (I). Chapter One: Requesting the Buddha.
Homage to the Buddha Vairocana, the Ocean of Great Wisdom.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Bhagavān was dwelling on Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean, within the city of Laṅkā atop its summit—that mountain being composed of various precious substances, with diverse jewels interspersed so that its radiance blazed forth like a mountain of gold illuminated by hundreds of thousands of suns.

Furthermore, there were immeasurable flower gardens and fragrant trees, all consisting of precious incense forests. As a gentle breeze blew upon them, shaking the branches and moving the leaves, hundreds of thousands of wondrous fragrances were simultaneously diffused, and hundreds of thousands of exquisite sounds were issued forth at once.

Amidst the winding, layered cliffs, there were everywhere celestial halls, numinous chambers, and grottoes, composed of countless varieties of jewels; they were so transparent inside and out that even the radiance of the sun and moon could not manifest within them. These were all places where the sages and worthies of antiquity contemplated the Dharma as it truly is and attained the Way—where he now gathered together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas, all having come from various Buddha-lands in other directions.

These bodhisattvas are fully endowed with the power of immeasurable sovereign samādhis and supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), roaming and transforming with vigorous ease. Having thoroughly and ultimately realized the five dharmas, the self-nature, and the two kinds of non-self, they are headed by the Mahāsattva Mahāmati. All Buddhas have personally anointed their crowns, conferring upon them the rank of Buddhahood. Skillfully understanding that their own minds constitute the objective realm, they manifest universally through various gateways of liberation—according to what is appropriate for those to be saved and what is appropriate for them to see—in accordance with the diverse minds and forms of various sentient beings, and following their various thoughts and differing conceptions.

At that time, the Bhagavān was teaching the Dharma in the palace of the Naga King Sāgara. After seven days had passed, he crossed over to the southern shore. At that moment, immeasurable nayutas of Śakras, Brahmās, and various Naga Kings, along with a boundless multitude, all followed him toward the southern shore of the sea.
At that time, the Bhagavān gazed afar at Mount Malaya and the city of Laṅkā; his radiant countenance was serene and joyful like a moving mountain of gold. With a gracious smile, he spoke these words:

"The Buddhas of the past—the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas—preached within the city of Laṅkā on the summit of Mount Malaya the Dharma realized through the noble wisdom of one's own inner body, which is free from all false views and discursive thought (vitarka-vicāra), and which is not the sphere of practice for outsiders, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas.
I, too, shall preach this Dharma for Rāvaṇa, the king of the Yakṣas, and others who are preeminent, within the city of Laṅkā on Mount Malaya."
At that time, Rāvaṇa, the Yakṣa King, heard the voice of the Tathāgata through the Buddha’s supernatural power.

Then the Bhagavān, having departed from the palace of the Nāga King Sāgara and crossed the great ocean, was surrounded by and respectfully honored by many nayutas of immeasurable Śakras, Brahmās, and various nāga kings.

At that time, the Tathāgata observed the ocean waves of the *ālayavijñāna* of sentient beings, which are stirred by the fierce winds of various objective conditions, causing the waves of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to arise in accordance with their conditions.
At that time, Rāvaṇa, the King of Yakṣas, spoke this self-exhortation:

"I should invite the Tathāgata to enter the city of Laṅkā, so that for a long night I may bring great benefit and secure the swift attainment of peace and happiness for myself among gods and humans, as well as for all other gods and men."

At that time, Rāvaṇa, the Yakṣa King and Lord of Laṅkāpura, together with his retinue, mounted a flower-palace and proceeded to where the Tathāgata was. He and his followers descended from the palace and circumambulated the Buddha three times. They delighted the Tathāgata with various kinds of music; the musical instruments they held were all fashioned from great blue *indranīla* jewels, interspersed with great *vaiḍūrya*, *musāragalva*, and other precious gems, and wrapped in priceless colored cloths. With voices like those of Brahmā and in immeasurable varieties of tones, they sang praises of all the Tathāgata’s virtues and spoke these verses:
"The mind possesses the treasury of Dharma, Free from the defilement of the view of selflessness;
The World-Honored One speaks of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), The Dharma known within the inner mind."
Through pure dharmas one attains the Buddha-body, the dharma realized within one’s own body;
the transformation body manifests a transformation body, and when the time arrives, it enters Laṅkā.
In this city of Laṅkā now, immeasurable Buddhas of the past—
As well as the sons of the Buddhas, they enjoy immeasurable bodies.
When the World-Honored One preaches the Dharma,
immeasurable yakṣas are able to manifest immeasurable bodies, desiring to hear the sound of his preaching.
At that time, Rāvaṇa, King of Laṅkā, having praised the various virtues of the Tathāgata with the diverse and wondrous sounds of the duṭuka lute,
further praised the Tathāgata with the exquisite tones of gāthās, speaking these verses:
“For seven days, the Tathāgata remained Amidst the fierce beasts of the great ocean;”
Having crossed the sea to the other shore, he emerged and immediately stood there.
King Rāvaṇa, together with his wife, the yakṣas,
and his immeasurable retinue, as well as his great-wisdom ministers, [approached him].
Śukrabalaṇa and all such hosts of devas,
each manifesting immeasurable supernormal powers,
arrived together at the place where the Buddha was, riding in exquisite flower palaces.
Having arrived, he descended from the Flower Palace and paid homage and made offerings to the Buddha.
Relying on the power of the Buddha’s sustaining grace,
he then spoke his own name before the Tathāgata:
"I am a ten-headed rākṣasa.
I pray that you will deign to show compassion for me and for the sentient beings of this city;
please accept this city of Laṅkā and Mount Malaya."
The immeasurable Buddhas of the past, within this city of Laṅkā,
upon various jewel mountains, expounded the Dharma realized through their own bodies.
The Tathāgata, too, should likewise do so here upon these jewel mountains.
Just as all the Buddhas of the past have likewise taught this Dharma,
I pray that you, together with the sons of the Buddhas, shall proclaim this pure Dharma;
both I and the assembly at Laṅkā all desire to hear it.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra was praised by the Buddhas of the past;
it is the realm of internal wisdom, transcending all spoken names and designations.
I recall the infinite Tathāgatas of the past.
Surrounded by the sons of the Buddhas, he has preached this sūtra.
On this very day, the Tathāgata should likewise preach this profound Dharma for us and for all the assemblies.
The future World-Honored Ones, And the sons of the Buddhas as well,
Upon this mountain of jewels, Shall likewise preach this profound Dharma.
This present city of Laṅkā Is subtle and exquisite, surpassing the celestial palaces.
The walls are not of earth or stone, but are covered with nets of various jewels.
These yakṣas and others have, under past buddhas,
practiced and abandoned all faults, ultimately abiding in the Mahāyāna.
With a mind of virtuous reflection, in accordance with mindfulness of reality as it is;
out of compassion, may the Buddha speak for the sake of all yakṣas.
May the Buddha, Teacher of Gods and Humans, enter Mount Malaya.
The yakṣas and their wives desire to attain the Mahāyāna;
the rākṣasas such as Ghaṭakarṇa and others also dwell within this city;
they have all made offerings in the past to immeasurable billions of buddhas.
Now I further vow to make offerings to the present Great Dharma King;
desiring to hear of the practices of the inner mind, and desiring to attain the Mahāyāna.
May the Buddha take pity on me and upon this assembly of yakṣas.
Together with all the sons of the Buddhas, we enter this city of Laṅkā.
My own palaces, wives, children, and retinues;
my jeweled crowns, various necklaces, and all manner of ornaments—[all these I offer].
The Aśoka grove, with all its various delights,
and the flower palanquin upon which I rode— I offered these to the Buddha and the great assembly.
Before the Tathāgata, there was nothing that I did not relinquish.
May the Great Muni, out of compassion, accept this for our use;
may I and all the sons of the Buddha receive the Dharma taught by the Buddha.
May the Buddha, moved by pity, graciously accept it for our use and speak it for us.
At that time, the Honored One of the Three Realms, having heard the yakṣa’s request,
immediately spoke for the sake of the yakṣa concerning the Buddhas of the past and future:
"O Yakṣa, as for the Buddhas of the past, within this mountain of supreme jewels..."
Out of compassion for the yakṣas, he taught the Dharma realized within his own body.
Future Buddhas will likewise, within these jewel mountains,
teach this profound Dharma for the sake of the yakṣas and others.
Yakṣa, this precious mountain is for those who practice according to reality;
only those who practice by directly perceiving the Dharma can dwell here.
Yakṣa, I now tell you: both I and the sons of the Buddhas [dwell here].
"Out of compassion for you all, I accept your request and shall speak.
Having thus briefly answered, the Tathāgata remained in silent tranquility;
Rāvaṇa the rākṣasa then offered the Buddha his flower palace.
The Tathāgata and the sons of the Buddha, having accepted [the offerings], immediately mounted them;
Rāvaṇa the yakṣa likewise mounted his own flower-palace.
With various celestial maidens and music, they delighted the Buddha as he proceeded to that city.
Having arrived at that wondrous city, Rāvaṇa the yakṣa,
along with his yakṣa wife, yakṣa sons, and daughters,
further brought forth superior offerings, all of which were exquisite and subtle.
They made offerings to the Tathāgata and to the sons of the Buddhas;
all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas accepted those offerings.
Rāvaṇa and his hosts likewise made offerings to the Dharma-preacher.
Observing the Dharma that has been taught, [he realized] the realm personally realized within his own body.
He made offerings to the Great Sage and repeatedly requested, saying:
"Great Being, you are able to question the Buddha regarding the realm of practice within one's own body."
I, along with the hosts of yakṣas, the sons of the Buddhas,
and all who listen, together entreat you, O Benevolent One, to inquire.
The Great Being’s teaching of the Dharma is supreme, and his practice is likewise most excellent.
I revere the Great Being and inquire about the Buddha’s supreme conduct:
how one leaves behind the extremes of all non-Buddhists and also transcends the faults of the two vehicles;
how one explains the purity of the internal Dharma and reaches the ultimate stage of the Tathāgata.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, he further manifested a mountain city;
towering with hundreds of thousands of features, its magnificent adornments rivalled Mount Sumeru.
There were immeasurable billions of flower gardens, all consisting of groves of various precious gems.
The fragrance spreads far and wide, its sweet scent never heard before.
Within each and every mountain of jewels, the body of a Buddha is manifested;
there also dwell the Rāvaṇas and hosts of yakṣas.
The Buddha-lands of the ten directions, And the bodies of all Buddhas;
The sons of the Buddha and the yakṣa kings All gather upon that mountain.
As for all the multitudes within this city of Laṅkā, [They too have gathered there.]
All saw themselves entering the transformed Laṅkā;
through the miraculous power of the Tathāgata, it was likewise like that Laṅkā,
with its mountains and groves, adorned with jewels in the same way.
In each and every mountain, there was a Buddha, And all of them were questioned by one of great wisdom;
The Tathāgata explained for them all The Dharma realized within his own body.
Having uttered hundreds of thousands of wondrous sounds And finished preaching this sutra-dharma,
The Buddha and all his sons were entirely hidden and no longer appeared.
Rāvaṇa the yakṣa suddenly saw himself in his own original palace, seeing nothing else at all.
And he reflects thus:
"Who was it that saw?
Who is it that preaches the Dharma?"
Who is it that hears?
What dharma do I perceive,
such that these things occur?
Those various Buddha-lands, as well as the bodies of the Tathāgatas—
where have all these wondrous things gone now?
Are they merely memories from a dream?
Is this something created by illusion?
Is it a real city or a city of the gandharvas?
Is this a vision caused by cataracts?
Is it the rising of a mirage?
Or is it like the birth of a stone woman in a dream?
"Do you see a fire-wheel?
Or do you see the smoke of a fire-wheel?
What is it that I see?"
Again, he reflected deeply:
"The essence of all phenomena is thus; it is solely the realm of one's own mind, which can be realized and known by the inner mind."
Yet all ordinary beings, shrouded and obstructed by ignorance,
discriminate with a deluded mind and are unable to realize it.
Both the seer and the seen are entirely unapprehendable.
The speaker and that which is spoken—such things as these do not exist.
The true essence of the Buddha-dharma is neither existent nor non-existent;
the characteristics of phenomena are always thus, being merely the conceptualization of one’s own mind.
If one perceives things as real, that person does not see the Buddha;
nor can one who dwells in a discursive mind see the Buddha.
When one does not perceive the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), such a one is called a Buddha.
If one can see in this way, that person sees the Tathāgata.
When the wise contemplate all objective realms in this manner, they transform their bodies to attain the wondrous body; this is precisely the Bodhi of the Buddha.
At that time, Rāvaṇa, the ten-headed Rākṣasa king of Laṅkā, having seen the fault of the discriminating mind, did not abide within that discriminating mind.

By the power of roots of goodness from past lives, they realize all treatises as they truly are and perceive the true mark of all phenomena as it truly is. Without following the teachings of others, they skillfully contemplate and awaken to all phenomena through their own reflection; they are able to distance themselves from all false views and awaken to them, and they are well able to practice the dharmas of true practice. Within their own bodies, they can manifest all various forms and images, thereby attaining the ultimate liberation of great skillful means.

They skillfully know the superior and supreme self-nature and characteristics of all the stages; they delight in contemplating the self-nature of mind, thought, and consciousness; they perceive the severance of the continuous body within the triple world; they are free from the eternalist views of all non-Buddhists; and through wisdom, they truly and as-it-is know the Tathāgata-garbha.
Firmly abiding in the Buddha-ground with the true wisdom of the inner mind, he heard a sublime voice emerging from the midst of space and from within his own body, which spoke these words:
“Excellent, excellent!
"O King of Laṅkā!
All practitioners should cultivate and train exactly as you do.
He further spoke these words:
“Excellent, King of Laṅkā!
The dharmas and non-dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are just as you perceive them; if they were not as you perceive them, that would be called the view of nihilism.”
"O King of Laṅkā!
You should distance yourself from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and practice according to reality the true mark of all dharmas;
you should now cultivate the internal dharma and not cling to the signs of external meanings or false views."

"King of Laṅkā! You must not practice the spheres of cultivation of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or various non-Buddhists; you should not abide in any of the samādhis of other non-Buddhists; you should not delight in the various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of all non-Buddhists; you should not abide in the false views of the Vedas of all non-Buddhists; you should not be attached to the power of negligence and self-indulgence within the royal throne; and you should not be attached to the power of mastery in meditative concentration and supernormal faculties."
Lokagarbharāja!

Such matters as these are all the practices of those who practice according to reality; they can subdue all heterodox arguments of external paths, destroy all false and delusive views, overturn all errors of viewing a self, and transform all subtle movements of consciousness to cultivate the practice of the Mahāyāna.
"King of Laṅkā!

You should enter the stage of the Tathāgata within your own body and cultivate the practice of suchness. One who practices in this manner will attain the progressively higher and more purified dharmas."
O King of Laṅkā!

Do not abandon the path you have realized; cultivate well the samādhis and samāpattis. Do not become attached to the states of samādhi of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists as supreme bliss, like the ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhist practitioners who follow the ways of the hair-path (mārga); do not engage in such conceptual discrimination.

“Lokagarbharāja! Non-Buddhists are attached to the view of self; because they possess the mark of a self, they engage in false discrimination. These non-Buddhists perceive the marks of the four great elements and become attached to form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects as being substantially real. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas perceive ignorance-conditioned formations as being substantially real; they give rise to a mind of attachment and depart from true emptiness. Engaging in false discrimination, they are exclusively attached to the existence of dharmas, thereby falling into the mind that discriminates between the seer and the seen.”
O King of Laṅkā!

This supreme Dharma of the Path enables sentient beings to engage in internal contemplation and observation; it enables sentient beings to attain the supreme Mahāyāna and to give rise to the three realms of existence.
Lakṣaṇā-rāja!

This practice of entering the Mahāyāna can shatter the various cataracts and the various waves of consciousness of sentient beings, so that they do not fall into the various views and practices of the non-Buddhists.
Lokagarbharāja!

This is the practice for entering the Mahāyāna, not the practice of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Those who follow the practices of the non-Buddhists act based on the notion of a self within the internal body; because they perceive the two dharmas of consciousness and form as being real, they see them as subject to arising and ceasing.
Excellent, King of Laṅkā!
Contemplate this meaning; to contemplate it as you do is itself to see the Buddha.
At that time, Rāvaṇa, the King of Laṅkā, again had this thought:

"I should ask the Buddha about the practice of reality, which turns away from all the practices of the non-Buddhists; regarding the objective realm contemplated through internal cultivation, there must be a superior dharma beyond the responsive deeds performed by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas."

When those who practice according to reality realize the Dharma, they attain the ultimate bliss of samādhi; if one attains that bliss, they are called a practitioner of reality. Therefore, I should now question the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion.

The Tathāgata can burn away the fuel of afflictions until it is exhausted, and the sons of the Buddha likewise can burn them away; the Tathāgata knows the mental tendencies and afflictions of all sentient beings; the Tathāgata reaches everywhere to the state of omniscience; and the Tathāgata is able to know and understand, as they truly are, these characteristics and the absence of characteristics.

I should now, by means of my wondrous supernormal powers, behold the Tathāgata; having beheld the Tathāgata, that which I have not yet attained I shall attain, and that which I have already attained I shall not lose; I shall obtain the non-conceptual samādhi and samāpatti, and I shall attain the growth and fulfillment of the sphere of the Tathāgata’s practice.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing in accordance with reality that the time had come for the King of Laṅkā to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), out of compassion for the ten-headed Rākṣasa king, restored his hidden palace to its original state and manifested his body within the mountain city adorned with various jeweled nets.

At that time, the ten-headed Rākṣasa King of Laṅkā saw that all the palaces had returned to their original state. In every mountain, everywhere, he saw Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, with bodies wonderfully adorned by the thirty-two marks, dwelling within those mountains; he saw his own body appearing before all these Buddhas.

Furthermore, he saw all the Buddha-lands and various kings who, contemplating the impermanence of the body and being bound by the five desires for the sake of craving royal power, wives, children, and retinues—with no prospect of liberation—abandoned their kingdoms, palaces, consorts, elephants, horses, and treasures to give them to the Buddhas and the Saṃgha, entering mountain forests to leave the household life and study the Way.
He also saw sons of the Buddha in the mountain forests practicing with courageous diligence, casting themselves before hungry tigers, lions, and rākṣasas in their quest for the Buddha-way.
Furthermore, I saw sons of the Buddha beneath forest trees reciting and chanting the sutras and expounding them for others in their quest for the path of the Buddha;
I also saw Bodhisattvas mindful of suffering sentient beings, seated at the site of enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, contemplating the path of the Buddha;
and I saw before each Buddha a noble being, the Bodhisattva Mahamati, expounding upon the realm of internal bodily cultivation.
He also saw him surrounded by all the hosts of yakṣas as he spoke these names and phrases.

At that time, the World-Honored One observed the present assembly with his wisdom-eyes rather than his physical eyes; like a lion king casting a majestic glance, he laughed aloud with a "ha ha. From the *uṣṇīṣa* on his crown, he emitted immeasurable light, and from his shoulders, flanks, waist, thighs, chest, the *śrīvatsa* mark, and all his pores, he likewise radiated all manner of infinite light—like rainbows in the sky, like the thousand rays of the sun, or like the blazing, fierce flames of the great conflagration at the end of an eon. Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others in the void gazed upon the Tathāgata and saw the Buddha sitting upon Mount Sumeru, facing the summit of Laṅkā Mountain, laughing aloud with a "ha ha."
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and others thought to themselves:

"For what cause and for what reason has the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—who has attained mastery over all dharmas—never before laughed so loudly with 'ha-ha' laughter? Furthermore, why does he now emit immeasurable light from his own body and remain in silence, focusing his mindfulness on the realm of internal wisdom without regarding it as superior, gazing like a lion at King Laṅkā while contemplating the practice of suchness?"

At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having previously received the request of King Rāvaṇa of Laṅkā, called to mind the King of Laṅkā and understood the mental activities and dharmas of all the great Bodhisattvas. He observed that the minds of all future sentient beings would delight in teachings expressed through names and words, becoming deluded and giving rise to doubts by grasping at things exactly as they are described, and becoming attached to the practices of all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—who have transcended all activities of the mind and consciousness—laughed with a great laugh in order to sever the doubts of that great assembly.
He then asked the Buddha:
"For what cause, for what condition, and for what reason does the Tathāgata laugh so loudly?
The Buddha addressed the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati:
"Excellent! Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!"
Excellent, Mahāmati!

You are able to observe the deluded conceptualizations and false views of the world; you truly understand the matters of the three periods of time that you inquire about. Your question is just like the questions of the wise, being for the sake of benefiting both yourself and others.
"Mahāmati!

This King of Laṅkā previously inquired about these two dharmas from all the Buddhas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past; now, in the present as well, he likewise wishes to inquire of me regarding these same two dharmas."
Regarding these two dharmas, none of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths have ever known their characteristics.
Mahāmati! This ten-headed rākṣasa also inquired about these two dharmas from all future Buddhas.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing [the king's thoughts], intentionally questioned King Rāvaṇa, saying:
"O King of Laṅkā!
Whatever you wish to ask me, you may now inquire according to your doubts; I am able to answer all of them, severing your doubts and causing you to attain joy."

"O King of Laṅkā! You have severed the mind of false conceptualization and attained the skillful means of contemplation that counteracts the stages. With wisdom as it truly is, you are able to enter the samādhi of the blissful practice of the internal body’s true marks. The Buddha then takes hold of your body, causing you to dwell well within the blissful realm of śamatha; you transcend the impure defilements of the samādhis of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and are able to abide in the stages of Acalā, Sādhumatī, and Dharmameghā. Skillfully knowing the dharma of non-self as it truly is, you sit upon the throne of the Great Jewel Lotus King, attain immeasurable samādhis, and receive the office of a Buddha."
"O King of Laṅkā!

Before long, you shall see yourself likewise seated upon such a king of lotus thrones, abiding by the natural law (*dharmatā*). Surrounded by an immeasurable retinue of kings of lotuses and an immeasurable retinue of bodhisattvas, each seated upon their own king of lotus thrones, they will encircle you and gaze upon one another; before long, each shall individually attain that inconceivable state."

This refers to the practice of giving rise to the expedient means of the single practice while abiding within the various stages; therein one is able to perceive inconceivable realms and behold the immeasurable and boundless varieties of dharmic characteristics of the Tathāgata stage, which have never before been seen by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, or Brahmā.

At that time, having heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had granted him permission to ask his questions, King Laṅkā—surrounded by immeasurable celestial maidens upon the mountain adorned with various jewels and a great precious lotus of stainless, immeasurable radiance—manifested immeasurable varieties of diverse flowers, diverse fragrances, powdered incense, and ointments; he manifested jeweled banners, streamers, canopies, crowns, necklaces, and ornaments for the body;
he further manifested various exquisite and wonderful ornaments never before seen or heard of in the world;

and he further manifested immeasurable varieties of musical instruments that surpassed all the musical instruments possessed by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others.
Furthermore, they manifested all manner of articles of pleasure corresponding to the three realms—the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;

they also manifested all kinds of supreme and wondrous articles of pleasure corresponding to the buddha-lands of the ten directions. They manifested immeasurable great jewel nets that completely covered all the assemblies of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and they further erected immeasurable banners of various jewels.

After King Rāvaṇa had performed such miraculous transformations, his body rose into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees. Abiding in mid-air, he rained down various kinds of music, various flowers, various fragrances, and various garments, filling the sky like a torrential downpour as an offering to the Buddha and his sons. Having finished raining down these offerings, he descended from above and sat in mid-air upon the second great precious lotus-king, the Mountain of Various Jewels, which was as radiant as lightning.
At that time, having seen him seated, the Tathāgata smiled and granted the King of Laṅkā permission to inquire about two kinds of dharmas.
Then the King of Laṅkā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I have already asked these two kinds of dharmas of the past Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and those Blessed Ones have already explained them to me.
World-Honored One!
Now, in the present, I also ask the Tathāgata regarding these names and phrases; the Tathāgata should ultimately explain them to me."
“World-Honored One!
These two dharmas spoken by the emanated Buddha who has manifested through transformation are not the fundamental Tathāgata.
World-Honored One!”
"Regarding the realm of the bliss of samādhi cultivated by the Fundamental Tathāgata, it does not speak of external objects apart from mind and consciousness.
Excellent, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata himself has attained mastery over all dharmas; we pray that the World-Honored One, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will explain these two dharmas. All the sons of the Buddha, as well as my own self, likewise desire to hear them."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the king's thoughts], immediately addressed King Laṅkā, saying: "King Laṅkā!
You have asked about these two dharmas."
At that time, the Yakṣa King further donned various golden crowns, necklaces, and golden ornaments, and spoke these words:
“The Tathāgata has often said:
‘Even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more so non-dharmas.’”
"World-Honored One!
In what sense do you speak of 'abandoning two dharmas'?
World-Honored One!"
"What is the Dharma?
What is non-Dharma?
World-Honored One!"
Why are there two aspects to the dharma of relinquishment?
Because one falls into the midst of conceptualized marks.
Through false discrimination, one perceives existence and non-existence; where there is no greatness, one perceives greatness.
World-Honored One!

The Ālayavijñāna is known by the name "consciousness-characteristic. Its essential nature and characteristics are like the appearance of hair-tufts in the empty sky; it is the object of knowledge for those who possess the wisdom that exhausts impurity.
“World-Honored One!
If dharmas are thus, how can they be abandoned?
The Buddha told King Laṅkā:
“Lakṣaṇa-rāja!

Do you not see that jars and such things are impermanent phenomena subject to decay and destruction? Yet, foolish commoners (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) discriminate among the various characteristics of their objective realms.”
O King of Laṅkā!
Why do you not grasp it in this way?

The distinction between phenomena and non-phenomena exists only according to the conceptualizing mind of ordinary worldlings; it is not something to be seen through the realized wisdom of the noble ones.
O King of Laṅkā!

Setting aside various phenomena such as jars and the like, they are what the minds of ordinary worldlings (bāla-pṛthagjana) conceive to exist; it is not that the noble ones (ārya) consider them to be existent dharmas.
O King of Laṅkā!

For example, when a single flame burns through palaces, gardens, groves, grasses, and trees, one perceives various colors and flames of fire, each distinct from the others. Depending on the various kinds of fuel—whether grasses or trees, long or short—one discriminates and perceives signs of superiority or inferiority. Why, in this case, do you not likewise understand that there are distinctions between phenomena and non-phenomena?
O King of Laṅkā!
It is not only within a single continuous body that flames are seen to possess various distinct characteristics.
O King of Laṅkā!

Just as from a single seed, within a single continuum, there arise the various distinct characteristics of sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and forests, so too do all internal and external phenomena produced—such as ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—possess distinctions according to their production within the three realms.

There are differences in the characteristics of present pleasure, form, speech, coming and going, and superior wisdom; yet, while the objective sphere is of a single characteristic, one grasps at its marks, perceiving inferior, middling, or superior characteristics, as well as defiled, pure, wholesome, or unwholesome characteristics.
O King of Laṅkā!

It is not only within various phenomena that one perceives differentiated characteristics; even within the internal realization of those who have awakened to the path of reality as it is, there are perceptions of various distinct characteristics—how much more so for the various differentiated characteristics of the non-discriminative [distinction between] dharmas and non-dharmas?
"O King of Laṅkā!
There are various distinct characteristics of phenomena and non-phenomena.
O King of Laṅkā!"
What is meant by "dharmas"?

It refers to the views of all non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and ordinary worldlings who, based on the notion of real causal substances as their foundation, give rise to various dharmas. Such dharmas as these should be abandoned and left behind; do not grasp at their marks to produce discrimination, nor perceive the dharmas of one's own mind and reckon them as real.
O King of Laṅkā!

There is no such real dharma as a jar, yet foolish ordinary beings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*) falsely discriminate it. Dharmas are fundamentally without marks; to know and contemplate them according to reality is called "abandoning all dharmas."
“Lakṣaṇasamudgata! What is that which is not the Dharma?

It refers to the absence of any characteristic of a self-body (*ātman*), wherein one merely extinguishes the false conceptualizations and discriminations of one’s own mind. Yet, ordinary beings perceive real dharmas and unreal dharmas; the Bodhisattva perceives them as they truly are and thus abandons what is not the Dharma.”
Furthermore, Lord of Laṅkā! What, moreover, constitutes that which is not a dharma?

It refers to things such as the horns of a rabbit, a horse, a donkey, or a camel, or the son of a barren woman—entities that are without body and without characteristics. Yet, foolish worldlings grasp at them and take them to be non-existent; they employ names for worldly purposes. These are not to be grasped as characteristics like those of dharmas such as a jar, which can be relinquished. The wise do not engage in such false conceptualization; even the names of dharmas such as "rabbit horns" are to be relinquished. Therefore, one relinquishes both dharmas and non-dharmas.
"O King of Laṅkā!
You have now asked me how one abandons both dharma and non-dharma;
I have already finished explaining this."
“Lakṣaṇasamudgata! You said:

“Lokendra! What you call the past is a mark of discrimination; the discrimination of the future and the present is likewise so. Lokendra!”

I say that the true nature of *tathatā* (suchness) being "as-it-is" is itself a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Just as one might conceptually construct form as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one should practice the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*) in order to realize authentic gnosis. Therefore, do not conceptually construct the Tathāgata as a body of wisdom or an essence of wisdom; do not construct such things within the mind, and do not grasp at notions of self, person, life, and so forth within the mental faculty.
What is meant by "non-discrimination"?
Within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one perceives various objects; such as forms and appearances, do not grasp them, and do not discriminate that which is to be discriminated.
"Furthermore, Lord of Laṅkā!
Just as various forms are painted upon a wall, so too it is with all sentient beings.
Lord of Laṅkā!"
All sentient beings are like grass and trees, without karma and without conduct.
O King of Laṅkā!
All phenomena and non-phenomena are neither heard nor spoken.
Lokarāja! All worldly dharmas are like illusions, yet the heterodox and ordinary people do not know this. Lokarāja!

If one can see in this way—that is, seeing according to reality—this is called right view; if one sees otherwise, it is called wrong view; and if one makes conceptual distinctions, it is called grasping at duality.

O King of Laṅkā! It is like a reflection in a mirror seeing itself as a reflection; it is like a shadow in water seeing itself as a shadow; it is like the moon, a lamp, or a light within a room seeing its own shadow as a shadow; it is like an echo in the air producing a sound from itself and grasping it as a sound. To grasp dharmas and non-dharmas in such a manner is entirely false conceptualization and discrimination.
Therefore, by not knowing dharma and non-dharma, one increases falsehood and fails to attain quiescence.

Quiescence is called the single mind; the single mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha. Entering the realm of wisdom within one's own body, one attains the samādhi of the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

the view of the sun, moon, and constellations and the view of non-sun, moon, and constellations; the view of the truths and the view of non-truths.

The view of fruition is not the view of fruition; the view of cessation is not the view of cessation; the view of arising from the attainment of cessation is not the view of arising from the attainment of cessation;
the view of remedy is not the view of remedy; the view of marks is not the view of marks; the view of factors is not the view of factors;
the view of skillful knowledge is not the view of skillful knowledge; the view of dhyāna is not the view of dhyāna; the view of delusion is not...
Deluded views, manifest views and non-manifest views, protective views and non-protective views,
clan-based views and non-clan-based views, seer views and non-seer views, royal views and non-royal views,
seizing views and non-seizing views, real views and unreal views, predictive views and non-predictive views, and the icchantika views.
The view of non-icchantikas is not the view of icchantikas; the view of male and female is not the view of male and female;
the view of flavors is not the view of flavors; the view of action is not the view of action; the view of the body is not the view of the body; the view of awakening is not the view of awakening;
the view of movement is not the view of movement; the view of the faculties is not the view of the faculties; the view of the conditioned is not the view of the conditioned; the view of causes...
The view of effect is not the view of cause; the view of the Akaniṣṭha heaven is not the view of the Akaniṣṭha heaven;
the view of time is not the view of time; the view of groves and forests is not the view of groves and forests; the view of various things is not the view of various things;
the view of speech is not the view of speech; the view of a bhikṣu is not the view of a bhikṣu; the view of a bhikṣuṇī is not the view of a bhikṣuṇī.
The view of a nun, the view of one who maintains [the teachings], the view of one who does not maintain them, the view of letters, and the view that is not of letters— Mahāmati,
these one hundred and eight views were taught by the Buddhas of the past; you and all other bodhisattvas should train yourselves accordingly.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Three: On the Collection of All Buddha-Dharmas (2–4), Part One.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing do the various consciousnesses have?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati!"
The arising, abiding, and ceasing of the various consciousnesses cannot be known by those who lack analytical discernment.
Mahāmati, each of the various consciousnesses has two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Mahāmati! There are two kinds of cessation of the various consciousnesses:
first, the cessation of appearances; [second, the cessation of the underlying nature].
Second is the cessation of continuity. Mahāmati,
the various consciousnesses further abide in two ways:
First, abiding by way of characteristics;
second, abiding by way of continuity. Mahāmati!
The various consciousnesses have two modes of arising:
first, arising as characteristics;
second, arising through continuity.
Mahāmati! There are three kinds of consciousness.
What are these three kinds?
First, the consciousness of the evolving aspect;
second, the consciousness of the karmic aspect;
third, the consciousness of the cognitive aspect.
Mahāmati! There are eight kinds of consciousness, which, when briefly explained, consist of two types.
What are these two?
The first is the consciousness that discerns;
the second is the consciousness that discriminates phenomena. Mahāmati!
Mahāmati, just as various forms and images are seen within a clear mirror,
so too does the discerning consciousness perceive various reflected images. Mahāmati!

The *ālayavijñāna* (the consciousness that cognizes) and the *pravṛttivijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates objects)— these two types of consciousness are without distinction in their characteristics and mutually serve as causes for one another.
Mahāmati, the *ālayavijñāna* is the cause of inconceivable perfuming and transformation.
Mahāmati! The discriminating consciousness (vijñapti-vijñāna) takes objects as its cause through discrimination.
It is due to the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (prapañca) from beginningless time, Mahāmati!
When the false discrimination of the ālayavijñāna and its various habitual perfumings are extinguished, the sense faculties are also extinguished.
Mahāmati, this is called the extinction of characteristics.
Mahāmati!
As for the cessation of continuity: when the cause of continuity ceases, continuity ceases; when the cause ceases and conditions cease, continuity ceases. Mahāmati!
This refers to that which relies on phenomena and that which relies on conditions.
"Relying on phenomena" means the habitual perfuming of beginningless conceptual proliferation and false discrimination.
"Relying on conditions" means the discernment of objective realms by the consciousness of one's own mind.
Mahāmati!
For example, a lump of clay and its atoms are neither different nor not different; likewise, gold and its ornaments are neither different nor not different.
Mahāmati! If the lump of clay were different [from its constituent parts], it would not be produced by them; yet in reality it is so produced, therefore they are not different.
If they were not different, there would be no distinction between the lump of clay and its atoms.
Mahāmati! If these evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the *ālayavijñāna* were of different characteristics, they would not arise from the *ālayavijñāna*.
If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the *ālayavijñāna* should also cease; yet the *ālayavijñāna*, in its own characteristic, does not cease.

Therefore, Mahāmati, the specific characteristics of the various consciousnesses cease; when their specific characteristics cease, the karmic characteristic ceases. If their specific characteristics were to cease, the ālayavijñāna would have to cease.
Mahāmati! If the ālayavijñāna were to cease, this would not differ from the nihilistic conceptual proliferation of the non-Buddhists. Mahāmati!

Those non-Buddhists speak thus: "When the consciousness that continues through the succession of all objective spheres ceases, and once that successive consciousness has ceased, all consciousnesses are extinguished."
"Mahāmati! If the evolving consciousness were to cease, then all the various consciousnesses that have existed since beginningless time would likewise cease.
Mahāmati!"

The various non-Buddhists claim that the successive consciousnesses arise from a creator; they do not say that consciousness arises based on the conjunction of the eye, visible forms, space, and light, but rather assert the existence of a creator.
Mahāmati! What is the creator of the non-Buddhists?
The Supreme Person (Puruṣa), Īśvara, Time, atoms, and so forth are the creators.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are the seven?
First, the self-nature of accumulation;
second, the self-nature of nature;
third, the self-nature of characteristics.
Fourth, the self-nature of the great nature;
fifth, the self-nature of the causal nature;
sixth, the self-nature of the conditional nature.
Seventh is the accomplishment of the self-nature of nature.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are seven kinds of ultimate truth.
What are the seven?
First, the realm of the mind;
second, the realm of wisdom.
Third, the realm of wisdom;
fourth, the realm of the two views;
fifth, the realm that transcends the two views.
"Sixth, the sphere of transcending the stage of the Buddha’s sons;
seventh, the sphere of internal practice for entering the stage of the Tathāgata. Mahāmati!"
This, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of the ultimate truth-mind of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.

Based on this mind of the ultimate reality of the self-nature of phenomena, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas ultimately attain both worldly and world-transcending [wisdom]. With the Buddha-eye of wisdom, they establish all dharmas according to their common characteristics and specific characteristics; these establishments do not coincide with the false views of external paths.
Mahāmati!
How does one not share the same views as the heterodox?
It means that while one discriminates the false perceptions of the objects of one's own mind, one fails to realize that these are merely the perceptions of one's own mental constructs.
"Mahāmati!
All foolish ordinary people, lacking any substantial reality as the ultimate truth, propound the theories of the two views.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
Listen attentively now; I shall explain for you how false discrimination is regarded as a real entity, in order to sever the three kinds of suffering.
What are these three?
They are the cessation of the causal conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma, and the realization that the objects perceived by one's own mind are like illusions.
Mahāmati!
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak thus:
"That which was originally non-existent arises from the beginning, manifesting in dependence upon cause and effect."
Furthermore, he spoke thus:

"There truly exists a persisting entity; because it relies upon various conditions, there are the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), bases (āyatanas), arising, abiding, and ceasing, for that which arises must cease."
"Mahāmati! Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas assert that the essence of the continuum is fundamentally beginningless, yet exists as birth, cessation, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, its fruit, and the truths."
"To destroy all dharmas is the doctrine of annihilationism; this is not what I teach.
Why? Because [the fruit] shall be attained in this very life before long."
Because the fundamental basis is not perceived. Mahāmati,
it is like a broken jar that can no longer serve the function of a jar.
Mahāmati!
It is like a scorched seed that does not produce sprouts and so forth. Mahāmati!
Those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are extinguished; the past aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are extinguished, and those of the present and future are likewise extinguished.
Why is this? Because they are seen through the false conceptualization of one's own mind.
Mahāmati! This is because there is no substantial continuity of those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. Mahāmati!
If various consciousnesses arise based on three factors that were originally non-existent from the beginning, why does turtle hair not produce [anything], and why does sand not yield oil?

Your established definitive position is thus self-contradictory; your assertions regarding existence and non-existence, as well as the cause and effect established through arising, are likewise destroyed.
Mahāmati!

If, based on these three dharmas as causes and conditions, one were to produce the self-characteristics of the causes and effects of all phenomena—including the various marks and analogies of existence and non-existence across the past, present, and future—one would speak thus, relying on the stage of scriptural authority and personal realization through contemplation, and by means of one's own views熏習 (vāsanā) within the mind.
Mahāmati!
Foolish ordinary people are just like this: harmed by evil views and with minds deluded by false views, they lack wisdom yet falsely claim to speak as one who possesses all-knowledge.
“Mahāmati! Furthermore, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who perceive all dharmas as being devoid of intrinsic nature;
and because they are like clouds, fire-wheels, and *gandharva*-cities, they are neither born nor extinguished;”
Because they are like illusions, mirages, and the moon reflected in water;
because they are like dreams, appearing through the internal and external mind based on false conceptualization and discursive proliferation from beginningless time;
and because they are free from the causes and conditions of objects seen through the false conceptualization of one's own mind.
Because it is free from the conceptualization of what is spoken and the phenomena spoken about;
because it is free from the body, the requisites for life, and the dharmas of maintenance and application;
and because it is free from the appropriation of objects associated with the ālayavijñāna.
Because one enters the realm of tranquility;
because one is free from the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
and because one contemplates and observes that one's own mind is what constitutes arising.
“Mahāmati!
In this way, such a bodhisattva will before long attain a mind of equality regarding both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!”
You have skillfully employed expedient means to develop further expedients, observing that all realms of sentient beings are entirely like illusions and like reflections in a mirror;
they arise without causes or conditions and are devoid of internal objects,
for external objects are but what one's own mind perceives.
Because they successively enter the state of signlessness;
because they successively enter the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) that range from stage to stage;
and because they have faith that the three realms are the illusory manifestation of their own minds.
Mahāmati!
This is because such practitioners shall attain the illusion-like samādhi and enter the tranquil realm of their own minds.
Because they have reached the realm of the further shore;
because they are free from the dharma of an agent or arising;
and because they have attained the vajra-samādhi.
Because they enter the body of the Tathāgata;
because they enter the emanation-body of the Tathāgata;
and because they enter the body adorned with the powers, superknowledges, masteries, great loving-kindness, and great compassion.
Because it enters all buddha-lands;
because it enters what all sentient beings delight in;
and because it is free from the spheres of mind, intellect, and consciousness.
Because they attain the wondrous body through the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Mahāmati!
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice in this manner will certainly attain the unsurpassed, wondrous body of a Tathāgata.
Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva who wishes to realize the body of a Tathāgata should remain far removed from the mind that clings to the dharmas produced by the causal conditions of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas);
and should remain far removed from the false conceptualizations and frivolous discourses concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing.

All phenomena are mind-only; this should be understood as follows: because one sees that the causes of the triple world have existed since beginningless time through false discrimination and conceptual proliferation;
because one contemplates the Tathāgata-ground as quiescent and non-arising;
and because one advances toward the noble practice within one's own body.
Mahāmati! Before long, you shall attain mastery over the mind through the ultimate realization of effortless practice;
and like a mani jewel manifesting in various forms, you shall enter the subtle minds of all sentient beings.
Because it enters the stage of following the mind;
and because it causes all sentient beings to enter the stages in succession.
For this reason, Mahāmati!
"All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully understand the internal dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, expound the Dharma-gate of the correspondence between the self-natures of mind, intellect, mentation, and the five dharmas—the sphere of practice for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—so that they may remain far removed from the conjunction with the realms of false views arising from their own minds."
Because it is able to shatter all linguistic metaphors and the characteristics of substantial forms;

because it is the Dharma-mind taught by all Buddhas for the sake of the Bodhisattvas within the great ocean on Mount Malaya in the city of Laṅkā, teaching the observation of the realm of the great ocean waves of the ālayavijñāna, and teaching the Dharma as spoken by the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
“Mahāmati! There are four causes and conditions for the arising of visual consciousness.”
What are these four?
First, because one does not realize that one’s own internal body grasps at objective realms;
second, because of the attachment to the proliferation of false conceptualizations regarding the realm of form, which have been perfumed since beginningless time.
Third, because the intrinsic nature of consciousness is thus;
fourth, because of the delight in seeing various forms and appearances. Mahāmati!

These are called the four kinds of causal conditions by which great surging waves arise from the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*, capable of generating the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). Mahāmati!
Just as visual consciousness arises, so too do all evolving consciousnesses arise simultaneously through the sense organs and pores, like the various images appearing in a mirror at once.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is that which arises sequentially according to causes and conditions.
Just as the ocean of the mind is stirred by a violent wind against objects so that waves of consciousness arise—because the causal signs of phenomena are never severed; thus it is.
Because they are mutually inseparable;
because the substance of karma binds one through mutual influence;
and because one does not realize the true nature of form.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because the five groups of consciousness arise,

that which does not depart from the causes of those five consciousnesses and which is characterized by the discernment of objects is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it arises continuously together with those causes.
Mahāmati! The five consciousnesses and the mind-consciousness do not form this thought:
"We mutually serve as causes for one another."

"One's own mind perceives through false discrimination and grasps at various objects; yet these objects, each distinct yet not differing in their essential nature, all appear as the objects of discrimination.
Thus, while those consciousnesses undergo subtle arising and ceasing, the practitioner who has entered samādhi fails to perceive or know this subtle perfuming, and the practitioner thinks to himself:
'I have extinguished all consciousnesses and entered samādhi.'"
"However, the practitioner does not enter samādhi by extinguishing the various consciousnesses. Mahāmati!
It is the mind that accumulates perfumed seeds which is not extinguished; it is the various consciousnesses that grasp external objects which are extinguished."
Mahāmati!

Such subtle activity of the ālayavijñāna cannot be known by any other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of external paths, except for the Buddha-Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have entered the stages;
even those who have attained the power of samādhi cannot awaken to it, because they do not know the characteristics of the various stages.
Because they do not know how to skillfully determine the distinctions between wisdom and expedient means;
because they are unable to awaken to the way all Buddhas and Tathāgatas gather all roots of goodness;
and because they are unable to understand the conceptual proliferation regarding the distinctions within their own manifested realms.
Because they are unable to enter the cave of the ālayavijñāna, which is like a dense forest of various [phenomena]. Mahāmati!
Only those who practice according to reality—whether of inferior, middling, or superior capacity—are able to discern and see that these are false perceptions within their own minds.
Because they are able to confer the position of Tathāgata upon others in immeasurable lands;
because they have attained immeasurable sovereign powers, supernormal knowledges, and samādhis;
and because, by relying on spiritual friends and the retinue of Buddha-sons, they are able to perceive the realms of the self-nature of mind, thought, and mentation.
The great ocean of birth and death is discriminated as having karma, craving, and ignorance as its causes and conditions.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
those who practice according to reality should seek out and draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Just as the great ocean waves arise from the forceful wind,
The surging billows roll through the dark abyss without ceasing for a moment."
The ālayavijñāna is likewise: stirred by the winds of objective realms, the various waves of consciousness surge and arise in succession.
Blue, red, salt, conch, milk, flavors, and rock honey—[all appear therein].
The various flowers and fruits are like the radiance of the sun and moon;
neither different nor not different, they are like waves arising from the ocean.
The seven consciousnesses are likewise: they arise in conjunction with the mind (citta).
Just as when the ocean water moves, various waves arise;
so too is the ālayavijñāna, from which all various consciousnesses are born.
The mind (manas), the thought (citta), and the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) are taught for the sake of [distinguishing] various characteristics.
The various consciousnesses have no distinct characteristics; they are not the characteristic of the seer or the seen.
Just as the waves of the ocean are without differentiation, so it is with the consciousnesses and the mind; even their difference cannot be found.
"The mind (*citta*) can accumulate all karmas; the intellect (*manas*) can contemplate the objects thus accumulated;
consciousness (*vijñāna*) can discern what is to be known; and the five sensory consciousnesses manifest discrimination.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha in verse:
“Blue, red, and all such forms and images— Self-consciousness perceives them thus;
The dharma of the mutual relation between water and waves— Why is it explained in this way?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Blue, red, and all various colors—none of these exist within the waves;
they are taught as the transforming consciousnesses and minds, spoken of according to the characteristics of ordinary beings.
Those karmas do not exist at all, for one's own mind is free from the graspable."
The graspable and the grasper are like those waves;
The body, the means of subsistence, and the environment—sentient beings perceive these as mere consciousness.
Therefore, the manifest evolving consciousnesses are similar to the waves upon water.
When the waves of the great ocean surge and leap, they can be distinguished;
yet when the ālayavijñāna undergoes transformation, why is it not perceived?
Ordinary beings lack wisdom; the ālayavijñāna is like the ocean.
"The turning of the waves corresponds to phenomena; therefore, it is explained through analogy.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again spoke in verse:
"The rising sun shines equally upon all—upon beings of inferior, middling, and superior capacity."
"When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he speaks of reality for the sake of ordinary beings.
Since the Buddha has attained the ultimate Dharma, why does he not speak of reality?
"If one were to speak of the absolute truth, that mind would lack any reality."
Just as the waves of the ocean, The images in a mirror,
and dreams, Appear simultaneously, So too are the objects of the mind;
Yet because their conditions are not all present at once, They appear in succession.
Consciousness cognizes what is to be cognized; the mind [discerns] the "so" and the "not-so.
But as for me, through direct perception, I see that such things do not exist within meditative concentration.
It is like a skilled painter and the painter’s disciple.
Spreading out colors to depict various images, my preaching of the Dharma is likewise.
The colors originally possess no patterns; it is neither by brush nor by vessel that they are formed.
Yet, for the sake of teaching sentient beings, I have painted these various images with intricate detail.
Verbal expression is apart from reality, and reality is apart from names;
having attained the state of reality, I know it within my own body as it truly is.
Free from the characteristics of the perceiver and the perceived, I explain it according to reality for the sake of others.
This is taught for the sake of the Buddha’s heirs; the foolish discriminate otherwise.
All varieties are like illusions; they are seen, yet not real.
Such various teachings are spoken according to whether things are factual or non-factual.
It is taught for the sake of this person, yet it is not taught for that one;
just as a skilled physician prescribes medicine according to the condition of each patient,
so the Tathāgata teaches sentient beings according to their minds and capacities.
"It is not the realm of false conceptualization, nor is it the portion of the Śrāvakas;
the World-Honored Tathāgatas speak of the realm of their own self-awakening.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva wishes to know their own mind as being free from the false discrimination of the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper, they should distance themselves from clamor and the hindrance of sleep; during the first and last watches of the night, they should constantly awaken themselves and practice skillful means; they should remain free from all the conceptual proliferations of the non-Buddhists and free from the characteristics of the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and thus thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of false discrimination manifested by their own mind.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Regarding the establishment and maintenance of the characteristics of the mind through wisdom by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, they should diligently cultivate and study the three aspects of supreme noble wisdom."
Mahāmati! What are the three characteristics of supreme noble wisdom? They are: the characteristic of non-existence;
[the characteristic of being beyond words]; and the characteristic of the ultimate reality.
The characteristic of the self-vow and sustaining power of all Buddhas;
the characteristic of internal realization through the noble wisdom of one's own body.
Having practiced this, one is able to abandon the characteristic of the "lame donkey" wisdom and attain the practice of the three characteristics of the eighth stage of the Superior Sons (*jin-zu*).
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of non-existence?
It refers to observing the characteristics of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and followers of external paths.
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the self-vow by which all Buddhas maintain [the teachings]?
It refers to the fact that all Buddhas originally made a vow to maintain all dharmas.
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the internal, noble wisdom realized through self-awareness?
It is the state of non-attachment toward the characteristics of all phenomena, attaining the body of the illusion-like samādhi, and proceeding toward the stages of the Buddhas for cultivation.
Mahāmati! These are called the three characteristics of the supreme noble wisdom.
One who accomplishes these three characteristics is able to reach the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
"Therefore, Mahāmati!
Those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who seek the three characteristics of supreme noble wisdom should train themselves in this way.

At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, and sustained by the power of the Buddha-Tathāgata’s empowerment, questioned the Tathāgata regarding the essence of the Dharma-gate called the "Discrimination of the Practice of Noble Wisdom."
“World-Honored One!

We pray that you will explain for us the essence of the Dharma-gate of the discrimination of the practice of noble wisdom, which is taught through the discrimination of the one hundred and eight views. May the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, based on these one hundred and eight views, distinguish and explain for all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the differences in the practice of the essence of the discrimination of self-characteristics and common characteristics within false imagination.”

Mahāmati, because the bodhisattvas have skillfully attained this differentiation of the practice of the self-nature of dharmas through false conceptualization and discrimination, they are able to purify both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of dharmas; they are well-versed in the various stages (*bhūmi*); they transcend the bliss of the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), samādhis, and attainments (*samāpatti*) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and they attain the practice of the inconceivable realm of all Buddha-Tathāgatas.
Because they have attained the practice of the true body of the Buddhas' Dharma-body, which is free from the practice of the self-characteristics of the five dharmas;
and because they have attained the well-determined station of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which is accomplished through the realm that is like an illusion.
"Because all lands attain the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata from the Tuṣita Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha realm.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:

"There is a class of heterodox practitioners with false views who cling to emptiness and non-existence. They falsely conceptualize that the causes of knowledge are twofold—having intrinsic nature and lacking intrinsic nature—and they discriminate that things like rabbit horns do not exist. Just as rabbit horns do not exist, they claim that all dharmas likewise do not exist."
Mahāmati!

Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who perceive the four great elements as having the reality of substantial entities; they perceive each of them as having distinct characteristics and, seeing that rabbit horns do not truly exist, they falsely and delusively cling to the conceptual discrimination that cow horns truly exist.
Mahāmati!
Those various non-Buddhists fall into two views; not knowing that all is but mind-only, they increase the realm of their own minds through false conceptualization and discrimination. Mahāmati!

Just as the body, the objects of livelihood, and the vessel-world are merely the conceptual constructions of the mind, one cannot conceptually construct a rabbit’s horn apart from existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! One cannot conceptually construct any phenomena apart from existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! If there is someone who, being free from [the notions of] existence and non-existence, speaks thus:
"There is no conceptualization of a rabbit's horn."

"One cannot conceptually differentiate that there is no rabbit's horn; that person perceives it as a dependent cause, and thus cannot conceptually differentiate that there is no rabbit's horn. Why is this?"
Mahāmati!

Even when one examines subtle atoms until no substantial entity is perceived, and having departed from the sphere of the noble ones' wisdom, one cannot conceptually differentiate the existence of an ox's horns.
At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!”
“Foolish ordinary beings do not perceive the characteristics of conceptual differentiation; yet, through inferential cognition, they conceptually differentiate that those people ‘do not see.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: “Mahāmati!”
That person does not possess signs when observing the discriminating mind. Why is this?
Because it is due to false discriminative thought that there arises a discriminative thought based upon horns.
Mahāmati!

Based upon the false horn, there arises discriminative thought; therefore, by relying on the causal basis and departing from the nature of dependent relativity, one does not perceive the phenomenon [of a cow], for that [cow] has no horn.
Mahāmati! If there were further conceptualization apart from the conceptualizing mind, it would exist independently of the horns; it would not exist because of the horns.
Mahāmati!
If one does not depart from that conceptualizing mind, those phenomena—even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom—will not be seen to possess any substantial reality.
Mahāmati! Apart from the mind, those phenomena cannot exist, for the existence or non-existence of those two [subject and object] cannot be apprehended.
If that is so, Mahāmati, what dharmas do you perceive as existing,
and what dharmas do you perceive as non-existent?
If one does not view existence and non-existence in this manner, one cannot differentiate between existence and non-existence.
What is the meaning of this?
One sees the horns of a cow and sees the absence of horns on a rabbit; yet, one must not differentiate them in such a way.
Mahāmati! Because the cause is dissimilar, the meaning of existence and non-existence is not established.
This is because the meanings of existence and non-existence as asserted by the various heterodox teachers, ordinary worldlings, and śrāvakas are both unestablished.

“Mahāmati! Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who, seeing that form has a cause, falsely imagine and cling to its characteristics such as length and shortness; they see space as being without characteristics or boundaries, and they perceive all material forms as being distinct from space and possessing their own boundaries.”
Mahāmati! Space is itself form, because the great form enters into space. Mahāmati!
Form is itself emptiness, because this phenomenon exists in dependence upon that phenomenon, and that phenomenon exists in dependence upon this phenomenon;
for one distinguishes emptiness by depending on form, and one distinguishes form by depending on emptiness.
Mahāmati! The four great elements arise with their own distinct characteristics and do not abide in space; yet, Mahāmati, it is not that space is absent within the four great elements. Mahāmati!
The horn of a rabbit is also like this: because there is the horn of an ox, one says that the horn of a rabbit does not exist.
Mahāmati! Furthermore, if that ox-horn were analyzed into atoms, the characteristics of those atoms could not be perceived; what kind of phenomena would then exist?
Which specific phenomena are non-existent?
Are they said to exist or not?
If one contemplates them in this manner, it is the same for all other phenomena.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: “Mahāmati!
You should abandon such false conceptualizations as the horns of a rabbit and the horns of an ox, as well as the views that space and form are distinct.”
"Mahāmati!
You, too, should teach the various bodhisattvas the state of being free from characteristics such as those of a rabbit's horns.
Mahāmati!"
You should understand that these are the marks of false discrimination perceived by your own mind. Mahāmati!
You should, among the lands of all Buddhas, for the sake of the sons of the Buddha, explain that all these illusory objects are manifestations of what is seen within your own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Form does not exist within the mind; The mind perceives existence based on objects.
Internal consciousness is seen by sentient beings As the body, the means of livelihood, and the dwelling place."
Mind, mentation, and consciousness, The self-nature and the five dharmas;
The purity of the two kinds of selflessness— Thus has the Tathāgata taught.
Long and short, existence and non-existence, and so forth, Arise from one another in mutual succession.
Through non-existence, existence is established; through existence, non-existence is established.
By analyzing the substance of atoms, one does not give rise to the false imagination of form.
When the mind merely dwells in its place of rest, evil views cannot purify it.
"It is not the realm of false cognition, nor is it known even by the Śrāvakas;
it is that which is taught by the Tathāgata—the realm of self-realization.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, in order to purify the stream of his own mental manifestations, again requested the Tathāgata, saying these words:
“World-Honored One!
How is the stream of one’s own mental manifestations purified?
Is it purified sequentially?”
"Is it simultaneous?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Mahāmati!"
The stream of one's own mental manifestations is purified gradually and sequentially,
not all at once. Mahāmati,
it is like the fruit of the *āmra* tree, which ripens progressively and not instantaneously.
Mahāmati!
The stream of the manifestation of one's own pure mind in sentient beings is likewise thus: it becomes purified gradually, not all at once;
just as a potter fashions various vessels, achieving them through gradual stages rather than simultaneously.
Mahāmati!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of sentient beings in exactly this way: they purify them gradually, not all at once.
Mahāmati!
For example, just as the great earth gives rise to all forests, medicinal herbs, and myriad things, which grow gradually rather than being perfected all at once;
so too, Mahāmati, do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of sentient beings: they purify them gradually, not all at once.
Mahāmati!
It is like a person who studies various arts and crafts—such as music, song, dance, calligraphy, and painting—understanding them gradually rather than knowing them all at once.
Mahāmati!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, likewise purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of sentient beings in this same way: they purify them gradually, not all at once.
Mahāmati!
Just as a bright mirror, free from a discriminating mind, simultaneously manifests all forms and images;

so too is the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One: he purifies the stream of mental manifestations within the minds of sentient beings without discrimination. This purification occurs all at once rather than gradually, causing them to abide in a state of tranquility free from conceptualization.
Mahāmati!
It is like the sun and moon, whose circular forms and radiance simultaneously illuminate all visible objects, not sequentially.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise; in order to cause sentient beings to abandon the faults of the habitual tendencies of views and afflictions within their own minds, he simultaneously manifests the inconceivable wisdom of the most supreme realm.
Mahāmati!
For example, the ālayavijñāna discriminates and manifests the objective world, one's own body, means of subsistence, and the container-world all at once, rather than sequentially.
Mahāmati!

The Reward Buddha-Tathāgata is also like this: at one time, he brings all realms of sentient beings to maturity and establishes them in the ultimate celestial pure and wondrous palaces, which are places for practicing purity.
Mahāmati! It is like this:
while the Dharma-buddha and the Reward-buddha emit various radiances, the Transformation-buddha illuminates all worlds.
Mahāmati!
The inner body of noble practice, the luminous dharma-body, illuminates and eliminates the worldly false views of existence and non-existence in the same way.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the Dharma-Buddha and the Reward-Buddha speak of all dharmas by way of their specific and general characteristics.
Because of the manifestation of the signs of habitual tendencies within one's own mind;
because of the bondage of the signs of false conceptualization and discursive proliferation;
and because the phenomena as they are spoken of do not possess such an intrinsic nature.
Mahāmati!
It is like a magician who conjures all manner of various forms; foolish people grasp at them as real, yet those forms cannot be found in reality.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The essence of false dharmas arises from clinging to the existence of reality based on the dharma of causes and conditions, and is produced through discrimination.
Mahāmati!

Just as a skilled illusionist relies upon grass, wood, tiles, and stones to perform various feats, and through the power of incantations and manual skill, brings about the appearance of all kinds of sentient beings with their physical forms, features, and characteristics— these being called "illusory persons"—
