sentient beings see these various illusory forms and colors and cling to them as being real people, yet in reality, no person exists there at all.
Mahāmati!
Although sentient beings see them and take them to be persons, there is no real personhood. Mahāmati!
The nature of dependent origination is likewise subject to mental discrimination, for one perceives the various illusory manifestations of the mind. Why is this?
Because one clings to false appearances through the habitual perfuming of the discriminating mind.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the essence of false discrimination. Mahāmati!
This is called the manner in which the Reward Buddha (vipākabuddha) preaches the Dharma. Mahāmati,
as for the Dharma-Buddha preaching the Dharma, it is because he is free from the nature of mental association.
Because it is the realm of internally realized noble practice, Mahāmati,
this is called the characteristic of the Dharma-Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
“Mahāmati! It is because the emanation-buddhas (nirmāṇa-buddha) speak of giving, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
and because they explain the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), and liberation.”
Because they establish the practice of distinguishing between consciousness and perception,
I have taught the sequential characteristics of the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) of the various non-Buddhists, Mahāmati!
This is called the characteristic of the teaching of the Dharma by the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the teaching of the Dharma by the Dharmatā Buddha is because it is free from objective referents (*ālambana*).
Because they are free from the observer and the observed;
because they are free from the characteristics of the object of action and the means of cognition. Mahāmati!
Because it is not the domain of ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths;
for those external path practitioners cling to the false characteristic of a self.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
Thus, one should train in this way regarding the superior characteristics of practice through internal self-awakening within the body.
Mahāmati! You should abandon the view that the appearances of your own mind are not real.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of distinguishing characteristics of the Śrāvaka-yāna: namely, the realization of the noble marks within one’s own body;
and the attachment to the discrimination of substantial entities based on false appearances."
Mahāmati! What is the noble mark realized within one's own body by the śrāvakas?
It is the sphere of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
Because true reality is free from desire and is quiescent;
because of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas);
and because of specific and general characteristics (svalakṣaṇa and sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
Because they do not perceive the characteristic of extinction regarding the internal or external; because they see phenomena as they truly are;
and because, having attained the samādhi of the mind, they attain the non-retrogressive liberation through the meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, fruits of the path, and samāpattis.
Because they are free from the inconceivable transformation-death of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-pariṇāma-vipariṇāma-maraṇa*),
and because they have internally realized the noble practice of blissful conduct while abiding on the stage of the śrāvaka. Mahāmati!
This is called the noble mark realized within one's own body by the śrāvakas.

Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the samādhi of the blissful Dharma of the noble practices internally realized by the śrāvakas; yet, he does not grasp at the bliss of the gate of quiescent emptiness, nor does he grasp at the bliss of *samāpatti*. Because he has compassion for sentient beings, he exerts himself through the power of his original vows; therefore, although he knows [these states], he does not take them as the ultimate.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the bliss of the noble practice realized within one's own body by the śrāvakas. Mahāmati!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice the gate of the bliss of noble realization within their own bodies, yet they must not grasp at or cling to it.
Mahāmati! What is the false appearance of the Śrāvakas' conceptualization that clings to the existence of things?
That is to say: because of the characteristics of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion in the four great elements, as well as the characteristics of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth;
because there is arising despite the absence of a creator;
and because of specific and general characteristics.
Because the Āgamas, which accord with careful deliberation, have been well-expounded by the former Victors;
yet, based on those teachings, one falsely clings to them as being substantially existent. Mahāmati!
This is called the śrāvaka’s conceptual attachment to the existence of things and their adherence to false appearances.

Mahāmati! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should understand and relinquish those śrāvaka teachings; having relinquished them, he enters the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*); having entered the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena, he enters the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*). Having observed the characteristic of selflessness, he enters the successive stages (*bhūmi*) one after another.
Mahāmati!
This is called the false appearance of the Śrāvakas' conceptual attachment to the existence of things.
Mahāmati!
"What I have said regarding the two characteristics of the Śrāvaka-yāna has now been fully explained.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The Dharma spoken by the World-Honored One is eternal and inconceivable; it is the Dharma realized within one's own body as the realm of the noble ones, the Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also speak of eternal and inconceivable causes and effects.
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati!"
The various non-Buddhists assert that what is eternal and inconceivable cannot constitute cause and effect.
Why is this? Mahāmati!
The various non-Buddhists claim that the eternal is inconceivable because it does not correspond with the self-characteristics of causes.
Mahāmati, if the eternal and inconceivable as claimed by the various non-Buddhists did not correspond with the self-characteristics of causes, what kind of dharma would this be?
What dharma is it that emerges through realization?
Therefore, non-Buddhists cannot claim that [the self] is eternal and inconceivable.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Regarding the claim of non-Buddhists that [the self] is permanent and inconceivable: if it were associated with causes possessing their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it would necessarily be impermanent and inconceivable, because it would possess the characteristic of having a cause;
therefore, it cannot be established as permanent and inconceivable.
Mahāmati!

I speak of the permanence that is inconceivable and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that is inconceivable; it corresponds to the cause and effect of the characteristics of ultimate truth because it is free from existence and non-existence, and because its characteristics are realized through internal personal experience (*pratyātma-adhigama*).
Because it possesses those characteristics;
because it accords with the characteristic of the cause for the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna*), as it is free from existence and non-existence;
and because it is unconditioned, it accords with the analogies of space, nirvāṇa, and cessation.
Therefore, it is eternally inconceivable.
For this reason, Mahāmati,
when I speak of the eternal and inconceivable, it is not the same as the theories of the eternal and inconceivable held by the non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati!

This permanence is inconceivable; the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are indeed of the nature of permanence, because they have realized it through the internal body of the noble wisdom of the Buddhas, and because it is not within the realm of the mind, the intellect, or the mental consciousness.
"Mahāmati!
For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice the dharma of the noble wisdom realized within one's own body, which is eternal and inconceivable.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
The various non-Buddhist paths are eternal and inconceivable; because they are associated with the causal characteristics of impermanent phenomena, they are therefore impermanent.
However, because they do not derive their name from causal characteristics, these eternal dharmas are inconceivable.
Mahāmati!

If the various non-Buddhists claim that which is eternal and inconceivable exists, they speak of "eternity" based on the perception of existence and non-existence; they assert its eternity by means of knowledge derived from analogy regarding those phenomena.
Mahāmati!
I am also like this: by means of these very dharmas, one forms views of existence and non-existence, and that which is impermanent should be considered permanent. Why is this?
Because they lack a cause.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,

when the various non-Buddhists claim that things are permanent and inconceivable because they are associated with causal characteristics, their assertion— that the self-characteristics of a cause exist or do not exist— is equivalent to the horns of a rabbit.
Mahāmati!
This permanence and inconceivability are merely false conceptualizations of the various non-Buddhists. Why is this so?
Because the rabbit's horn does not exist and is merely a false conceptual construction;
because its own causal characteristics are absent, Mahāmati!
The eternal is inconceivable because it is realized within one's own body through the nature of causes;
because it is free from the existence or non-existence of that which is produced;
therefore, it is eternally inconceivable because it lacks external characteristics.
Because they are associated with the notion of permanence, Mahāmati!

Those non-Buddhists perceive the absence of external signs and, through inferential knowledge, conceive of that which is permanent and inconceivable as being eternal. Yet those non-Buddhists do not truly understand permanence and inconceivability, because they [mistakenly] take their own causal characteristics for the characteristics of that [true cause].
Because it is the state of realization through the noble wisdom of one's own internal body,
Mahāmati, that teaching of mine should not be explained to those outsiders.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fear the suffering of the conceptualization of birth and death and seek nirvāṇa, because they do not know that there is no distinction between the world and nirvāṇa.

They discriminate between all dharmas and non-dharmas, and by extinguishing their faculties, they do not grasp at future states; taking the false grasping of objective realms to be nirvāṇa, they do not know the dharma of practice realized within one's own body."
Because they do not understand the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*, Mahāmati!

Therefore, those deluded people speak of three vehicles of Dharma, yet they cannot know that it is only through the cessation of mental conceptions that one attains the state of cessation. Thus, those ignorant and foolish people do not understand that the realms perceived by the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present are but the manifestations of their own minds.
Because they cling to external mental objects, Mahāmati,
those deluded people constantly revolve and do not cease within the wheel of birth and death in the world.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present all teach that all phenomena are unarisen. Why is this?
This is because one perceives the existence or non-existence of phenomena within one's own mind;
for if one is free from existence and non-existence, no phenomena arise.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
All phenomena are unarisen, Mahāmati!
All phenomena are like the horns of a rabbit or the horns of a donkey or a camel.
Mahāmati! Foolish ordinary beings conceptually discriminate and differentiate all phenomena; therefore, all phenomena are unarisen. Mahāmati!
The intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena are unarisen, because they are the sphere of noble wisdom realized within one's own body;
they are not the sphere of dualistic conceptualization by ordinary beings regarding their own nature.
Mahāmati! This is because the ālayavijñāna constitutes the self-nature and characteristics of the body, the objects of enjoyment, and the receptacle world, as well as their coming and going;
and because it manifests through the transformation of the grasper and the grasped.
This is because all ordinary beings fall into the dualistic mind of arising, abiding, and ceasing,
and thus conceptualize the existence or non-existence of all phenomena. Mahāmati!
"You should understand such dharmas for this reason.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
I have taught the fivefold nature of the vehicles as the dharma of realization."
What are the five?
First, the dharma realized by those of the śrāvaka-vehicle nature;
second, the dharma realized by those of the pratyekabuddha-vehicle nature; [and so forth].
Third, the realization of the dharma of those with the nature of the Tathāgata vehicle;
fourth, the realization of the dharma of those with an indeterminate vehicle nature;
fifth, the realization of the dharma of those without a [fixed] nature.
Mahāmati! What is the realization of the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle?
It refers to the teaching of the dharmas of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).
Because he teaches the dharmas of the realization-wisdom regarding specific and general characteristics, the pores of his body are filled with serene joy;
he delights in cultivating the wisdom of characteristics rather than cultivating causal conditions, for they are not mutually exclusive characteristics.
Mahāmati! This is because it is the dharma realized by those whose nature belongs to the Śrāvaka vehicle. Those Śrāvakas have attained a false realization of wisdom;

they are free from the arising of gross afflictions, yet they are not free from the afflictions of the perfuming of ignorance. Seeing the marks of their own personal realization, they claim that from the first stage up to the fifth and sixth stages they are free from all afflictions, on the grounds that these are the same as what they themselves have abandoned.
Because they are perfumed by ignorance and afflictions,
and because they fall into the inconceivable death of transformation,
they speak as follows:
"Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
By such statements as these, one enters into the realization of the non-self of persons, even to the point of generating the thought that one has attained nirvana.
"Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are other non-Buddhists who seek to realize nirvāṇa and speak thus:
'One perceives the self, the person, the sentient being, the life-span, the agent, the experiencer, and the puruṣa.'"
They take this to be nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati, furthermore,
there are other non-Buddhists who, seeing that all phenomena exist in dependence upon causes, give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!
Those various non-Buddhists have neither nirvāṇa nor liberation, because they do not perceive the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). Mahāmati!
This is called the nature of an outsider within the Śrāvaka vehicle; it is the production of the notion of detachment regarding that which is not detached.
Mahāmati! You should transform this false view through the practice of reality.
“Mahāmati, what is the realization of the nature of the Pratyekabuddhayāna? It is when,
upon hearing the teaching on the realization of the Pratyekabuddhas, one’s body hairs stand on end and one weeps with flowing tears because of a lack of delight in worldly clamor.”
Because they contemplate all phenomena of causes and conditions;
because they do not cling to any phenomena of causes and conditions;
and because when they hear it said that their own various supernatural powers involve diverse transformations of separation and union, their minds enter into accordance with them.
"Mahāmati!
This is called the dharma realized by those of the pratyekabuddhayāna nature; you should understand it as being taught in accordance with the pratyekabuddhas. "Mahāmati!"
What is the dharma realized by those of the Tathāgata-vehicle lineage? Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of dharmas realized by those of the Tathāgata-vehicle lineage.
What are the four?
First, realizing the true nature of phenomena;
second, departing from the realization of the true nature of phenomena.
Third, the nature of the noble wisdom personally realized within one's own body;
fourth, the nature of the Dharma as realized through the supreme and wondrous adornments of external lands.
Mahāmati!

Mahāmati, if, when hearing this teaching on each and every dharma, one perceives that it is merely the inconceivable realm of the external body, its supports, and the vessel-world—all of which are manifestations of the ālayavijñāna-mind—and is neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid; then, Mahāmati, [one is a true follower].
"You should know,
Mahāmati! These are people who have realized the nature of the Tathāgata-yāna."
This is called the characteristic of the person who realizes the Dharma through the nature of the Tathāgata-vehicle.
"Mahāmati! What is the realization of the Dharma through the indeterminate vehicle-nature?"
"Mahāmati!
If a person hears this teaching of the three kinds of dharmas and finds delight in any one of them, you should teach accordingly.
Mahāmati!"

The teaching of the three vehicles is for the purpose of initiating the stages of practice; the teaching of the distinctions between the various dispositions is not the ultimate stage, as it is intended to establish the ground of ultimate quiescence that can be fully realized.
Mahāmati!
Those three types of persons attain purification by being free from the habitual tendencies of the afflictive hindrances;
they attain the practice of the bliss of samādhi by realizing the non-existence of a self in phenomena.
“Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas ultimately realize the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Practicing the untainted [path] against the stream, Those who go and return, and those who do not return;”
The Arhats worthy of offerings—such as these have their minds distracted by delusions.
I speak of the three vehicles, the one vehicle, and the non-vehicle;
the noble ones understand them according to reality, whereas ordinary worldlings cannot know them.
The gateway to the ultimate truth is far removed from dualistic teachings;
it establishes the three vehicles for those dwelling in the state of tranquility.
It comprises the various dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless samādhis.
The non-conceptual meditative absorption and the cessation absorption are likewise both absent within the mind.
"Mahāmati! What is the vehicle of no-nature?"
This refers to the icchantikas. Mahāmati!
As for the icchantikas, they lack the nature for nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because within liberation they do not give rise to faith and thus do not enter nirvana,
Mahāmati!
There are two kinds of icchantikas. What are the two?
The first is those who have incinerated all roots of goodness.
Second, out of compassion for all sentient beings, one makes the vow to exhaust the entire realm of sentient beings.
Mahāmati, what is meant by "burning away all roots of goodness"?
This refers to slandering the Bodhisattva-piṭaka by saying:
"That is not a teaching that accords with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or liberation.
By abandoning all roots of goodness, one therefore fails to attain nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!
One who, out of compassion for sentient beings, makes the vow to bring the realm of sentient beings to an end—this one is a bodhisattva.
Mahāmati!

The Bodhisattva makes a vow through skillful means: "If all sentient beings do not enter nirvana, I likewise shall not enter nirvana. For this reason, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not enter nirvana.
“Mahāmati!
These are called the two kinds of icchantikas who lack the nature for nirvāṇa. For this reason, one must definitively recognize the conduct of the icchantika.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Of these two kinds of icchantikas, which kind of icchantika never enters nirvana?
The Buddha told Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
“Icchantikas never enter nirvāṇa. Why is this?

Because they thoroughly understand that all dharmas are originally in a state of nirvāṇa; for this reason, they do not enter nirvāṇa, yet they are not icchantikas who have abandoned all roots of goodness.”
Why is this? Mahāmati!

Those icchantikas who have abandoned all roots of goodness, if they encounter Buddhas, spiritual friends, and the like, will give rise to the bodhicitta and produce various roots of goodness, thereby attaining nirvāṇa.
Why is this? Mahāmati!
It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not abandon any sentient beings.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
the bodhisattva-icchantika never enters nirvāṇa.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Fascicle II.
The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Three: The Collection of All Buddha-Dharmas, Part Two.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully understand the intrinsic characteristics of the three dharmas.
Mahāmati!"
What are the three dharmas regarding their essential characteristics?
First, the characteristic of the names of false discrimination;
second, the characteristic of the self-characteristic of the essence of dependent origination.
Third is the characteristic of the essence of the dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of names based on false discrimination?
This refers to the false conceptualization of the characteristics of all phenomena based on names; this is called the characteristic of false conceptualization of names.
Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the self-nature of the causal-conditioned body of phenomena?
Mahāmati!
As for the characteristic of the self-nature of the causal-conditioned dharma-body, it arises from objective phenomena.
Mahāmati!

Regarding the essential nature, objective sphere, and phenomenal characteristics of the law of dependent origination, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have taught that there are two kinds of distinctions in false discrimination.
What are these two kinds?
First, the false attachment to the conceptual proliferation of names;
second, the false attachment to the characteristics of names, the characteristics of perceived objects, and the characteristics of phenomena.
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of the false attachment to names, the characteristics of objects, and the characteristics of things?
They refer to the specific and general characteristics of those very internal and external phenomena.
Mahāmati! This is called the two kinds of self-characteristics of the essence of dependent origination; because one contemplates that dharma based upon that dharma as it arises, Mahāmati!
this is called the self-characteristic mark of the essence of dependent origination.
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the essence of the Dharma of the ultimate truth?

It refers to the sphere of activity and the range of practice of the noble wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas, which is free from the characteristics of names, the characteristics of objects, and the characteristics of phenomena.
"Mahāmati!
This is called the characteristic of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), the Tathāgata-garbha mind of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Name, mark, and the objects of discrimination, as well as dharmas having two aspects—these are the characteristics of conventional reality.
True Suchness and correct, wondrous wisdom—these are the characteristics of the ultimate truth. “Mahāmati!

This is called the Dharma-gate of observing the specific characteristics of the five dharmas; it is the mark of the internal realization attained through the practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which you and all other Bodhisattvas should study in this manner.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully contemplate the two characteristics of non-self.
Mahāmati!"
What are these two kinds?
First, the wisdom of the selflessness of persons;
second, the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of the selflessness of persons?
It refers to being free from the notions of "self" and "mine," because the aggregates, elements, and sense bases are merely a collection;
and because [the person] arises from ignorance, karma, and craving.
Because of false attachment to the eye, forms, and so forth;
because of seeing all sense organs, the physical world, bodies, and dwellings as manifestations of one's own mind;
and because of the conceptualization and re-conceptualization by one's own mind.
Because it discriminates and discriminates consciousness;

because it is moment-to-moment, successive, and distinct in its prior and posterior states—light, fickle, and shifting—like a river, a seed, a lamp flame, or wind and clouds; because it delights in impure objects like a monkey or a fly;
and because it is insatiable like fire.
Due to the habitual perfuming of the objects of conceptual proliferation since beginningless time,
they produce various forms and various bodies within the three realms, like a mechanical wheel or a pulley, or like a phantom rising from a corpse.

Mahāmati! Such skillful means of wisdom that contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena is called the characteristic of the realm of wisdom that well understands the selflessness of persons. Mahāmati!
What is the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena?
It is the discernment, in accordance with reality, of the characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). Mahāmati!

The Bodhisattva observes that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are devoid of self and what belongs to a self; these collections of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are bound together by the ropes of karma and craving, and because they arise through causes and conditions, they are without self and without an agent.
Mahāmati!

Because the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are devoid of both common and distinct characteristics, they are designated by names based on the discrimination of unreal characteristics. Foolish ordinary beings falsely discriminate these characteristics as being existent; however, those who have realized the truth do not see them as existent.
Mahāmati!

When a bodhisattva thus observes that mind, intellect, and consciousness are devoid of the essential characteristics of the five dharmas, and that all causal conditions are non-existent, this is called the characteristic of the realm of wisdom that well-knows the selflessness of all phenomena.
Mahāmati!

Once a bodhisattva has well understood the selflessness of all phenomena, they observe suchness and cultivate the practice of tranquility; before long, they shall attain the first stage, the Stage of Joy.
Having skillfully observed the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), these successive stages become increasingly luminous until he attains the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

Once the Bodhisattva dwells upon that Stage of the Dharma-Cloud, he sits upon a great king of lotus thrones adorned with an intermingling of immeasurable jewels; this great jewel palace is produced from the realm of reality as an illusory manifestation (*yathābhūta-māyā-viṣaya*). Surrounded by all his fellow sons of the Buddha who pay him respectful homage, the Buddhas of the ten directions extend their hands to confer empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) and bestow upon him the rank of a Buddha, just as a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) anoints the crown of his heir apparent, thereby transcending the stage of the sons of the Buddha.
Having transcended the stage of the Buddha-sons, one contemplates all Buddha-dharmas and practices them as they truly are, thereby attaining mastery over all dharmas.
Having attained such mastery, one is said to have realized the unsurpassed Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, because of seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the selflessness of dharmas as they truly are. Mahāmati!
"You and all bodhisattvas should train yourselves in this way.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Bhagavān, there are characteristics of the slander of existence and non-existence; I pray that you will explain them for me. Bhagavān!
If I and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear this, we shall be able to leave behind the false views of existence and non-existence and quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one distances oneself from the establishment of false views of annihilationism and eternalism, and is thus able to establish the true Dharma of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having again accepted the request of the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, spoke these verses:

“In the mind there is neither annihilation nor permanence; The body, the means of subsistence, and the dwelling place— It is only because of delusion regarding the mind and a lack of wisdom That one perceives existence where no object exists.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further proclaim the meaning of these verses, addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: “Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of characteristics of establishment and denial.”
What are the four? First, establishing the characteristic of non-existence;
second, establishing the characteristic of non-right view.
Third, the establishment of the characteristic of non-existent causes;
fourth, the establishment of the characteristic of non-existent substance. Mahāmati!
These are called the four kinds of establishment.
"Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of slander?"
Mahāmati!
When one examines the dharmas established by false views and fails to perceive their true nature, one slanders all dharmas by asserting that "everything is non-existent.
Mahāmati!
This is called establishing the characteristic of denial.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
what is the characteristic of establishing that which does not exist?

This refers to the conceptualization of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) as non-existent phenomena, because from beginningless time they have been mere conceptual proliferations (prapañca) lacking any reality;
yet one clings to their common and specific characteristics, asserting that these phenomena are thus and so, ultimately never different.
Mahāmati! It arises based on the attachment resulting from the habitual perfuming of afflictions throughout immeasurable lifetimes. Mahāmati!
This is called establishing the characteristic of non-existence.
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of establishing what is not right view?
Mahāmati!

Within those aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, there is no self, person, sentient being, life-span, agent, or experiencer; yet, based upon these, one establishes false views, claiming that such things as a self exist.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of establishing what is not right view. Mahāmati!
What is the establishment of the characteristic of non-existent causes?

It means that the initial consciousness does not arise from a cause; it is originally unarisen yet arises later like a magical illusion. Originally there was no causal substance, yet it exists because of the eye, visible forms, light, and attention; once arisen, it subsequently ceases.
Mahāmati! This is called the establishment of the characteristic of a non-existent cause. Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of the denial of dharmas through the establishment of non-existent entities?
It refers to the attachment to establishing [the existence of] space, cessation, and nirvāṇa as being without action and without substance. Mahāmati!
Because those three dharmas are free from existence and non-existence, Mahāmati!

All dharmas are like the horns of a rabbit, a horse, a donkey, or a camel, or like a mass of hair [seen by the visually impaired]; they are free from the characteristics established as existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! The characteristics of establishing [existence] and slandering [non-existence] arise because ordinary people engage in false discrimination;
they do not know that these are merely what is seen by the mind, and thus perceive all phenomena as being real, which is not the vision of the noble ones.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the denial of dharmas by establishing what has no real essence. Mahāmati!
"You should remain far removed from false views, for they establish the characteristics of slandering the Dharma.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas realize the mind, the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the five dharmas, and the two kinds of selflessness as they truly are, they manifest various types of forms for the sake of bringing peace and security to sentient beings. Just as those [forms] are illusory and devoid of conceptual discrimination, yet appear in various ways based upon the law of dependent origination,"

Mahāmati! It is the same for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: relying upon sentient beings, they manifest various forms like a wish-fulfilling gem, appearing within the great assemblies of all Buddha-fields in accordance with the mental inclinations of all sentient beings; for they are like illusions, dreams, echoes, the moon reflected in water, or images in a mirror;
and because they are detached from all dharmas, being neither arising nor ceasing, and neither eternal nor annihilated.
The present Buddha-Tathāgata appears because he is free from the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
upon hearing all the Buddha-dharmas, one immediately attains immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of profound samādhis.

Having attained samādhi, by the power of that samādhi, they travel from one buddha-field to another to make offerings to the Buddhas; they manifest birth within various palaces to praise the Triple Gem; they manifest as the body of a Buddha surrounded by a great assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas, causing all sentient beings to enter into the realization that objects are but the manifestations of their own minds; and they teach that external objects are neither non-existent nor existent, so that beings may distance themselves from the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Buddha-son, when seeing the world, One sees only mind and no external dharmas;
The various categories of existence are not created by the body, But are accomplished through the attainment of power and mastery.”
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the Buddha, saying:

“I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain for us the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and absence of self-nature in all dharmas. Once I and all the assembly of Bodhisattvas have understood the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and absence of self-nature in all dharmas, we shall abandon the false imaginings of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
At that time, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain this to you in detail.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati, saying: "Mahāmati!"
"Emptiness," Mahāmati, is a term for the essence of imagined phenomena.
Based on the attachment to the essence of imagined phenomena, one speaks of emptiness, non-arising, lack of essence, and non-duality.
Mahāmati! There are seven kinds of emptiness.
What are these seven?
First, the emptiness of marks;
second, the emptiness of all phenomena as being both entities and non-entities;
third, the emptiness of conditioned activity.
Fourth, the non-practice of emptiness;
fifth, the ineffable emptiness of all phenomena;
sixth, the great emptiness of the noble wisdom of the ultimate truth.
Seventh is the emptiness of this and that (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).
Mahāmati, what is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)?
It means that all dharmas are empty of both their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), being seen as mutually accumulated together. Mahāmati!

When one examines each dharma’s specific and general characteristics, not a single dharma can be apprehended. Being free from the two characteristics of self-characteristic and other-characteristic, there is no characteristic to abide in or to perceive; therefore, it is called "emptiness of specific characteristics."
Mahāmati! What is the emptiness of all phenomena regarding existence and non-existence?
It refers to the arising of dharmas that possess a real intrinsic nature and characteristics.
Mahāmati!

The self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty of both existence and non-existence; therefore, it is called the emptiness of the self-nature and characteristics of things being both existent and non-existent.
Mahāmati!
What is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)?
It refers to the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are devoid of self and what belongs to self (*ātman-ātmīya*), yet they arise based upon causes, karma, and activity. Mahāmati!
Therefore, it is called the emptiness of activity (*pracāra-śūnyatā*). Mahāmati,
what is the emptiness of non-activity (*apracāra-śūnyatā*)?
That is to say, Mahāmati, within the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), nirvāṇa has never functioned;
this is called the emptiness of non-functioning.
Mahāmati! What is the emptiness of the ineffability of all phenomena?
It refers to the fact that all phenomena, when conceptually discriminated by false imagination, are inexpressible in words.
Mahāmati! This is called the ineffable emptiness of all dharmas. Mahāmati!
What is the ultimate noble wisdom of great emptiness?
It refers to the emptiness of dharmas realized within one’s own internal noble wisdom, which is free from the faults of the habitual tendencies of all false views. Mahāmati!
This is called the great emptiness of noble ultimate wisdom.
Mahāmati, what is that which is empty of this or that (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)?

This means that regarding whichever dharma-bases there may be, if those dharmas do not exist where this dharma exists, or if this dharma does not exist where those dharmas exist, for this reason they are said to be empty, Mahāmati.

In the past, when I was a doe, I explained to others that when one says a palace is empty, it is called "empty" because there are no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep; it is called "not empty" because there are bhikṣus and so forth. Yet, the essence of the palace does not exist, and the essence of the bhikṣus likewise cannot be found. Furthermore, those elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep do not simply not exist elsewhere.
Mahāmati!

In this way, the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena are likewise unattainable, as they cannot be separated from this or that location; therefore, I speak of "this-and-that emptiness" (itaretara-śūnyatā). Mahāmati!
These are called the seven kinds of emptiness.
Mahāmati, among these,
the emptiness of one thing in relation to another is the most coarse and superficial.
“Mahāmati!
You should abandon those various forms of emptiness; there is no need to cultivate them.
Mahāmati said:
"What is it that is not born? "Mahāmati!
It is not that its own essence is not born; rather, it is called 'born' in accordance with conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), while it is said to be 'not born' because it is fundamentally unborn."
Mahāmati said:
"What is the characteristic of non-existence?
[The Buddha replied: "Mahāmati!"

When I speak of the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), I mean that the essence of all phenomena is fundamentally unarisen; therefore, I say that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, yet their continuity does not abide for even a single moment.
Mahāmati! Because one perceives various distinct characteristics,
all phenomena (dharmas) are devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics.
Mahāmati said:
"What is called the characteristic of non-duality?
[The Buddha replied: "Mahāmati!"

Regarding the characteristics of the two dharmas: they refer to the length and shortness, or the black and white, of the sun's shadow; since such dharmas as these each have their own distinct names, one cannot say they are non-dual.
Mahāmati! Just as in the world there are two aspects to all dharmas, including nirvāṇa,
so it is, Mahāmati!
What is nirvāṇa?
In that place there is no world. Where is the world?
In that state, there is no nirvāṇa, because it possesses the characteristics of a distinct cause; therefore, I say that all dharmas are non-dual.
That all dharmas are non-dual means that there is no duality between the world and nirvāṇa.
"Therefore, you should practice and study the emptiness of all phenomena, because they are non-arising, without intrinsic nature, and non-dual.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"I have always taught the Dharma of emptiness, Which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence."
Birth and death are like illusions and dreams, yet karma is never lost.
Space and nirvana—the cessation of these two—is likewise;
they arise from the conceptualization of ordinary beings, while the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: “Mahāmati!

All phenomena are empty, unarisen, without self-nature, and characterized by non-duality; they enter into the sūtras spoken by all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, for all dharma-gates expound this very meaning.”
Mahāmati!
All sūtras are differentiated and revealed in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings.
Mahāmati!
For example, just as a mirage deludes birds and beasts, who through false attachment conceive the notion of water, yet in that mirage there is actually no water.
Thus it is, Mahāmati!

The teaching of the Dharma in all sūtras is likewise: it is intended to bring joy to ordinary beings through the conceptualizations of their own minds; it is not that the true wisdom of the noble ones resides within verbal expressions.
"Mahāmati!
You should conform to the meaning and not become attached to the names, words, and phrases that have been spoken.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
World-Honored One!

As stated in the sūtras, the Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature and endowed with the thirty-two marks; it dwells within the bodies of all sentient beings, yet is enveloped by the garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, defiled by the unreal stains of greed, hatred, and delusion—like a priceless jewel wrapped in soiled clothing. Furthermore, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has declared it to be eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging.”
“World-Honored One!

If that is so, the non-Buddhists also speak of a self (*ātman*) as a divine self that is permanent and unchanging; likewise, the Tathāgata also speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha as permanent, even unto unchanging.”
“World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists also speak of a permanent creator that exists spontaneously without depending on various conditions, being omnipresent and indestructible.
If this were so, there would be no distinction between the Tathāgata and the teachings of the non-Buddhists.”
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati!
When I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha as permanent, it is not the same as the *ātman* (self) held by the non-Buddhists."
Mahāmati!

When I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha using such terms and phrases as emptiness, the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), nirvāṇa, non-arising and non-ceasing, signlessness, and wishlessness, these are designated as the Tathāgatagarbha.
Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the sake of all foolish ordinary beings who would give rise to fear upon hearing the teaching of non-self, speaks of the tathāgatagarbha;
yet this tathāgatagarbha is without discrimination, quiescent, and signless—it is called the tathāgatagarbha.
“Mahāmati!
Bodhisattvas of the future and present should not cling to the characteristic of a self.
Mahāmati!”
For example, a potter relies upon a lump of clay, fine dust, a wheel, a string, and the skillful effort of human hands and tools to produce various vessels.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is likewise: that dharma which is selfless and devoid of all marks of conceptual discrimination is described by means of wisdom and skillful means as the *tathāgatagarbha*, or as "selflessness," or as the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*) and "nirvāṇa. Through various names, phrases, and expressions, he manifests this just as that potter produces various vessels.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
I say that the Tathāgatagarbha is not the same as the "self" (ātman) asserted by the non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati!

When I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is for the sake of those non-Buddhists who are attached to a self; I employ the term "Tathāgatagarbha" in order to attract them, so that those non-Buddhists may abandon their attachment to the mind of false conceptualization regarding a personal soul (ātman), enter the three gates of liberation, and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāmati!

For this reason, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas teach the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, when I speak of the existence of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is not the same as the non-Buddhists' attachment to a self (ātman).
Therefore, Mahāmati!

In order to cause one to leave behind all the false views of the outsiders, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have made this teaching: you should practice and study the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s characteristic of non-self.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The person, the self, and the aggregates; The various conditions and the subtle atoms;
Intrinsic nature and the creation of Īśvara— These are merely the mind’s false discriminations."
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, observing all sentient beings of the future, again requested of the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound for the sake of the bodhisattvas the Dharma of practice according to reality; when those bodhisattvas hear the teaching on the Dharma of practice according to reality, they shall thereby achieve the status of practitioners who act in accordance with reality."
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Mahāmati!
There are four kinds of dharmas by which one is named a great practitioner of reality as it is (yathābhūta-pratipannaka)."
What are the four?
First, because of skillfully knowing that what is seen is the manifestation of one's own mind;
second, because of being far removed from arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Third, because they skillfully understand the existence and non-existence of external phenomena;
fourth, because they delight in cultivating the wisdom of internal realization. Mahāmati!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they achieve the status of a great practitioner of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-pratipatti*).
Mahāmati, what are they?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates that the triple world is nothing but the creation of the single mind;
that it is free from "self" and "what belongs to self";
and that it is without movement and without cognition.
Because it is free from grasping and abandoning;
because it arises from the mind of conceptual proliferation, which has been habituated by the three realms through false attachments since beginningless time;
and because it is constantly bound by various forms and activities.
Because the body, the means of subsistence, and the vessel-world appear as false within the six realms of existence, Mahāmati,
this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ skillful knowledge of the appearance of what is manifested by one’s own mind.
Mahāmati!
How do all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing as being far removed?
It is by contemplating all dharmas as being like illusions and dreams.
All phenomena do not arise because both self and other are non-existent, for they are known and perceived as mere manifestations of one's own mind;
because there are no external dharmas;
and because the various consciousnesses do not arise, as one contemplates that causes and conditions have no accumulation.
Because they see that the three realms exist due to causes and conditions;
because they do not perceive any internal or external phenomena as having substantial reality;
and because they remain far removed from the false views regarding the arising of all phenomena.
Because they enter into the illusory nature of all phenomena;

at that time, the Bodhisattva is said to have attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) of the first stage (*bhūmi*), as they are far removed from the essential characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five dharmas;

they attain the body of mind-as-wish (*yathā-icchita-manomaya-kāya*) of the two kinds of selflessness, up until the attainment of the eighth Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) and its body of mind-as-wish.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason is it called the ‘body of mind according to wish’?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Go as you wish with speed; reaching wherever you think of it without any obstruction is called the 'body of sovereign will' (kāya-vaśitā).
Mahāmati!"

As for the term "as one wishes" (yathā-icchā): even when facing stone walls, mountain barriers, or obstacles extending for immeasurable hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of *yojanas*, by recollecting the various realms previously perceived and binding them within one's own mind, one cannot be obstructed and proceeds with sovereign ease.

Mahāmati! The body of will is likewise so: having attained the sovereign spiritual power of the illusion-like samādhi, one adorns that body and advances toward all categories of noble wisdom. The body proceeds without obstruction wherever the mind desires, because it takes as its objective sphere the power of mindfulness regarding original vows, for the sake of transforming all sentient beings.
Mahāmati! This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s distancing from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Mahāmati!
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva skillfully understand the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding external phenomena?
It is because the bodhisattva perceives all phenomena as being like a mirage, like a dream, and like the optical illusion of falling hairs;
and because they have been permeated by the habitual tendencies of various conceptual proliferations, discriminations, and delusive imaginings resulting from attachments since beginningless time.
Because they see that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, and thus practice to seek realization of the realm of noble wisdom.

Mahāmati, this is called a bodhisattva who skillfully understands the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding external phenomena; such a person is one who has accomplished the great practice of reality as it is.
“Mahāmati!
You should train yourself in this manner.
At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain the characteristics of the causes and conditions of all dharmas.

May I and all the bodhisattvas thoroughly understand these characteristics so that we may be free from the false conceptualizations and discriminations of improper views such as existence and non-existence, and avoid the errors of regarding dharmas as arising either sequentially or simultaneously.”
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva: "Mahāmati!
All dharmas have two kinds of characteristics arising from causes and conditions, namely: the internal and the external."
Mahāmati!

As for the characteristics of the collection of external causal conditions, it is like this: due to the conditions of clay lumps, pillars, wheels, ropes, human effort, and skillful means, a jar is produced.
Mahāmati!

Just as a jar is produced through causes and conditions such as a lump of clay, so too are threads, cloth, grass mats, seeds, sprouts, and milk; through human effort, milk produces curd, from curd comes butter, and from butter one obtains ghee.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the accumulation of causes and conditions of external dharmas; it should be understood as proceeding from the lower to the higher. Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of the internal collection of causes and conditions?
Mahāmati, it refers to ignorance, karma, and craving; such dharmas as these are called the characteristic of the internal collection of causes and conditions.
Mahāmati!

It is because of ignorance and so forth, as well as the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, that they are termed the "characteristic of the collection of causes and conditions"; yet all ordinary beings, through false discrimination, perceive them as having distinct characteristics.
Mahāmati!
There are six kinds of causes. What are the six?
First, the causal condition;
second, the continuous causal condition;
third, the characteristic causal condition.
Fourth, the producing cause;
fifth, the revealing cause;
sixth, the relative cause.
Mahāmati! As for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), once it has acted as a cause, it is able to produce internal and external phenomena. Mahāmati!
The cause of continuity (*saṃtati-hetu*) is that which can take as its object the seeds of the internal and external aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. Mahāmati!
The cause of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-hetu*) is that which can produce the successive sequence of activities within continuity without interruption.
Mahāmati!
As for the causal agent, it acts as a sovereign cause, like a wheel-turning monarch.
Mahāmati!
The "revealing cause" (*pariniṣpattihetu*) is that which can manifest phenomena once they have arisen from conceptual construction, like a lamp illuminating forms and so forth. Mahāmati,
the "relative cause" (*apekṣāhetu*) is that which, at the time of cessation, does not perceive the arising of false dharmas, because the continuity of those phenomena has been severed.
Mahāmati!
These various dharmas are falsely discriminated by the deluded minds of ordinary people.
Mahāmati!
These dharmas do not arise sequentially, nor do they arise simultaneously.
Why is this? Mahāmati!
If all phenomena were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between cause and effect, because the distinct characteristics (*kāyalakṣaṇa*) of cause and effect would not be perceived.

If they were to arise sequentially, one could not speak of sequential arising so long as the characteristic has not yet been attained, just as one cannot speak of a "father" when a son does not yet exist.
Mahāmati! Foolish ordinary people, observing with their own minds that the successive continuity [of phenomena] is not logically consistent, speak thus:
"The causal condition, the immediate condition, the object-condition, and the dominant condition are able to produce all dharmas."
"Mahāmati! In this manner, all phenomena are sequentially non-arising.
Mahāmati!"
False conceptualization grasps the essential nature and characteristics of phenomena, yet they do not arise whether simultaneously or sequentially.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
because one perceives the body and the necessities of life within one's own mind, Mahāmati!
Because self-characteristics, common characteristics, external dharmas, and non-dharmas do not exist, they do not arise sequentially or simultaneously.
Mahāmati! It is only because the deluded consciousness gives rise to the perceptions of one's own mind that they appear.
“Mahāmati!
You should abandon the views of those who maintain that things arise from causes and conditions, or that phenomena arise either sequentially or simultaneously.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
“Because of causes and conditions, nothing is not produced; because it is not produced, it does not cease.
The causes and conditions of production and cessation are empty; there is neither production nor cessation.
To refute these various causes and conditions, the foolish grasp at them as false and delusive.”
Because there is no arising from conditions that lack objects, all phenomena do not originate.
Since within the three realms the deluded mind is permeated by habitual tendencies,
and causes and conditions are fundamentally non-existent, they neither arise nor cease.
Seeing all conditioned phenomena as the barren woman’s son or flowers in the sky, one turns away from the grasped and the grasper; thus, deluded false views do not arise.
Both manifestation and the fundamental are primordially unarisen; even conditions are fundamentally non-existent.
"All such dharmas as these are empty and non-existent in their own essence;
they have no place of abiding, yet for the sake of the world they are said to exist.
At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the World-Honored One will expound for us the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Dharmas of the Discrimination of Verbal Designations.

If I and all the Bodhisattvas can skillfully know this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Dharmas of the Discrimination of Verbal Designations, we shall be able to penetrate both the two kinds of dharmas—namely, speech and its meaning—and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
“Having attained enlightenment, [his] speech and its meaning shall enable all sentient beings to attain pure understanding.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent, Mahāmati!”
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of false conceptual speech."
What are the four? First, discourse on signs;
second, discourse on dreams; [third, discourse on dreams of the dream state; fourth, discourse on the transformation of the transformation state].
Third, the false attachment to verbal expression;
fourth, beginningless verbal expression. Mahāmati!
Discourse based on signs arises from clinging to the various signs of form and so forth. Mahāmati!
Discourse based on dreams refers to recollecting previously experienced false objects; having awakened from the dream, one realizes that it arose based on those unreal, false objects.
Mahāmati! Attachment to verbal expression arises from recollecting what was previously heard and the karma that was performed. Mahāmati!
Regarding "beginningless verbal expression," it arises from the habitual perfuming of the seeds of afflictions through attachment to conceptual proliferation since beginningless time. Mahāmati!
As for my statement that there are four kinds of false attachments to verbal expression, I have already finished explaining them.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested the Tathāgata on this matter, addressing the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
I pray that you will once more explain for me the characteristics of the four kinds of false attachment to speech. From where do the speeches of sentient beings arise?"
"How does one emerge? By what cause does one emerge?
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
“Mahāmati! Because it proceeds from the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, teeth, and jaws, sound is produced through their conjunction.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the nature of the false and illusory speech within the mouth different from [the mind], or is it not different?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Mahāmati! That which is false in speech is neither different nor not different [from the object]. Why is this?
Mahāmati! Because speech arises from those signs of false dharmas. Mahāmati!
If language were different [from its object], it would arise without a cause. Mahāmati!
If they were not different, speech would be unable to clarify the preceding object.
"Mahāmati!
It is said that speech can cognize the objects before it; therefore, it is neither different nor not different.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is speech itself the ultimate truth?
Or is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Verbal expression is not itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is this?"
Mahāmati!

In order to cause the ultimate truth (paramārtha) to conform to language so that it may enter the realm of the noble ones, there is speech that speaks of the ultimate truth; however, language itself is not the ultimate truth.

Mahāmati! The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is that which is internally realized by noble wisdom; it is not a dharma of verbal expression, for it is the domain of wisdom, and it is through verbal expression that one can understand that domain.
Mahāmati!

That which is called speech regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing that does not abide for even a single moment; it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions.
Mahāmati!
Those who rely on the conjunction of causes and conditions cannot realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Why is this? Because they lack both self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and other-characteristics (*paralakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, Mahāmati,
language cannot fully express the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
Following one's own mind, one perceives external phenomena as being devoid of any conceptual differentiation; therefore, one is unable to realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
For this reason, Mahāmati, you should abandon the various marks of false conceptualization arising from verbal expression.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All phenomena are fundamentally illusory, And possess no real intrinsic nature;
Therefore, through all words and speech, One cannot express existence or non-existence."
Emptiness and non-emptiness—these ordinary beings cannot know;
all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics, and it is said that sentient beings are likewise so.
To discriminate between existence and non-existence is like illusions, dreams, and the like.
Observing all phenomena, he does not abide in nirvana,
nor does he abide in the world, like a king or a householder.
To delight his children, he fashions various birds and beasts out of clay.
First one gives illusory things, and afterwards bestows the reality;
I teach various dharmas, such as the reflections in the mirror of the self-dharma;
to delight the sons of the Buddha, I subsequently explain the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all bodhisattvas and myself, explain that which is free from existence and non-existence, identity and difference, conjunction and disjunction, being and non-being, neither-being-nor-non-being, permanence and impermanence—that which cannot be traversed by any heterodox teachers, because it is the sphere of activity of the self-realized awakening of noble wisdom.”
Because they are free from phenomena characterized by specific and general marks;
because they enter into the ultimate reality of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
and because the stages (*bhūmi*) proceed through successive levels of purification.
Because it is the characteristic of entering the stage of the Tathāgata;
because it is the characteristic of the spontaneous practice of immeasurable realms, like a wish-fulfilling jewel, through the power of original vows;
and because it is the characteristic of perceiving the distinctions among all phenomena as manifestations of one's own mind.

May I and all bodhisattvas alike be free from such false conceptualizations of common and distinct characteristics, and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; having attained bodhi, may we provide all sentient beings with the requisites for peace and happiness, causing them all to be fully satisfied.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
“Excellent, excellent! Excellent indeed, Mahāmati!”
Out of compassion for all devas and humans, and for their great peace, happiness, and benefit, you have been able to question me on such a matter as this.
Excellent, excellent!
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Foolish ordinary beings are unable to realize that what they see is merely their own mind. They cling to the various external phenomena as being truly existent. Therefore, they falsely discriminate between identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence, based on the habitual tendencies of their own minds and relying upon this falsely discriminating mind."
Mahāmati!

It is like a herd of animals, driven by thirst, who—relying on a shimmering mirage and with their own minds deluded—conceive the notion of water and run hither and thither, unaware that it is not water.

Mahāmati! Thus, ordinary people with foolish minds perceive the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing, yet they fail to discern them correctly. Due to the habitual tendencies of false attachment and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from beginningless time, their minds are tormented and deluded by the fever of greed, hatred, and ignorance. They crave and seek after various objective realms of form; therefore, ordinary people fall into views of oneness and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, being-both and being-neither, permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Mahāmati!

It is like ordinary people who, seeing a city of the Gandharvas, conceive the notion that it is a real city; they see it because of the habitual perfuming of the seeds of the notion of a city, which have arisen from beginningless false discrimination.
Mahāmati! That city is neither a city nor not a city.
Mahāmati!

All non-Buddhists are likewise; because of the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation from beginningless time, they cling to the notions of oneness and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and being and non-being, as well as permanence and impermanence.
Mahāmati! This is because they do not realize that it is merely the false perception of their own minds. Mahāmati!

For example, suppose a person, while dreaming, sees various men and women, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; cities and villages, oxen and buffaloes, gardens and groves, trees, and various mountains, rivers, springs, streams, and bathing pools; as well as palaces and towers, all magnificently adorned, vast, grand, and extensive. Seeing himself within them, he suddenly awakens; having awakened, he still recollects that vast city.
Mahāmati! What do you think?
Would such a person be called a noble one (ārya)?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"It is the same with all foolish worldlings, non-Buddhists, and those with false views; they likewise cannot awaken to the knowledge of all phenomena because they perceive them as dreams and slumbering within their own minds.
They cling to views of oneness and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and the views of permanence and impermanence."
Mahāmati! It is like a painted image, which is neither high nor low;
yet, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people falsely perceive all phenomena as having height and depth.
Mahāmati!

In future ages, based on the mental habituation to the false views of various non-Buddhists, there will increase the false discrimination of identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Mahāmati! Those outsiders, who destroy themselves and cause others to be destroyed, speak these words:
"All dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; existence and non-existence are quiescent."
Such a person is called one of wrong view.
Mahāmati!
Those non-Buddhists slander the dharma of cause and effect; because of their false views, they uproot all roots of goodness and the pure causes of the white dharmas.
Mahāmati!

Those who seek the supreme Dharma should distance themselves from those who preach such doctrines; for their minds are attached to the dualistic views of self and other, they cling to false dharmas and fall into slander, establishing wrong views and entering the evil realms.
Mahāmati!
It is like a person with cataracts who sees the appearance of floating hairs in the empty sky and says to others:
"It is thus, it is thus—blue, yellow, red, and white; why do you not observe them?"
"Mahāmati! That mass of hairs is fundamentally without intrinsic nature. Why is this so?"
Because there is both seeing and not seeing.

Mahāmati, it is likewise with the false conceptualizations of the various non-Buddhists based on their minds of false views; they falsely cling to the notions of identity and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, non-existence and non-non-existence, permanence and impermanence, as they give rise to all phenomena.
Mahāmati!

It is like raindrops produced by the falling rain that resemble crystal beads; foolish ordinary people, through deluded perception, become attached to them, giving rise to the notion that they are beads and running hither and thither in pursuit of them.
Mahāmati! Those water bubbles are neither jewels nor non-jewels. Why is this?
Mahāmati, because there is grasping and non-grasping,

it is likewise with those externalists who, due to the habitual tendencies of false mental discrimination, assert that non-existent phenomena arise based on causes and conditions, while others further claim that existent phenomena perish.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Those various non-Buddhists establish three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism, and they speak thus:
'The reality of the Dharma realized within by the noble ones exists as something apart from the two natures, because it is [otherwise] a false discrimination.'"

"Mahāmati! Departing from mind, mentation, and consciousness, one immediately attains the body of the noble lineage (*āryagotra*). In practicing all activities, such a mind does not exist, because one is free from the false objects of the grasped and the grasper as seen by one's own mind;
because one enters the stage of the Tathāgata and personally advances toward the realization of noble wisdom."
One who practices according to reality does not give rise to a mind of existence or non-existence.
Mahāmati! This is because one who practices according to reality will necessarily attain such a realm.
Mahāmati!
If one grasps at the existence or non-existence of phenomena, that constitutes the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span.
Mahāmati!
To speak of the existence or non-existence of self-characteristics and common characteristics is called the teaching of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, not the teaching of the *dharmakāya* Buddha.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the *nirmāṇakāya* Tathāgata teaches such dharmas in accordance with the views and minds of deluded ordinary beings to lead them into practice; it is not for the purpose of establishing the practice of reality as it is, nor for demonstrating the blissful practice of the samādhi of the noble wisdom realized within oneself.
Mahāmati!
It is like a person seeing the reflection of a tree in water.
Mahāmati!
That is neither a shadow nor not a shadow.
Why? Because it exists when there is a tree, and does not exist when there is no tree.
Mahāmati!

It is likewise with those non-Buddhists who, based on a mind of false views, are perfumed by delusive conceptualization; they discriminate between identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence, all because of their delusive conceptual discrimination.
Why is this? Because they do not realize that what is seen is nothing but the manifestation of their own minds. Mahāmati!
For example, just as a bright mirror reflects all forms and images according to conditions without a discriminating mind,
so it is, Mahāmati!
That [mirror] is neither an image nor not an image.
Why is this? Because one who has conditions can see, whereas one without conditions cannot see. Mahāmati!
"O Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people perceive the existence or non-existence of images through the conceptual discriminations of their own minds.
Likewise, O Mahāmati,

all outsiders perceive the mirror-like images of their own mental constructions through the conceptual discriminations of their own minds, because they see them as being identical, different, both, or neither."
Mahāmati!
It is like an echo, which is heard through the conjunction of people, mountains, rivers, water, wind, space, and houses; that echo which is heard is neither existent nor non-existent. Why is this?
Because of the sound of the śrāvakas, Mahāmati! All non-Buddhists,

due to the habitual tendencies of false discrimination within their own minds, perceive oneness and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
Mahāmati!

It is like a great earth where there are no grasses, trees, gardens, or forests; due to the combination of sunlight and dust motes, one perceives the movement of water waves, yet those water waves neither exist nor do not exist.
Why is this? Because it causes sentient beings to experience both joy and lack of joy. Mahāmati!

All non-Buddhists and ignorant worldlings are likewise thus; due to the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation from beginningless afflictions of the mind, they discriminate regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing; identity and difference; conjunction and disjunction; existence and non-existence; neither existence nor non-existence; and permanence and impermanence. This is because, within the gateway of the sages' internal realized wisdom, these are manifested as the phenomena of a mirage and the thirst of craving.
Mahāmati!

It is like a person who, by the power of incantations, raises up a corpse or a wooden automaton that lacks any sentient essence; yet, through the power of a piśāca or the skill of a craftsman, these perform acts of coming and going. Fools and ordinary people, however, cling to them as being truly existent because of their coming and going.
Mahāmati!

It is likewise with the foolish commoners and the various non-Buddhists who fall into the mind of false views; they cling to the delusions of identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
Therefore, these commoners and non-Buddhists falsely construct such dharmas.

Therefore, Mahāmati, you should remain far removed from [the notions of] arising, abiding, and ceasing; oneness and difference; bothness and not-bothness; existence and non-existence; neither-existence-nor-non-existence;
and permanence and impermanence, because these are merely conceptual constructions of the noble wisdom realized within oneself.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The five aggregates and consciousness Are like the reflection of a tree in water;
Like what is seen in illusions and dreams— Do not rely on mental consciousness to grasp them."
All phenomena are like hair-tufts in the air, like the delusion of water in a mirage;
when one observes the three realms, everything is like an illusion or a dream.
If one can contemplate in this way, through such practice, one attains liberation.
Like a beast in summer yearning for water, the agitated mind is deluded;
though there is no reality of water there, through false conceptualization it perceives it as water.
Just so, from the seeds of consciousness, perceptions arise when stirred by objects.
The deluded grasp at these as real; those phenomena arise like a visual impairment.
Through beginningless ignorance in the world, they grasp at objects as if holding them in their embrace.
Just as one uses a wedge to extract a wedge, [the Buddha] deceives ordinary people into entering the Dharma.
Like illusions, zombies, and mechanical devices, Like dreams, lightning, and clouds—always thus;
Viewing the world in this way, One severs existence and attains liberation.
In a mirage within the empty sky, There are no cognitions that perceive.
Contemplating all phenomena in this way, one does not cling to any dharma.
All consciousnesses are merely names, for they are empty of characteristics;
seeing the aggregates as like falling hairs, what phenomenon could one differentiate?
Paintings and the optical illusions of floating hairs, Illusions, dreams, and the city of the Gandharvas;
The fire-wheel and the water of the mirage— These exist not in reality, yet are seen as existing.
Permanence and impermanence, unity, Duality, and neither: [all are likewise].
Bound by causes from beginningless time, the minds of ordinary beings are deluded.
Within mirrors, jewels, water, and the eyes, various kinds of images appear;
they falsely perceive various forms, like dreams or the son of a barren woman.
"All dharmas are without reality, like the water in a mirage that a deer craves.
