Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach the Dharma free from the four kinds of views; that is to say, they are free from the views of identity, difference, both, and neither, and they remain far removed from the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati!
All Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach the Dharma based on the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), tranquility (śānti), and liberation (vimokṣa).
Mahāmati!

All Buddhas and Tathāgatas teach the Dharma based on the ultimate realm; they do not teach the Dharma by relying on self-nature, Īśvara, causelessness, atoms, or time. They do not teach the Dharma by relying on such things.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Buddhas teach the Dharma to eliminate two kinds of hindrances: the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Just as a great caravan leader leads a multitude of people and gradually establishes them in a place of ultimate security and tranquility never before seen, so too do they gradually establish [beings] so that they may skillfully understand the distinct characteristics of the vehicles and the stages (*bhūmi*)."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four?
First, the dhyāna practiced by ignorant ordinary beings;
second, the dhyāna that contemplates meanings;
third, the dhyāna that recollects suchness.
The fourth is the dhyāna of all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati, what is the dhyāna practiced by ignorant ordinary beings?

This refers to the practitioners of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who contemplate the selflessness of persons through the characteristics of commonality and particularity, such as the skeleton;
who cling to various marks—impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and impurity—as being fixed, ultimate, and unchanging;

and who, through such a sequence, progress from these prior contemplations to higher and higher stages up to the liberation of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and the Cessation Attainment. This is called the dhyāna of ignorant ordinary people, non-Buddhists, Śrāvakas, and the like.
“Mahāmati! What is the dhyāna of examining meaning?
It refers to observing the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the non-self of persons.”
Because one perceives that the specific and general characteristics, as well as the self and other characteristics, of foolish ordinary beings and non-Buddhists lack reality;
and because one contemplates the meaning of the stages of practice regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) in their proper sequence.
"Mahāmati!
This is called the dhyāna of examining the meaning. Mahāmati!"
What is the meditation on suchness (*tathatā*)?

It refers to observing the causes and conditions of false discrimination, knowing the two kinds of selflessness as they truly are, and correctly discerning that all phenomena lack any substantial nature or characteristics; at that time, one does not abide within a mind of discrimination and attains the state of tranquility.
"Mahāmati!
This is called the dhyāna of contemplating suchness. Mahāmati!"
What is the contemplation of the Tathāgata-dhyāna?
It is because one enters the stage of the Tathāgata as it truly is;
and because one enters the characteristics of the noble internal wisdom of the body, the three kinds of emptiness, and the practice of the three kinds of bliss.
It is able to accomplish the inconceivable tasks for the sake of sentient beings.
Mahāmati! This is called the Tathāgata-dhyāna of investigative observation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Ordinary beings practice the dhyāna of common conduct; They practice the dhyāna of observing the characteristics of meaning;
They practice the dhyāna of contemplating True Suchness; And they practice the dhyāna of the ultimate purity of the Buddha.”
Like the forms of the sun and moon, The characteristics of the padma lotus and the ocean,
And the signs of the exhaustion of fire in space— The practitioner contemplates in this way.
Such various signs as these Cause one to fall into the teachings of the non-Buddhists.
They also fall into the practices of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
To abandon all of these is to be without anything at all;
at that time, throughout the lands of the ten directions, the hands of the Buddhas’ true suchness—
"Touching the crown of that practitioner's head, he enters the signless True Suchness.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When you speak of 'nirvāṇa, nirvāṇa,' what dharma is being designated by the name 'nirvāṇa'?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati!"
What is called *nirvāṇa* refers to the transformation and cessation of the essential nature and characteristics of all consciousnesses;
the transformation of the habitual tendencies of various views;
and the transformation of the habitual tendencies regarding the phenomena of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—this is termed *nirvāṇa*.
Mahāmati! This is because I and all the Buddhas teach that the nature of the realm of this dharma of nirvāṇa is emptiness.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
What is called "nirvāṇa" refers to the sphere of practice of noble wisdom within one's own body;
it is because it is free from the false discrimination of existence and non-existence. Mahāmati!
Why is it impermanent?
It is because it is free from the discrimination of specific and general characteristics of phenomena; therefore, it is impermanent, Mahāmati.
Why is it not annihilation?
Because all noble ones—past, future, and present—realize it within their own bodies; therefore, it is not annihilation. Mahāmati!
Mahāmati, parinirvāṇa is neither death nor extinction. Mahāmati,
if parinirvāṇa were a phenomenon of death, it would necessarily entail the bondage of birth.
Mahāmati! If parinirvāṇa were a phenomenon subject to extinction, it would necessarily fall into the category of conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).
Therefore, Mahāmati!
Parinirvāṇa is neither death nor extinction, for it is the refuge of those who practice according to reality.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, that which is called nirvāṇa is neither to be grasped nor to be abandoned; it is not here nor there; it is neither annihilation nor permanence; it is neither a single meaning nor manifold meanings. For these reasons, it is named nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
As for the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas, it is called the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas because they perceive all dharmas by examining their specific and general characteristics.
Mahāmati!

The nirvana of pratyekabuddhas does not delight in clamor and bustle; seeing that all objective realms are impermanent, without pleasure, without self, and without purity, they do not give rise to inverted perceptions. Therefore, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas conceive the notion of nirvana regarding what is not the ultimate state.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
I shall explain to you the essential characteristics of two dharmas. What are these two?
First, attachment to the essential characteristics of verbal expressions;
second, attachment to the essential characteristics of worldly affairs. Mahāmati!
What is the attachment to the essential nature of verbal expression?
It arises from the habitual tendencies of verbal proliferation (prapañca) attached to expressions since beginningless time. Mahāmati!
What is attachment to the essential characteristics of worldly phenomena?
It is the failure to know, as it truly is, that external objects are merely the manifestations of one's own mind.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

Because all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide through the sustaining power of two kinds of vows, they pay homage to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and inquire about matters of doubt.
Mahāmati! What are the two kinds of sustaining power of the vow?
First, the sustaining power based on samādhi and samāpatti.

Second, they attain bliss throughout their entire bodies; this refers to the power of empowerment and sustenance when the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, place their hands upon the crowns of their heads. Mahāmati!

Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas dwelling in the first stage receive the sustaining power of all the Tathāgatas, it is called "entering the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Radiance of the Great Vehicle."
Mahāmati!

Once the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have entered the Samādhi of the Radiance of the Mahāyāna, at that time the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions, through the sustaining power granted to those bodhisattvas, manifest their bodies, speech, and minds.
Mahāmati!
It is like the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Vajragarbha and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who have accomplished such marks of merit.
Mahāmati!
Thus, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by virtue of abiding in the power of samādhi and samāpatti within the first stage;
and by virtue of the power of the roots of goodness accumulated through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas;
successively and in accordance with reality, achieve the realization of the characteristics of the remedial dharmas of each stage.

When the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (Dharmameghā-bhūmi), he dwells in the palace of the Great Jewel Lotus King, seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by a retinue of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of similar rank. His body is adorned with jeweled crowns and necklaces, possessing a radiance like that of Jāmbūnada gold, Campaka flowers, the sun and moon, or the most excellent lotus color.

"At that time, all the Buddhas of the ten directions each extended their hands from afar and stroked the crowns of the heads of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas upon the lotus-king thrones, just as the Sovereign King of Attainment, Śakra, and the Wheel-Turning King perform the consecration by pouring water upon the crown of a crown prince to confer his station."
Mahāmati!

Those bodhisattvas who have received their position, along with their retinue of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, obtain joy throughout their entire bodies because the Tathāgata has rubbed the crown of their heads with his hand; therefore, it is said that the power of sustaining [them] comes from the Tathāgata’s hand rubbing the bodhisattvas’ crowns.
Mahāmati! These are called the two kinds of sustaining powers of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Mahāmati!
By relying on these two kinds of sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to observe the bodies of all Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati, if these two kinds of sustaining power did not exist, one would not be able to see the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati!
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were able to preach the Dharma apart from the two kinds of sustaining power, then foolish ordinary people should also be able to preach the Dharma.
Why is this? It is because it is not by attaining the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas. Mahāmati!

By the power of the sustaining presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Tathāgatas, mountains, rivers, stone walls, grasses, trees, gardens, groves, and various kinds of musical instruments, as well as cities, towns, villages, palaces, and dwellings, are all able to produce the sound of the Dharma being taught, and naturally emit the sounds of music.
Mahāmati!
How much more so for those with minds—beings who are deaf, blind, or mute—to be freed from all suffering and affliction.
Mahāmati!
"The sustaining power of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, brings immeasurable benefit, peace, and happiness to sentient beings.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"

World-Honored One, for what reason do the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas exercise their power of sustaining support when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into samādhi-samāpatti and enter the various stages?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is for the sake of guarding against the karmic activities of Māra and the distraction of the afflictions;
and for the sake of not falling into the meditative stages of the Śrāvakas."
It is for the sake of personally realizing the stage of the Tathāgata within one's own body;
it is for the sake of increasing the realization of the Dharma within one's own body. Mahāmati!
Therefore, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas provide the sustaining power for all bodhisattvas. Mahāmati,

if the Tathāgatas did not provide this sustaining power for the bodhisattvas, they would fall into the realms of externalists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and māras, and thus would not attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Therefore, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, out of their great compassion, embrace all bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Bodhisattvas rely upon their own bodies, Through the purity of the power of their original vows."
Entering samādhi and receiving empowerment, from the first stage to the tenth;
the Buddhas, honored among men, sustain them through their divine power.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Three.
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Three: The Collection of All Buddha-Dharmas, Part Three.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the World-Honored One has taught, the twelve links of dependent origination arise from causes producing effects; it is not said that they arise through the power of the deluded discrimination and views of one’s own mind.”
World-Honored One!
If that is so, then the non-Buddhists also say that an effect arises from a cause.
World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists claim:
"All phenomena arise from causes such as primal nature (svabhāva), the Lord (īśvara), time (kāla), or atoms (paramāṇu).
The Tathāgata also teaches that all phenomena arise in dependence upon causes and conditions, yet he does not teach the existence of any self-established phenomenon.
“World-Honored One!
The non-Buddhists also say:
‘All phenomena arise from existence and non-existence.’”

The World-Honored One has declared that all dharmas are originally non-existent; arising through causes and conditions, they perish once produced. The World-Honored One has taught that from ignorance as a condition there arise volitional formations, continuing thus up to existence, and that all dharmas arise in dependence upon eye-consciousness and the other [sense-consciousnesses].
As the World-Honored One has said, there are also dharmas that arise without causes.

Why is this? They do not arise from causes; they arise simultaneously, without priority or posteriority. For the World-Honored One himself has stated that this dharma arises from a false cause, and not through sequential production.
World-Honored One!
If that were so, the Dharma taught by the non-Buddhists would be superior while that of the Tathāgata would not be. Why is this?
“World-Honored One!

The non-Buddhists claim that causes and conditions can produce effects even when they are non-existent. Yet the Tathāgata teaches that the cause depends on the effect and the effect also depends on the cause; if this were so, then causes and conditions would be without cause and without effect.”
“World-Honored One!
If that were so, these causes and effects would follow one another endlessly.
Yet the World-Honored One has said that ‘from this dharma, that dharma arises. If that were the case, then dharmas would arise without a cause.”
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: “Mahāmati!
I shall now explain that one dharma arises from another; this is not like the cause-and-effect established by the non-Buddhists, nor is it like the doctrine of causeless dharmas arising from causes.”
I do not hold such a view.
I teach that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they do not arise without causes and conditions, nor are they disordered, and there is no fault of infinite regress.
Why is this? Because there are no dharmas of either the grasper or the graspable. Mahāmati!

Because non-Buddhists do not know that what they see is their own mind, they cling to the phenomena of the grasper and the grasped; they neither know nor realize that all internal and external phenomena are merely the manifestations of their own minds.
Mahāmati!

Because those non-Buddhists do not understand that objects within their own minds are merely appearances, they perceive the existence or non-existence of things. Therefore, such faults belong to the non-Buddhists, not to me.
"I have always said that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; they do not arise without a cause.
Mahāmati spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
"There must be dharmas corresponding to the speech that is spoken,
World-Honored One!
If there were no dharmas, one would not speak words."
“World-Honored One!
For this reason, all phenomena must exist based on verbal expression.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are also verbal expressions concerning non-existent things; that is to say, such expressions as ‘the horns of a rabbit,’ ‘the hair of a tortoise,’ or ‘the son of a barren woman’ exist as conventional discourse within the world.”
That rabbit's horn is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is spoken of in words.
Mahāmati! Your claim that because there is verbal expression, all phenomena must exist, has already been refuted.
Mahāmati!
It is not the case that all Buddha-lands employ speech to teach the Dharma. Why is this?
Because all verbal expressions are merely the conceptual distinctions of the human mind,
therefore, Mahāmati,
there are Buddha-lands where looking straight ahead without blinking and having no speech at all is called "preaching the Dharma."
In some buddha-fields, directly manifesting signs is called teaching the Dharma;
in some buddha-fields, merely moving the eyebrows is called teaching the Dharma;
in some buddha-fields, solely moving the eyes is called teaching the Dharma.
In some buddha-fields, laughter is called the teaching of the Dharma;
in some buddha-fields, yawning is called the teaching of the Dharma;
in some buddha-fields, coughing is called the teaching of the Dharma.
Mahāmati, there are buddha-fields where the Dharma is taught by means of names and thoughts;
there are buddha-fields where the Dharma is taught by means of the body. Mahāmati!

Just as in the world-systems of No-Winking and Universal Fragrance, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, observing the Tathāgata Amitābha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—with eyes that do not blink for even a moment, attain the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and also attain immeasurable, supreme samādhi dharmas.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
You must not say that because there is verbal expression, there must necessarily be dharmas. Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata also sees within all worlds all classes of sentient beings, such as tiny insects, mosquitoes, gadflies, and flies, who accomplish their own tasks without speaking words.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Like space, a rabbit’s horns, And the son of a barren woman— Though they do not exist, there are words for them; Such is false conceptualization."
"Phenomena arising from the harmony of causes and conditions are produced through the discrimination of the ignorant;
not knowing phenomena as they truly are, they wander in saṃsāra within the three realms of existence.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One speaks of the Dharma as eternal; based on what dharma do you make such a statement?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
“Mahāmati! Based on delusive phenomena, I speak of them as permanent. Why is this?
Mahāmati!
Even the noble ones perceive the delusive phenomena of the world as not being a perverted mind.
Mahāmati!

For example, like a mirage, a fire-wheel, floating hairs, a city of the Gandharvas, a magical illusion, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror—those in the world who lack wisdom perceive these various forms because of their inverted views;
those with wisdom do not give rise to conceptual discrimination, yet it is not that they fail to see those delusive phenomena.
Mahāmati! Those possessed of wisdom do not give rise to a notion of reality regarding those various delusive phenomena. Why is this?
"Because they are free from the existence and non-existence of phenomena.
The Buddha again addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati!"
How is it that deluded phenomena are free from existence and non-existence?
It refers to the way foolish ordinary beings perceive various objective realms; they are like hungry ghosts who see water in the great ocean and the Ganges, yet do not actually see it.
Mahāmati!
This delusive dharma cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist.
Mahāmati!
Because other sentient beings perceive it as water, one cannot say that it does not exist.
Mahāmati, the matter of delusion is likewise; this is because the noble ones have transcended inverted views.
Mahāmati! That which is called the permanence of delusive phenomena is due to the differentiation of conceptualization. Mahāmati!
Because the phenomena of delusion manifest various appearances, yet the phenomena of delusion do not themselves differentiate between distinct categories.
Therefore, Mahāmati, the phenomena of delusion are eternal.
Mahāmati! Why is it that delusive dharmas are called "real"?
It is because within these delusive dharmas, the noble ones do not give rise to perverted thoughts, nor do they give rise to thoughts of reality.
Mahāmati!
When the noble ones perceive those delusive dharmas, they give rise to only a slight mental conception and do not produce the objective marks of noble wisdom. Mahāmati!
One who gives rise to even a slight conceptualization is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), not a noble one (*ārya*). Mahāmati!
To discriminate between those deluded phenomena as being either inverted or non-inverted gives rise to the two natures.
What are these two kinds?
First, that which can produce the nature of an ordinary person;
second, that which can produce the nature of a noble one.
Mahāmati!
Those of the noble nature can give rise to three kinds of differentiated natures, namely: the differentiated natures of the Śrāvaka, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Buddha-land.
Mahāmati!
How is it that ordinary worldlings, through their deluded discrimination of phenomena, can give rise to the disposition for the Śrāvaka vehicle?
Mahāmati!
This refers to the attachment to the specific and general characteristics of those delusive phenomena, which can bring about the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Mahāmati! This is called the delusive phenomena that can produce and bring about the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
Mahāmati!
How is it that ignorant ordinary beings, through their discrimination of delusive phenomena, can give rise to the disposition for the Pratyekabuddha vehicle?
Mahāmati!

That which is called clinging to those delusive phenomena, observing the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, and taking no pleasure in worldly clamor, is able to give rise to the disposition for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
Mahāmati!
This is called the delusive dharma that can produce and perfect the nature of the Pratyekabuddhayāna. Mahāmati!
How is it that the wise, by discerning those delusive phenomena, are able to give rise to the nature of the Buddha-vehicle? Mahāmati,
it is because they perceive that both the seer and the seen are merely one's own mind, and thus do not discriminate between existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati!
Observing the phenomena of delusion in this manner can give rise to and perfect the nature of the Tathāgata-vehicle.
Mahāmati!
This is what is meant by the meaning of "nature" (*dhātu*). Mahāmati,

what is it that all ordinary worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*)— by means of their conceptualization of those delusive phenomena and their perception of various things— are able to produce the potential for the vehicles (*yāna-dhātu*) found within the world?
Because one observes that all phenomena are thus and thus, determined and not otherwise;
therefore, Mahāmati,
those deluded phenomena are merely the various entities of dharmas falsely discriminated by ignorant, ordinary people.
Mahāmati!
That delusive dharma is neither a real entity nor a non-real entity. Why is this?
Mahāmati!

The noble ones observe those delusive phenomena without false conceptualization; therefore, the noble ones are able to transform the bodies and characteristics of mind, intellect, and consciousness, because they have abandoned the habitual tendencies of affliction.
Therefore, the Sage transforms that deluded dharma and names it *tathatā* (suchness).
Mahāmati! What kind of dharma is this called?
Mahāmati! This is called the dharma of suchness, because it is free from the dharmas of conceptual discrimination. Mahāmati!

For this reason, I shall further proclaim that the essence of the *tathatā* (suchness) is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because within that *tathatā*, those falsely constructed phenomena do not exist.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is that delusive dharma existent or non-existent?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Mahāmati,
because they are deluded regarding phenomena and cling to various marks, they are said to 'exist'."

If those delusive phenomena existed within the midst of false conceptualization, then all noble ones would never be free from them, because they would still be clinging to the false phenomena of existence and non-existence.
"Mahāmati!
Just as the non-Buddhists speak of the twelve links of dependent origination—claiming some arise from causes while others do not arise from causes—the meaning of this [teaching] is also like that.
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One!
If delusive phenomena are seen as being like illusions, then these delusive phenomena would be distinct from delusion itself, because delusive phenomena are able to produce other phenomena.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Mahāmati!
It is not that the fault of afflictions arises from delusive dharmas."
Mahāmati!
If one does not discriminate among delusive phenomena, no faults will arise.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
All illusory phenomena arise based on human effort, incantations, and arts; they do not arise from the afflictions of one's own mental discrimination.
Therefore, Mahāmati, those delusive phenomena do not give rise to any faults; it is only because foolish people perceive these delusive phenomena that [faults appear].
“Mahāmati!
It is the ignorant and foolish ordinary beings who, by clinging to false and subtle matters, give rise to various faults; this is not said of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The Noble One does not perceive delusion, nor is there any reality in the world;
delusion itself is reality, and the dharma of reality follows from delusion.
If any signs of arising were to appear, one would have abandoned all delusions."
"That itself is delusion; impurity is like a cataract.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, you must not say that because an illusion is non-existent, all phenomena are likewise non-existent like an illusion.
Mahāmati said:
"World-Honored One,
is it because of attachment to the illusory characteristics of all phenomena that you say all phenomena are like illusions?"
It is because of attachment to the inverted characteristics of all phenomena that one says "all phenomena are like illusions.
World-Honored One,
if one were attached to the characteristic of all phenomena being like illusions, then, World-Honored One, you could not say that all phenomena are like illusions.
If one speaks of things being like an illusion because of clinging to the inverted characteristics of phenomena, then it cannot be said that all phenomena are like an illusion. Why is this,
World-Honored One?
"World-Honored One, because various causes and characteristics of form are perceived,
there is no other cause for the perception of the various characteristics of form than that they are like an illusion."
"Therefore, World-Honored One,
one must not say that clinging to all phenomena is entirely like an illusion.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not that by clinging to the various marks of phenomena one says that all phenomena are like illusions.
Mahāmati! Because all phenomena are inverted and perish as swiftly as lightning, they are said to be like illusions."
Mahāmati!
All dharmas are like flashes of lightning—seen and then immediately extinguished—but ordinary people do not perceive this.
Mahāmati!

All phenomena are likewise thus: because one discriminates the common and specific characteristics of all phenomena by means of one's own mind, and because one fails to observe them correctly, one does not see them as they truly are, due to false attachment to phenomena such as form.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"One does not perceive dharmas such as form, yet speaks of the non-existence of illusory dharmas;
therefore, there is no contradiction with what is above or below."
"I teach that all dharmas are seen to have no intrinsic nature; they are like illusions, having no essence of arising.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

As the World-Honored One has taught that all dharmas are unarisen, yet has further stated that they are like illusions, will there not be a contradiction between what the World-Honored One has said previously and what he has said later?
For the Tathāgata has taught that all dharmas are not like illusions.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"When I say that all phenomena are unborn and like an illusion, there is no fault of contradiction regarding their temporal sequence. Why is this?"

Because all ignorant, ordinary worldlings do not perceive the nature of arising phenomena or non-arising phenomena, they are unable to realize whether their own minds exist or do not exist, nor whether external phenomena exist or do not exist.
Why is this? Because they are unable to see the dharma of non-arising, Mahāmati!
In this way, my teaching of all phenomena is without contradiction from beginning to end. Mahāmati!
I refute the positions of the non-Buddhists who establish a discordant theory of cause and effect; therefore, I teach that all phenomena are unarisen.
Mahāmati!
All the ignorant multitudes of externalists speak in this way, asserting that all phenomena arise from existence and non-existence;
they do not say that they arise from the causes and conditions of one's own mind’s conceptualization and attachment.
Mahāmati!
I teach that all dharmas are neither produced as existent nor produced as non-existent.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
I teach that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished. Mahāmati,
when I say that all dharmas exist, it is to protect my disciples and cause them to understand these two aspects of reality.
What are these two?
First, because of gathering in all the worlds;
second, because of protecting against all views of annihilationism.
Why is this? Because it is by depending on karma that there are various bodies which comprise birth within the six realms; therefore, I say that there are dharmas that encompass the world.
Mahāmati!

When I say that all phenomena are like illusions, it is for the sake of enabling all foolish ordinary beings to ultimately abandon the grasping at self-characteristics and common characteristics. Because these ordinary beings, with their deluded minds, cling to them and fall into false views, failing to realize that they are merely the false perceptions of their own minds, I cause them to abandon attachment to phenomena produced by causes and conditions; therefore, I say that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, lacking any substantial reality.

Why is this? If it were not explained in this way, foolish ordinary people would cling to a mind of false views, deceiving both themselves and others, because they would be separated from the true vision of all phenomena.
Mahāmati! What is dwelling in the vision of reality as it is?
It means entering into one's own mind and perceiving all phenomena [as such].
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If, as you say, all dharmas Are entirely unarisen,
Then this is to slander cause and effect, And not to see arising as it truly is."
"I teach that there are dharmas subject to birth, which sustain all worlds;
yet seeing all dharmas as identical to an illusion, one does not grasp at the characteristics of various views.
Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:

“Mahāmati! I shall now explain to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the characteristics of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*). Because the bodhisattvas skillfully understand the characteristics of names, phrases, and syllables, they will, by relying on these characteristics of names, phrases, and syllables, swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Having attained enlightenment, they will explain the characteristics of names, phrases, and syllables for the sake of sentient beings.”
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Excellent,
World-Honored One!”
"I only pray that you will explain this quickly. "Mahāmati,
what is called 'name-body' (nāmakāya)?"
That is to say, based on whichever various dharmas a name is established, the name-body (nāmakāya) consists of different names for things that have a single meaning.
Mahāmati! This is what I call the name-body.
Mahāmati! What is the phrase-body (*padakāya*)?
It is that which determines the meaning of things and realizes the ultimate sense.
Mahāmati! This is what I call the "body of phrases. Mahāmati!
What is the body of syllables (*vyañjana-kāya*)?
It is the ultimateity of phonemes and phrases, Mahāmati.

Furthermore, regarding the "body of names" (*nāmakāya*): it is that by which one discerns names and phrases based on various phenomena, because it is able to cognize their own specific characteristics.
Mahāmati! Furthermore, regarding the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*): it refers to the ultimate completion of the meaning of a phrase.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, as for the "body of names" (nāmakāya), it refers to the various syllables distinguished by their names, from the letter *a* up to the letter *ha*; this is called the body of names.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, as for the "body of syllables" (vyañjana-kāya), it refers to the length of sounds and the high or low pitch of vocal tones; this is called the body of syllables.
Mahāmati!

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the "body of phrases" (*padakāya*), it refers to tracks left on a path, such as the footprints of humans, elephants, horses, or various other animals; these are designated as "phrases."
Furthermore, regarding "names": this refers to the four formless aggregates (skandhas) which are spoken of in reliance upon names.
Mahāmati! Furthermore, regarding the characteristic of names: this refers to the ability to discern the characteristics of names.
Mahāmati! These are called the characteristics of the body of names, phrases, and syllables. Mahāmati!
"You should study these characteristics of names, phrases, and syllables, and expound them for others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The body of names, the body of phrases, And the distinctions of the body of syllables;..."
"Ordinary people, through their deluded attachments, are like elephants mired in deep mud.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, in future ages there will be those lacking wisdom who, because they do not know the Dharma as it truly is due to their minds of false views, will claim to be wise based on worldly treatises. When those who possess wisdom question them regarding the Dharma as it truly is—concerning the characteristics of false views such as identity, difference, both, or neither—"
Yet that foolish person speaks thus:
"This question is not correct; it is not a question asked with right mindfulness, namely: 'Are phenomena such as form eternal or impermanent, and are they one or different?'"
In this way, are nirvāṇa and conditioned phenomena one or different?
Within their characteristics, are the seer and the seen one or different?
Are the agent and the action one or different?
Among the four great elements, are form, odor, taste, and touch one or are they different?
Are the seer and the seen one or are they different?
Is a lump of clay and its subtle atoms one or are they different?
Is that which is known by the wise one or many?
Regarding such successive stages of characteristics as these, the Buddha’s higher and higher *avyākṛta* (unanswered) setting-aside responses—if one speaks thus, it constitutes slandering me.
"Mahāmati! I do not teach such a doctrine for the purpose of refuting the false views of the non-Buddhists. Why is this?"
Mahāmati!

The non-Buddhists and others assert that the body is identical to the life-force, or that the body and the life-force are distinct; such teachings as these, propounded by the non-Buddhists, are indeterminate matters (*avyākṛta*).
Mahāmati!
Because non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the meaning of cause and effect, they designate things as "indeterminate" (avyākṛta); it is not within my teaching that something is called indeterminate.
Mahāmati!

In my Buddha-dharma, there is a non-conceptual mind that is free from the false imaginings of the seer and the seen; therefore, within my teaching, there is no such thing as a "set-aside" answer (*sthāpanīya*).

Various non-Buddhists cling to the grasped and the grasper, not realizing that these are merely phenomena seen by their own minds. For the sake of those people, I speak of four types of questions, among which the set-aside answer exists; however, this is not found within my own dharma.
Mahāmati!
For the sake of all sentient beings, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, have four kinds of speech known as "setting aside the answer" (sthāpanīya). Mahāmati!

I have taught such a Dharma for the sake of waiting for the proper time; it is for those whose faculties are not yet matured, and not for those whose faculties are matured. For this reason, I have spoken of the meaning of setting aside a question.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
"All dharmas, if they were to arise apart from an agent and causes, would not be produced; because there is no agent, I therefore say that all dharmas are unarisen.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All dharmas have no intrinsic nature or characteristics."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do all dharmas lack any substantial reality or characteristic?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"When one observes all dharmas through one's own wisdom, one does not perceive the individual or general characteristics of those dharmas; for this reason, I say that all dharmas lack any substantial characteristic."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All dharmas likewise have no marks to be grasped.
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason are all dharmas likewise without the characteristic of grasping?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because neither specific characteristics nor general characteristics can be apprehended, I say that no dharma can be apprehended.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All dharmas likewise possess no characteristic of relinquishment."
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One,
for what reason do all dharmas also lack the characteristic of relinquishment?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"When one observes the specific and general characteristics of phenomena, there is no phenomenon to be abandoned; therefore, I say that all dharmas likewise possess no characteristic of abandonment."
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“All dharmas are not extinguished.
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are all dharmas non-extinguished?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Because one observes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature in their specific and general characteristics, I say that all phenomena are not extinguished.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All phenomena are impermanent."
Mahāmati said:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason are all dharmas impermanent?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All dharmas are characterized by the constant non-arising of the notions of permanence and impermanence; for this reason, I say that all dharmas are impermanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
"I teach that all dharmas are impermanent.
Mahāmati said,
"World-Honored One!"
"For what reason are all dharmas impermanent?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Because their characteristics do not arise, and because their essential nature does not arise; for this reason they are both permanent and impermanent. Therefore, I say that all dharmas are impermanent."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“There are four kinds of categorical responses: Direct answers, analytical answers, Responses by counter-questioning, and setting aside the question; These are used to subdue all non-Buddhists.”
Existence and non-existence arise; the Sāṃkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas declare them both to be indeterminate, for they speak thus.
When examined with correct wisdom, intrinsic nature is not to be found.
"Therefore, it cannot be spoken of, nor can it be said to have no essence or characteristics.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

We pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the distinct characteristics of the practices of the *srotāpanna* and the others. Having thoroughly understood the characteristics of the practice of the *srotāpanna* and the rest, we and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas shall know, according to reality, the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*; and in this manner and that manner, we shall preach it for the sake of sentient beings.

Once sentient beings have heard it, they shall enter the two marks of selflessness (*nairātmya*), purify the two kinds of obstructions, and progressively advance through the superior characteristics of each stage (*bhūmi*) to attain the practice of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable realm.
Having attained the locus of practice, like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), they shall, in accordance with the thoughts of sentient beings, experience the realms of body, speech, and mind.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall now explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
“Yes, we shall listen and receive it.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: “Mahāmati!
"There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the fruit of the srotāpanna.
Mahāmati said:
"What are these three kinds?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"They are the inferior, the middling, and the superior. Mahāmati!"
What is the lower stage of a srotāpanna?
It refers to one who undergoes rebirth seven times within the three realms of existence, Mahāmati.
What constitutes the middle?
It refers to those who enter nirvana after three or five births.
Mahāmati!
What is supreme?
It is to enter nirvana in this very life. Mahāmati!
These three kinds of *srotāpanna* have three kinds of fetters, namely: inferior, middling, and superior.
Mahāmati, what are these three fetters?
That is to say: the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals.
Mahāmati, by means of these three fetters, through successive stages of superior progress, one attains the fruit of arhatship.
Mahāmati! There are two kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-existent body). What are the two?
The first is that which is co-emergent;
the second is that which arises from false discrimination, such as the discrimination of dharmas based on causes and conditions.
Mahāmati!

For example, based upon the characteristics of various causes and conditions, false conceptualization gives rise to the notion of a "real characteristic"; yet within those causes and conditions, there is neither existence nor non-existence, because the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is not the true characteristic.
Foolish ordinary beings cling to various characteristics of phenomena, just as birds and beasts see a mirage and take it to be water.
Mahāmati! This is called the srota-āpanna’s discrimination of the view of a self-body (satkāya-dṛṣṭi). Why is this so?
Because of a lack of wisdom;
because from beginningless time they have falsely grasped at signs, Mahāmati!
This stain of the view of a self-body can only be abandoned by realizing the non-self of persons.
Mahāmati! What is the innate view of a self-body belonging to a stream-enterer?

What is meant by seeing both one's own body and the bodies of others refers to those two sets of four aggregates (*skandha*). When the formless aggregate arises together with the aggregate of form, it arises through the conjunction of causes and conditions based upon the four great elements and the four sense objects. Having understood this, the *srotāpanna* is able to abandon the false views of existence and non-existence and sever the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Once the view of a self-identity has been severed, the mind of craving does not arise.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) of a srotāpanna. Mahāmati!
What are the characteristics of doubt in a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*)?

It refers to having attained the realization of the Dharma and the mark of right vision; having first severed the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the mind of discrimination regarding the two views, one consequently does not give rise to doubt concerning all phenomena, nor does one give rise to a mind that regards other venerable ones as being marks of superiority, purity, or impurity.
Mahāmati! This is called the mark of doubt in a srotāpanna.
Mahāmati!
What is the mark of grasping at precepts by a srotāpanna?
It is because they clearly perceive the mark of suffering in the places where one is born; therefore, they do not grasp at the marks of precepts. Mahāmati!

Regarding the attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): this refers to ordinary worldlings who, through the observance of precepts, diligence, and various virtuous practices, seek pleasant realms and are reborn among the gods. The *srotāpanna*, however, does not grasp at such signs; rather, he grasps at the internal realization within himself, dedicating his efforts toward progressing toward the superior state. Free from all conceptual proliferations (*vikalpa*), he cultivates the constituent of untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*).
Mahāmati! This is called the mark of the precept-and-vow attachment of a srotāpanna. Mahāmati!
“The Srotāpanna severs the afflictions of the three fetters and is free from greed, hatred,
and delusion. Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
“World-Honored One!”
“The World-Honored One has spoken of many kinds of craving; what kind of craving does a *srotāpanna* abandon?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“A *srotāpanna* remains far removed from union with women; he does not create the causes for future suffering through the seeds of present pleasure, and he remains far removed from striking, slapping, kissing, embracing, and gazing.”
Mahāmati!
A srotāpanna does not give rise to such a mind of craving. Why is this?
Because they have attained the practice of the bliss of samādhi, Mahāmati!
the srotāpanna is free from such cravings as these, but not free from craving for nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin?

It refers to one who, upon seeing forms for the first time, gives rise to a mind that is not based on false conceptualization or views, because they have skillfully practiced the characteristics of dhyāna. Having come once more to this world, they sever suffering and enter nirvāṇa; this is called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of an Anāgāmin?

It means that regarding the marks of form (rūpa) in the past, present, and future, one gives rise to a mind free from existence and non-existence; because the latent tendencies (anuśaya) and the mind of false discrimination have been seen through, the various fetters (saṃyojana) do not arise, and since one does not return [to the desire realm], one is called an Anāgāmin.
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of an arhat?

It is called an arhat because one does not give rise to the conceptualizing thought that discriminates between the object of thought and the act of thinking, nor between samādhi, liberation, powers, superknowledges, afflictions, suffering, and so forth; for this reason, one is named an arhat.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One, you have spoken of three kinds of arhats; which of these is designated by the name ‘arhat’?”
Does the World-Honored One speak of an Arhat who has attained definitive nirvana?
Or an Arhat who has made the vow for Bodhicitta but whose roots of goodness have been forgotten?
Or an Arhat who is a manifestation created for the sake of transformation?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I speak of those śrāvakas and arhats who have attained definitive nirvāṇa, not of other arhats,
Mahāmati."

As for the "other arhats," this refers to those who were formerly practitioners of the bodhisattva path; furthermore, there are arhats emanated by the Buddha of Response and Transformation. By the power of their original vows, roots of goodness, and skillful means, they manifest within the great assemblies of various buddha-fields to adorn the great congregations of the Buddhas.
Mahāmati!

One discriminates various matters by speaking of going and coming; because one is far removed from the realization of the fruit, from the thinker, the object of thought, and the act of thinking, one speaks of the attainment of the fruit's characteristics based on seeing that which is seen as being one’s own mind.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
if a srotāpanna were to give rise to such a thought as, "These are the three fetters;
I am one who has abandoned the three fetters," [he would be a false claimant].
Mahāmati!
This is called seeing the three dharmas and falling into the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); if one is thus, one does not escape the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*). Mahāmati!
Therefore, a stream-enterer does not give rise to such thoughts.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,

if one wishes to be far removed from the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), one should distance oneself from the appearances seen by one's own mind and distance oneself from minor signs, because of the characteristics of the samādhi of tranquil extinction (*śamatha-nirodha-samāpatti*).
"Mahāmati! If it were not thus, those bodhisattvas would perceive all phenomena with their minds; [it is] because [all is] mind-only.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The various dhyānas and the four immeasurables, The formless attainments and samādhis;
The signless, the cessation, and the concentrations— None of these exist within their minds.
They practice the outflow-free path against the stream, And have attained the stage of once-returning.”
Those who go and return, and those who do not return, as well as Arhats, have their minds lost in delusion.
That which is contemplated, that which can be contemplated, and the one who contemplates—by remaining far removed from these, one perceives the True Reality;
it is only by means of this illusory mind that one can know and attain liberation.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are two kinds of knowledge.
What are these two?
The first is the wisdom of observation;
the second is the wisdom that dwells upon the grasping of signs through false discrimination. Mahāmati!
What is the wisdom of observation?

It refers to that wisdom which observes the essential characteristics of all phenomena and, being free from the four [extreme] positions, finds no phenomenon to be apprehended; this is called the wisdom of observation.
Mahāmati! What are the four dharmas? They are:
identity, difference, both, and neither; these are called the four dharmas.
Mahāmati! Apart from these four dharmas, no phenomena whatsoever can be apprehended. Mahāmati!
If one wishes to examine all phenomena, one should observe all dharmas by relying on four principles. Mahāmati!

Those who dwell in wisdom by means of false conceptualization and grasping at signs are those who, because they falsely discriminate the characteristics of the four great elements—namely, solidity, heat, moisture, and motion—become attached to them; they establish their views based on the characteristics of causes and analogies, taking what is not a real dharma to be real.
Mahāmati! This is called the wisdom that dwells upon and sustains the grasping of signs through false conceptualization. Mahāmati!
This is called the characteristic of the two kinds of knowledge. Mahāmati!

All Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas ultimately understand these two characteristics and advance toward the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). They skillfully know the characteristics of the stages of practice of true knowledge; having known them, they immediately attain the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and obtain one hundred samādhis. By the power of these samādhis, they see one hundred Buddhas and one hundred Bodhisattvas, can know the events of one hundred eons each in the past and future, and illuminate one hundred Buddha-worlds.

Having illuminated the realms of a hundred buddhas, he thoroughly understands the characteristics of the progressively superior wisdoms of the various stages. By the power of his original vows, he is able to manifest various supernatural powers with great agility. Within the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), he receives his consecration according to the rain of Dharma, realizing the stage of the Tathāgata’s internal ultimate wisdom-body (*dharmakāya*). Relying on ten immeasurable roots of goodness and vows, he manifests various transformations to teach and convert sentient beings; he displays various radiances from his own body because he has attained the bliss of samādhi through the wisdom realized by his own practice.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should skillfully understand the characteristics of the four great elements and the four sense objects.
Mahāmati!"
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the characteristics of the four great elements and the four objects? Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice in this way: that which is called "reality" refers to the absence of the four great elements, observing that the four great elements are fundamentally unarisen from the very beginning.
Having observed in this way, he further reflects:

"That which is called 'observation' is merely the mind's own perception of false cognition. Because one sees that external objects have no substantial reality, they are seen only by the discriminating mind as mere names. That which is called the triple world is devoid of the four great elements and the characteristics of the four sensory objects."
Having seen this, one abandons the four kinds of views; seeing the pure dharma, one is free from "I" and "mine," and abides within the dharmas of suchness according to their own characteristics.
Mahāmati!
"Abiding in the reality of the specific characteristics of phenomena" means abiding in the establishment of the specific characteristic of the non-arising of all phenomena.
Mahāmati, how can there be four objects within the four great elements?
Mahāmati!
That is to say, through the softening and moistening of conceptual discrimination, the water-element arises internally and externally.
Mahāmati!
The power of the growth of the warmth of false conceptualization gives rise to the internal and external fire element.
Mahāmati! The characteristic of lightness, movement, and vibration of false conceptualization gives rise to the internal and external wind element.
Mahāmati! From all the characteristics of solidity produced by false conceptualization and discrimination, the internal and external earth element arises, Mahāmati!

Through false conceptualization and discrimination, one gives rise to notions of "internal," "external," and "both" in relation to space; because of clinging to these false internal and external wrong views, the clusters of the five aggregates, the four great elements, and the four sense objects arise.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Consciousness is able to cling to various objects and seek after heterodox paths because it grasps those objects.
Mahāmati!”
The four great elements are fourfold, namely: form, fragrance, flavor, and tangibility.
Mahāmati, the four great elements have no cause.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature and form of earth—its length and shortness—do not give rise to the characteristics of the four great elements. Mahāmati!
All phenomena arise based on forms, sizes, positions, and appearances, for there are no phenomena that exist apart from forms, sizes, lengths, and shortness.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
The non-Buddhists falsely discriminate among the four great elements and the four sense-objects; such discrimination does not exist within my Dharma.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall explain to you the essential nature and characteristics of the five aggregates.
Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of the five aggregates?
They are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati! The four aggregates are without the characteristic of form; they are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Mahāmati!
Form arises dependent upon the four great elements, yet these four great elements possess mutually distinct characteristics. Mahāmati!
Since formless phenomena are identical to space, how could they possibly establish the numerical characteristics of four?
Mahāmati!
It is like space, which is free from numerical characteristics, yet is falsely discriminated as "this is space. Mahāmati!
The numerical characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) are detached from all marks; they are detached from the marks of existence and non-existence, and detached from the four marks.
It is the ignorant worldlings who speak of these numerical characteristics, not the noble ones (*ārya*).
Mahāmati!

I teach that all marks are like illusions; their various forms are free from the dependence on one or two [causes], being spoken of by way of conventional designations, just as dreams and reflected images do not exist apart from their bases.
Mahāmati! Just as the wisdom of the noble ones, through cultivation and discernment, perceives the five aggregates as false. Mahāmati!
This is called the five aggregates having no essence or characteristic of the five aggregates. Mahāmati!

You should now abandon such characteristics of false discrimination. Having abandoned them, you should teach for the sake of all bodhisattvas the dharma of tranquility that is free from the characteristics of all phenomena, in order to block the characteristics of the various views of the outsiders.
Mahāmati!

By teaching the Dharma of tranquility, one attains the realization of the pure characteristic of non-self and enters the Far-Reaching Ground (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*). Having entered the Far-Reaching Ground, because one has attained mastery over immeasurable samādhis and the body born of sovereign will, because one has attained the samādhi of the illusory nature of all phenomena, and because one progresses through the cultivation of sovereign supernormal powers, one functions with mastery for the sake of all sentient beings, like the great earth.
Mahāmati! It is like the great earth, which all sentient beings use according to their own inclinations. Mahāmati!
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s adaptation to the needs of sentient beings is likewise so.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
non-Buddhists speak of four kinds of nirvāṇa.
What are the four?
First, nirvāṇa as the essential nature;
second, nirvāṇa regarding the existence or non-existence of various characteristics.
Third, the nirvāṇa that is the realization of the existence or non-existence of one’s own body;
fourth, the nirvāṇa that is the cessation of the continuity of the individual and general characteristics of the aggregates. Mahāmati!
These are called the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists; they are not what I teach.
Mahāmati, that which I teach is the cessation of the discriminating consciousness that perceives false objects; this is called nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
has the World-Honored One not spoken of eight kinds of consciousness?”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I speak of eight kinds of consciousness.
Mahāmati said:
“If the Blessed One speaks of eight kinds of consciousness, why do you say only that the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) ceases, and not that the seven consciousnesses cease?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Because they exist in dependence upon that *manas* (the thinking mind), when the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cease, the seven consciousnesses also cease.”

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises through attachment and grasping at objects. Once arisen, it increases the *ālayavijñāna* through various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Because it functions together with the mental consciousness, it is free from the marks of "I" and "mine," yet it clings to false emptiness and gives rise to discrimination.

Mahāmati! Those two kinds of consciousness have no distinct characteristics; because they rely on the *ālayavijñāna* as their cause, they perceive objects as being of their own mind. Through false conceptualization and attachment, various states of mind arise, just as bundles of bamboo serve as mutual causes for one another. Like waves upon the great ocean, they arise and cease when blown by the wind of perceiving objects within one's own mind.
"Therefore, Mahāmati, when the manas-vijñāna is transformed and ceases,
the seven kinds of consciousness are also transformed and cease.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I do not grasp at nirvāṇa, nor do I abandon the characteristics of conditioned activity;
by turning back and extinguishing the deluded mind, one is said to attain nirvāṇa.
Relying on those causes and mindfulness, the mind ranges through various objects."
Consciousness acts as the cause for the mind and serves as its support.
Just as when the flow of water is exhausted, waves do not arise;
so too, when mental consciousness ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

I shall explain for you the distinct characteristics of the essence of false discrimination. You and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should skillfully discern and know these distinct characteristics of the essence of false dharmas; you should transcend the dharmas of the discriminator and the discriminated, skillfully know the dharma of internal personal cultivation, remain far removed from the externalist realms of the grasper and the grasped, stay distant from the various essences and marks of the causal conditions of false discrimination, and having distanced yourselves, no longer further discriminate the marks of the false."
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the differentiation of the essence of dharmas through false discrimination? Mahāmati!
The intrinsic nature and distinctions of unreal conceptualization consist of twelve types. What are these twelve?
The first is verbal conceptualization;
Second, the discrimination of what can be known;
third, the discrimination of signs;
fourth, the discrimination of meaning.
Fifth, discrimination of substantial entities;
sixth, discrimination of causes;
seventh, discrimination of views;
Eighth, the establishment of discrimination;
ninth, the arising of discrimination;
tenth, the non-arising of discrimination.
Eleventh, the discrimination of conjunction;
twelfth, the discrimination of bondage and non-bondage.
Mahāmati!
This is called the characteristic of phenomena that differentiates the specific characteristics of their own essence. Mahāmati,
as for verbal discrimination, it refers to the attachment to various kinds of speech and exquisite sounds.
Mahāmati! This is called verbal discrimination. Mahāmati!

That which can be known through discrimination refers to the mental deliberation that there must exist the characteristics of real entities corresponding to prior phenomena; it is that which the sages, through their cultivation, come to know, and based upon those phenomena, they give rise to speech.
"O Mahāmati! Such discrimination as this is called the discrimination of the knowable.
O Mahāmati!

Discrimination of characteristics refers to the grasping at various characteristics—such as heat, moisture, motion, and solidity—within those very objects of cognition as being real, just as various birds and beasts perceive a mirage in the sky as water.
Mahāmati! This is called the discrimination of names and signs. Mahāmati!
Discrimination of meaning refers to delighting in various real objects such as gold, silver,
and so forth. Mahāmati,
this is called discrimination of meaning.
Mahāmati!

As for the discrimination of self-nature, it refers to being single-mindedly preoccupied with the characteristics of the self-nature of existing phenomena, thinking, "This phenomenon is thus and so, and not otherwise. This is not the vision of right view; it is merely discrimination.
Mahāmati! This is called the discrimination of intrinsic nature. Mahāmati!

Regarding "causes for discrimination," this refers to various causes and various conditions by which the characteristic of non-existence is discriminated and the characteristic of existence is produced.
Mahāmati!
This is called discrimination based on causes. Mahāmati!

As for discrimination based on views, it refers to the attachment-based discrimination of heterodox outsiders who hold to views of existence and non-existence, identity and difference, both and neither.
Mahāmati! This is called the discrimination of views. Mahāmati!
"Establishing discrimination" means grasping at the marks of "self" and "what belongs to self" and proclaiming false dharmas.
Mahāmati, this is called establishing discrimination.
Mahāmati!
That which is called "discriminating arising" refers to the generation of a mind of attachment toward the existence or non-existence of things based upon various conditions.
Mahāmati!
This is called the discrimination of arising. Mahāmati!

As for the non-discrimination of arising, it means that all dharmas are originally unarisen; because they are fundamentally non-existent, they exist based on causes and conditions, yet there is no cause-and-effect [inherent within them].
Mahāmati! This is called the discrimination of non-arising.
Mahāmati!
Regarding "conjunction and discrimination": it refers to which various phenomena are conjoined, such as gold and thread together;
and which various phenomena are conjoined, such as the conjunction of gold and thread.
Mahāmati! This is called the discrimination of conjunction. Mahāmati!
Regarding the discrimination between bondage and non-bondage: it refers to the attachment to the causes of bondage as if they were actual bonds. Mahāmati!
It is like a person who, through skillful means, ties a knot in a rope; having tied it, he then unties it.
Mahāmati! This is called the discrimination between bondage and non-bondage. Mahāmati!

This is called the characteristic of the differentiation of the essence of dharmas through false conceptualization; because all ordinary beings cling to existence and non-existence by means of this characteristic of the differentiation of the essence of dharmas through false conceptualization, they cling to the various causes and conditions of the marks of dharmas.
Therefore, Mahāmati!

One discriminates the various characteristics of the essence of phenomena and, seeing these manifold phenomena, clings to them as real; it is like seeing various things based on an illusion, where ordinary people discriminate and perceive such phenomena as being different from the illusion itself.
Mahāmati! Among the various dharmas, I do not speak of them as being different from illusion, nor am I speaking of them as not being different. Why is this?
If illusion were different from the various phenomena, then the various phenomena should not arise based on illusion.

If illusion were identical to the various phenomena, then one should not perceive a distinction by seeing "this is illusion" and "this is the various phenomena. Therefore, I say they are neither different nor non-different.
"Therefore, Mahāmati!
You and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas must not discriminate that illusions are either real or unreal.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The mind is bound by its objects; cognition arises following those objects.
In the supreme state of tranquility, one gives rise to impartial wisdom.
Conceptualization and discrimination exist, yet they do not exist within the nature of dependent phenomena."
Grasping at false delusions, they do not know that things arise through the power of others.
All phenomena born of various conditions are like illusions and lack reality;
yet they harbor various conceptions, which are merely false discriminations and cannot be established.
Those perceptions are errors, all arising from the bonds of the mind;
the ignorant person lacks wisdom and discriminates the phenomena of dependent origination.
The very substance of these various false imaginings is itself the dharma of dependent origination.
Delusive thoughts are manifold, discriminated within a multitude of conditions.
There is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); a third [truth] arises without cause.
Delusive thoughts are said to constitute the conventional truth; their cessation is the realm of the sages.
For example, as a practitioner sees various things in a single object;
though that phenomenon has no variety, such is the nature of conceptualized marks.
Just as one with various cataracts in the eyes perceives manifold forms through false imagination; so it is with the world.
Cataracts have no color and are not form, yet the ignorant grasp at phenomena in this way.
Just as pure gold is free from dross, just as water is free from muddy turbidity,
and just as space is free from clouds, so too is the true Dharma pure.
There are no phenomena of false conceptualization, nor are there phenomena of dependent origination;
those who perceive through discrimination see both the grasping at existence and the denial of non-existence.
If false conceptualization were not real, and if dependent origination were real;
Phenomena that arise from causes are separated [from them], yet real phenomena give rise to real phenomena.
Causes are designated as "false phenomena," and one perceives all things arising through dependent origination;
since conceptualization and designation are inseparable, it is in this way that the false arises.
Delusion is fundamentally without reality; thus one transcends all false imaginings.
Only then does one know purity—this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
There are twelve kinds of false imaginings, and six kinds of dependent dharmas.
The realm realized within one’s own body is without distinction.
The five dharmas are the reality, and the three natures are likewise so;
when practitioners practice this, they do not depart from suchness.
Sentient beings and their causes and conditions—these are names for the discrimination of those dharmas;
the various marks of false conceptualization arise from those causes and conditions.
When true wisdom observes well, there are no conditions and no false conceptualizations.
In the ultimate sense there are no entities; how then could wisdom differentiate them?
If there were truly existent dharmas, they would be free from existence and non-existence;
if they are free from existence and non-existence, how could there be two dharmas?
The essence of the two dharmas is distinguished; there exist two kinds of dharma-essence.
Various things are seen through false imagination, while the realm of the pure sages is seen as the various manifestations of conceptual construction, discriminated within causes and conditions.
If one discriminates otherwise, one falls into the ways of the non-Buddhists.
To speak of delusion through delusive thought arises from the conjunction of views;
free from these two kinds of delusive thought, that is the true Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the practice of the noble wisdom realized within one’s own self, as well as the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, by means of which one does not rely on others to travel through all Buddha-lands and penetrate the Buddha-Dharma.”
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
“Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having departed from the conceptualization of dharmas as taught by various masters who rely on the names and words of the Āgamas, should sit alone in a quiet place and contemplate. Observing all dharmas through his own internal wisdom, he does not follow the teachings of others. Free from the false appearances of various views, he should diligently practice to enter the stages of the Tathāgata and realize the progressively superior wisdom.”
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the practice of the noble wisdom realized within one's own body. Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there is the characteristic of cultivating the One Vehicle within the three realms.
Mahāmati! What is the characteristic of the One Vehicle?
Mahāmati!
Because of realizing the path of the One Vehicle as it truly is, I speak of it as the One Vehicle.
Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of the path of the Single Vehicle as it is truly awakened to?

It is said that one does not discriminate between the objects of apprehension and the subject of apprehension, and does not give rise to abiding in such characteristics of phenomena, because one does not discriminate any phenomena whatsoever.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the path of the One Vehicle as realized according to reality. Mahāmati!
Thus, one awakens to the characteristics of the path of the One Vehicle; this has never been known by any outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or Brahmās, except for me alone.
“Mahāmati!
Therefore, I speak of it as the characteristic of the path of the One Vehicle.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason does the World-Honored One speak of the three vehicles and not the one vehicle?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to realize nirvāṇa through their own self-knowledge; therefore, I teach that there is only the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna). Mahāmati!

Because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas follow the Buddha’s teaching to become weary of and detached from the world, yet cannot attain liberation by themselves, I therefore teach that there is only the Single Vehicle.”
Furthermore, Mahāmati,

because all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have not yet abandoned the obstacle of knowledge, nor have they abandoned the obstacle of the habitual tendencies of karma and afflictions, I therefore speak of only the single vehicle (ekayāna).
Mahāmati!

Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and have not yet attained liberation from the inconceivable transformation-birth (*acintyapariṇāmikī-jāti*), I have taught the path of the One Vehicle for the sake of those Śrāvakas.
Mahāmati!

If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are free from all habitual tendencies of faults and realize the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), at that time, being liberated from all faults, they awaken from the intoxication of the samādhis and the outflow-free states (anāsrava). Having awakened, they cultivate all the merits within the supramundane outflow-free realm; having so cultivated, they attain the inconceivable Dharma-body of mastery.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The vehicle of the gods and the vehicle of Brahmā, The vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
And the vehicle of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas— I have taught all these vehicles."
Because the mind undergoes arising and ceasing, the various vehicles are not ultimate;
if that mind were extinguished, there would be neither vehicle nor one who rides it.
Since there is no distinction among vehicles, I speak of them as the One Vehicle.
In order to guide sentient beings, I have distinguished and taught the various vehicles.
There are three kinds of liberation, As well as the two forms of selflessness;
Without being free from the two kinds of obscurations, One is far removed from true liberation.
Just as a piece of wood floating on the ocean follows the turning of the waves,
so too do the śrāvakas drift about, tossed by the winds of the marks.
They have abandoned the secondary afflictions, yet remain bound by the latencies of the afflictions.
Relishing the bliss of samādhi, they dwell securely in the untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu).
There is no ultimate destination for them, nor do they ever regress;
having attained the body of samādhi, they remain unaware for immeasurable eons.
"Just as a person who is intoxicated awakens only after the wine has worn off;
so too, upon attaining the unsurpassed body of the Buddha, one realizes: 'This is my true Dharmakāya.
— *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Four: The Buddha-Mind (Part Five). Chapter Four: The Buddha-Mind.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "Mahāmati!
I shall now explain for you the distinctions in the practice of the mind-made body."
Mahāmati! Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (manomaya-kāya)."
What are these three?
First, the mind-made body attained through the samādhi of the bliss of samāpatti;
second, the mind-made body that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are.
Third, there is the body born of mind through the practice of non-effort within one's lineage.
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, the bodhisattva practices according to reality and attains the characteristics of the realized wisdom of the progressively higher stages.
Mahāmati! What is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) attained by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas through the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the bliss of samādhi?

It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages, wherein one practices various modes of conduct with a tranquilized mind.
