The bliss of meditative absorption—the manifestation of the evolving consciousnesses as waves upon the ocean-like mind—is called the arising of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Because one perceives that the objective realm is nothing but one’s own mind, one knows, in accordance with reality, the characteristics of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya). Mahāmati!
What is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are?

It refers to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), observes and realizes that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*), like illusions, and so forth, being entirely non-existent. Through the transformation of body and mind, he attains the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) and other gateways to the bliss of immeasurable *samāpatti*s, as well as immeasurable marks of power, mastery, and supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*). Adorned with exquisite flowers, moving as swiftly as one’s will, it is like an illusion, a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror; though not produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it possesses limbs and features that resemble those of the four great elements. Having attained sovereign mastery through all practices, he enters at will into the assemblies of the Buddha-lands.
Mahāmati!
This is called the mind-made body that realizes the characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are. Mahāmati!
What is the body born of mind that arises from the lineage and is characterized by non-conditioned practice?
It refers to the internal realization of all dharmas within oneself, because one delights in the true nature of phenomena and the blissful aspect of the characteristics of dharmas.
Mahāmati!
This is called the mind-made body born of the lineage, characterized by effortless practice. Mahāmati!
"You should observe and fully understand those three types of bodily characteristics.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"My vehicle is not a Great Vehicle; it is neither speech nor letters."
Neither truth nor liberation, yet not without a realm;
riding upon the Mahāyāna, they possess mastery over samādhi.
With various mind-made bodies, they are adorned with the flowers of sovereignty.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said, there are good sons and good daughters who commit the five deeds of immediate retribution.”
"Bhagavān! What are these five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantaryakarmāṇi*)?
And how is it that a son of good family or a daughter of good family, by performing the five deeds of immediate retribution, enters into the Avīci hell?"
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The five acts of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya) are as follows:"
First, killing one's mother;
second, killing one's father;
third, killing an arhat;
Fourth, causing a schism in the Saṃgha;
fifth, with an evil mind, drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
Mahāmati!
What is the mother of sentient beings?
It is the taking up of subsequent rebirth; it arises together with craving and delight, established like a mother who provides conditions. Mahāmati!
What is the father?
It is ignorance that acts as the father, giving birth to the village of the six sense bases. Mahāmati!
To sever those two kinds of roots that give rise [to existence] is called killing one's father and mother.
Mahāmati, what is meant by killing an Arhat?
This refers to how the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are like the poison of a rat that flares up; by uprooting the fundamental root of these enemies—the latent tendencies—they do not arise again.
Mahāmati, this is called "killing an Arhat."
Mahāmati! What is the schism of the Saṃgha?
It refers to the ultimate severance and destruction of the accumulation and conjunction of the five aggregates, which possess distinct characteristics; this is called the schism of the Saṃgha.
Mahāmati! What is meant by "shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind"?

It refers to perceiving the specific and general characteristics of external objects as the manifestations of one's own mind—the eightfold collection of consciousnesses—and, relying on the three gates of liberation that are free from outflows, ultimately severing these eight kinds of conscious Buddhas; this is called shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.
Mahāmati! These are called the five kinds of internal *ānantarya*.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family practices these *ānantaryas*, they are termed "those who have committed the *ānantaryas*," because those who commit the *ānantaryas* are said to realize the Dharma as it truly is.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
I shall explain to you the characteristics of the five external *ānantarya* offenses, so that when the Bodhisattvas hear this teaching, they will not give rise to doubt in future ages."
“Mahāmati! What are the five external acts of immediate retribution? They are:

killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha. Those who commit these acts of immediate retribution cannot realize even a single liberation among the three gates of liberation, except by relying on the sustaining power of the Tathāgata. Through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, who manifests as śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, or the Tathāgata himself, he effects repentance for the doubting minds of these five types of offenders. By severing this doubt, he causes them to give rise to roots of goodness and provides them with teachings through such manifestations.”
Mahāmati!

If one commits the five kinds of immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), one will ultimately be unable to realize entry into the factors of the path, except for those who—having seen that their own mind is merely illusory—become free from the conceptualizations of body, livelihood, and dwelling place, and the perception of "self" and "mine"; and who, throughout immeasurable and boundless eons, encounter spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) and, within the bodies of other paths, become free from the false views of their own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Craving is called the mother, Ignorance is the father;
The consciousness that cognizes objects is the Buddha, And the latent propensities are the Arhats.”
“The collection of aggregates is called the Saṃgha; it is characterized by uninterrupted continuity.
With no further interval of karma, one attains the uninterrupted state of True Suchness.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the Tathāgatas’ realization.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāsattva Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying:

“Mahāmati! By knowing the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena as they truly are, and by being able to know the two kinds of hindrances as they truly are, one becomes detached from the two kinds of afflictions.”
Mahāmati! This is called the Tathāgata’s knowledge of reality as it truly is. Mahāmati!
"Mahāmati, those Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who attain this Dharma are also called Buddhas.
For these reasons, Mahāmati, I teach the One Vehicle."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, The two obstructions, and the two afflictions, One attains inconceivable transformation; This is called the awakening of a Buddha.”
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
for what reason did the World-Honored One speak these words in the midst of the great assembly?"

"I am all the Buddhas of the past," and I have spoken various Jātaka sūtras; at those times, I was King Mūrdhaja, the six-tusked great elephant, the parrot bird, the seer Vyāsa, King Śakra, and the Bodhisattva Sunetra—thus, in hundreds of thousands of sūtras, I have spoken of these births.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: “Mahāmati!
Based upon four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha proclaims these words amidst the great assembly:”
"At that time, I was Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha.
What are these four? First, the equality of names; [and so forth].
Second, equality of speech;
third, equality of the Dharma;
fourth, equality of the body.
Mahāmati! It is because of these four kinds of equality that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak these words in the midst of the assembly.
Mahāmati!
What is the equality of syllables?

It means that whatever syllable the Buddhas of the past were called by—namely "Buddha"—I am likewise called "Buddha" by those same syllables. These syllables do not exceed those [past] syllables; they are equal to them, without difference or distinction.
Mahāmati! This is the equality of names. Mahāmati!
What is the equality of the speech of all Buddhas?
It means that just as the Buddhas of the past spoke the Dharma with sixty-four kinds of exquisite Brahma-voices, I too speak the Dharma with sixty-four kinds of subtle and wondrous Brahma-voices.
Mahāmati!

Future Buddhas will also preach the Dharma using sixty-four kinds of subtle and wondrous Brahma-voices; these voices will neither increase nor decrease, being non-different and without distinction, as exquisite as the Brahma-voice of the kalaviṅka bird.
Mahāmati! This is called the equality of the speech of all Buddhas.
Mahāmati!
What is the equality of the bodies of all Buddhas? Mahāmati!

My Dharma-body and Form-body, with their marks and signs of excellence, are no different and have no distinction from those of all other Buddhas; it is only for the sake of guiding sentient beings that the Tathāgatas manifest various bodies according to the diverse places of birth of those various beings.
Mahāmati! This is called the equality of the bodies of all Buddhas.
Mahāmati!
What is the equality of all Buddhas' dharmas?
It means that those Buddhas and I have attained the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth.
Mahāmati! This is called the equality of the dharmas of all Buddhas. Mahāmati!
Based on these four kinds of equal dharmas, the Tathāgata makes this declaration among the great assembly:
"I was King Mūrdhagata and others in the past."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni are I;
I speak of all the sons of the Buddha because they rely upon the fourfold equality.”
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As the Tathāgata has said:”
"On the very night I realized great enlightenment and on the very night I entered parinirvāṇa, I did not speak a single word in the interval.
The Buddha said, "It is not speech. World-Honored One, based on what meaning do you say such words? Why does the Buddha say that his words are not words?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata speaks these words based upon two kinds of dharmas."
What are these two?
I have explained them as follows:
first, the dharma realized through internal personal experience; [second, the dharma taught by others].
Second, by relying on the primordially abiding dharma (*pūrvasthita-dharma*).
Mahāmati, it is based on these two dharmas that I speak thus.
What is the dharma realized within one's own person?

It means that the dharmas realized by those past Buddhas and Tathāgatas, I likewise realize without increase or decrease; it is the practice of the various realms realized within one's own person, which is free from the characteristics of verbal conceptualization and detached from the two kinds of syllables.
Mahāmati! What is the primordially abiding dharma? Mahāmati!
It means that the path of original practice is level and smooth, just as gold, silver, pearls, and other such treasures are found there.
Mahāmati! This is called the primordial abode of the dharma-nature.
Mahāmati!

Whether the Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), and the realization of phenomena (dharmasamavasarana) abide eternally, like the original road to a city.
Mahāmati!

It is like a person traveling through a vast wilderness who sees the level, direct road leading back to his original city; he follows it and enters that city, and having entered it, experiences various pleasures and performs various activities.
"Mahāmati, what do you think?
Does that person first create this path and then enter the city?"
"Did they begin by creating various kinds of adornments?
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"No, World-Honored One."

“Mahāmati! Myself and all the Buddhas of the past, as well as the dharmatā, the dharmadhātu, the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthiti), the characteristics of phenomena (dharmanimitta), and the realization of phenomena (dharmasākṣātkriyā), are likewise eternally abiding.”

Mahāmati! It is based on this meaning that I have made such a declaration in the midst of the great assembly: "On the very night I attained Great Enlightenment and on the very night I entered Parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken between these two moments; nor has anything been spoken, will be spoken, or is currently being spoken."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"On what night I attained enlightenment, And on what night I entered parinirvāṇa—
Between these two moments, I have said nothing at all."
"I have realized the nature of phenomena within my own body; it is based on this that I speak.
The Buddhas of the ten directions and I—there is no difference between us regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the Buddha, saying:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and the great assembly of bodhisattvas, having heard this, may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Many people in the world fall into two views."
What are these two views?
First, the view of existence;
second, the view of non-existence.
Because they perceive the existence of phenomena and perceive the non-existence of phenomena, they conceive the notion of ultimacy regarding what is not ultimately real.
Mahāmati, how is it that worldly people fall into the view of existence?
This means that all phenomena arise from truly existent causes and conditions, not from non-existent ones; it is truly existent dharmas that arise, not non-existent dharmas.

Mahāmati, when people of the world speak in this way, they are said to be propounding causelessness and conditionlessness, and thereby slandering the world by asserting that all phenomena arise without cause or condition.
Mahāmati! How do people in the world fall into the view of non-existence?

It is by asserting that while greed, hatred, and delusion exist as real entities, they simultaneously claim that greed, hatred, and delusion do not exist, thus discriminating between existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! Furthermore, if there should be someone who speaks thus:
"There are no dharmas, because the characteristics of things are not perceived."
"Mahāmati! Furthermore, if someone were to say:
'The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are without greed, without hatred, and without delusion.'"
He further asked: "If both say that [the self] existed previously, between these two people, which one is superior and which one is inferior?
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said:
“If anyone says that greed, hatred, and delusion existed previously but are absent later, such a person is not in accordance with reality.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“Excellent!”
Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!
You have understood my question.
Mahāmati!

It is not merely that you claim desire, hatred, and delusion truly existed previously but later say they do not exist; in this regard, you are the same as the Vaiśeṣikas and others, and for that reason, you are inferior. Mahāmati!
Not only are they inferior, they extinguish all the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Why is this? Mahāmati!
Because, in reality, there are no internal or external dharmas;
because they are neither identical nor different;
and because the various afflictions are neither identical nor different.
Mahāmati!
The dharmas of greed, hatred, and delusion cannot be found within the internal body, nor can they be found among external phenomena; because they lack substantial reality, I do not admit them.
Mahāmati!
What I do not permit is the existence of greed, hatred, and delusion; therefore, such persons destroy the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, know the dharma of tranquility; because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not perceive dharmas, they lack the causes for that which binds and that which is bound.
Mahāmati!
If there is that which binds, there must necessarily be that which is bound; if there is that which is bound, there must necessarily be a cause for that which binds.
Mahāmati, one who speaks in this manner is said to advocate the annihilation of all dharmas.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of non-existence. Mahāmati!

Based on this meaning, I have stated in other sūtras: "It would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru and develop arrogance, than to say that all phenomena are empty and non-existent."
Mahāmati!

When those of overweening pride say that all dharmas are non-existent, they are negating all dharmas because they have fallen into the view of self-characteristics and common characteristics; because they see dharmas as the manifestations of their own minds;
and because they see external objects as impermanent.
Because various characteristics mutually differ from one another;

because one perceives the continuity of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as a substantial entity, which arises through the mutual succession of their respective causes, due to the false discrimination of one's own mind.
"Therefore, Mahāmati,
such persons destroy the teachings of all Buddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"Existence and non-existence are two extremes, which constitute the sphere of the mind;
Transcending all such spheres of phenomena, the equalizing mind is tranquil.
By not grasping at the spheres of phenomena, one extinguishes that which is neither existent nor non-existent."
As suchness is primordially existent, that is the realm of the noble ones.
That which was originally non-existent arises, and having arisen, it returns to extinction;
that which arises neither from existence nor from non-existence does not abide within my teaching.
Neither non-Buddhists nor Buddhas, neither I nor anyone else;
since it is not established through causes and conditions, how can one say it exists?
If it does not arise from causes and conditions, how can one say it does not exist?
Those with wrong views debate the arising of phenomena, Conceptually calculating existence and non-existence.
If one knows there is nothing that arises, One also knows there is nothing that ceases;
Observing that the world is entirely empty and quiescent, They do not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Teacher of Gods and Humans, will establish for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the practice of the True Dharma.”

Once I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have well understood the characteristics of practicing the True Dharma, we shall swiftly attain the realization of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, because we will not follow any illusory thoughts, observations, or demonic activities.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
“So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati: “Mahāmati!”
There are two kinds of dharmas by which all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas establish the characteristics of practicing the True Dharma.
What are these two?
First is the characteristic of establishing the true Dharma;
second is the teaching on the characteristic of establishing the true Dharma. Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of establishing the True Dharma?

It refers to the characteristics of the various supreme dharmas personally realized within oneself, which are free from words, language, and phrases; it is the ability to grasp the characteristics of the dharma of practice on the various stages of realization and untainted right precepts; it is to remain detached from the false conceptualizations and discursive thoughts of all non-Buddhists and the realms of all Māras; and it is to subdue all non-Buddhists and Māras while manifesting the dharma of one’s own internal realization through practice in accordance with reality.
Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of establishing the True Dharma.
Mahāmati!
What is the characteristic of establishing the teaching of the Dharma?

It refers to the exposition of the various teachings of the nine divisions of scripture, which are free from the conceptual grasping of oneness or difference, existence or non-existence. First, one teaches through skillful means in order to lead sentient beings to enter the state they delight in; that is, according to the faith of sentient beings in this or that teaching, one expounds this or that teaching.
Mahāmati! This is called the establishment of the characteristics of preaching the Dharma. Mahāmati!
"You and all bodhisattvas should practice and study such a true Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Establishing the Dharma of internal realization, And the names and characteristics of the spoken Dharma;"
If one can skillfully discern this, one will not follow the characteristics taught by others.
In reality, there are no external phenomena as ordinary beings discriminate them;
if all phenomena were merely false, for what purpose would one seek liberation?
Observing all conditioned phenomena, which continue in a succession of arising and ceasing, one increases the two views and fails to understand causes and conditions.
Nirvāṇa is free from consciousness; this alone is the single reality.
Contemplating the world as illusory, Like a phantom, a dream, or a plantain tree;
Though greed, hatred, and delusion exist, There is no agent who creates them.
From craving arise the aggregates; All that exists is like a phantom or a dream.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
We pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, will explain unreal conceptualization for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
"In what phenomena does unreal conceptualization occur?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
"Excellent!"
Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!

For the sake of bringing peace and security to all sentient beings, for the benefit of all sentient beings, for the happiness of all sentient beings, and out of compassion for all the world’s devas and humans, you have requested this matter of mine.
Mahāmati! Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All sentient beings who cling to unreal and false conceptualizations do so because they arise from perceiving various kinds of unreal phenomena, due to their attachment to the various objects of the unreal grasper and the graspable."
Because they enter into the arising of false conceptualizations from the perceptions of their own minds;

and because they fall into the factional assemblies of unrighteousness—the dualistic views of existence and non-existence—thereby increasing and perfecting the habitual tendencies of the false and divergent views of external paths.
Mahāmati!

Because of grasping at the meanings of external conceptual proliferations, false mind and mental factors arise; it is like a bundle of grass upon which one discriminates the dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self."
"Mahāmati!
For this reason, unreal conceptualization arises.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

If sentient beings cling to unreal and false conceptualizations, they arise from perceiving various false phenomena. They cling to all objects—the false grasper and the grasped—and enter into the perceptions of their own minds, giving rise to false conceptualizations. They fall into the midst of the partisan discrimination of the two views of existence and non-existence, increasing and perfecting the habitual tendencies of the false and divergent views of externalists. By grasping at the meanings of external frivolous discourses with unreal conceptualization, they give rise to false minds and mental factors, just like those who grasp at a bundle of grass as being 'self' and 'what belongs to self.'”
World-Honored One!

Just as those various external objects and various marks serve as bases for falling into the partisan views of existence or non-existence, one should remain free from the marks of such views of existence and non-existence.
World-Honored One!

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) should likewise be thus: it is far removed from the teachings spoken by the Noble Ones in the *Āgamas*, far removed from the sense-faculties (*indriya*), and far removed from the establishment of the three types of dharmas—namely, analogies, causes, and characteristics.
World-Honored One!
How is it that within a single locus, various kinds of conceptual discrimination and attachment arise, giving rise to various false conceptualizations?
For what reason do they fail to abide in the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), but instead give rise to discrimination through false conceptualization?
World-Honored One!
When the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma in this manner, it is not a teaching of equality, for it is taught without cause. Why is this so?
Because [things] arise in one place and do not arise in another.

If the Blessed One speaks in this way, he falls into two factions; for he gives rise to conceptualization through attachment to views and false discrimination. Since the Blessed One says that it is like a worldly magician who, depending on various causes and conditions, produces various forms and images, and since the Blessed One’s own mind involves false discrimination, and since the Blessed One speaks of various falsehoods—whether existent or non-existent—which cannot be described as being free from discrimination, such a Tathāgata falls into worldly discourse and enters the assembly of those with minds of wrong views.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I distinguish that what is false does not arise and does not cease. Why is this?"
Because they do not give rise to the conceptual characteristics of existence and non-existence,
and because they do not perceive any external existence or non-existence. Mahāmati!
Because one sees one’s own mind as it truly is, false discrimination neither arises nor ceases.

Mahāmati, what I have here spoken is intended solely for the sake of ignorant ordinary people; I speak of the discrimination of one’s own mind, wherein various discriminations arise according to prior mental states, and wherein there is attachment to the signs of various discriminated phenomena.

Why is this? If it were not explained, ignorant ordinary beings would not be free from the deluded perceptions of their own minds, nor from the attachment to views of self and what belongs to self, nor from the faults regarding causes, effects, and various causal conditions.

Because they perceive the two kinds of mind as they truly are, they will skillfully know the characteristics of all stages (*bhūmi*), skillfully know the internally realized realm of the Buddhas' own practice, and—by transforming the essence of the five dharmas and the perceived marks of discrimination—enter the stage of the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati!
For this reason, I say that all sentient beings alike cling to unrealities and give rise to deluded thoughts, mentally discriminating various objects within their own minds;
it is for this reason that all sentient beings must realize the meaning of reality as it is in order to attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All causes and all conditions, From these the world arises;
Those who falsely imagine and cling to the four positions Do not understand what I have taught."
The world does not arise from existence or non-existence, nor does it arise apart from existence and non-existence;
why do the deluded discriminate regarding phenomena that arise through dependent origination?
If one can see the world such that existence and non-existence are neither existent nor non-existent, [one sees reality].
By transforming the deluded mind, one attains the true Dharma of non-self.
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; therefore, they arise dependent upon causes and conditions.
These conditions themselves are the fruit; from the fruit, existence is not produced.
A fruit does not arise from a fruit; if it did, there would be two fruits.
If there were two fruits, it would be difficult to find a fruit within a fruit.
Free from both thought and the object of thought, one contemplates all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Seeing that all phenomena are mind-only, I therefore teach "mind-only.
As for the nature of the means of cognition and its forms, they are devoid of conditions and all [external] dharmas;
ultimately there is true purity—this is the measure I teach.
The "self" in conventional truth is a mere designation; it has no substantial reality.
The aggregates and the designation of "aggregates" are likewise designations, and these designations are not real dharmas.
There are four kinds of equality: equality of characteristics, equality of causes, equality of arising, and equality of selflessness.
These four equalities are the dharma for practitioners.
They overturn all views and transcend conceptualization and its objects;
because nothing is perceived and nothing arises, I teach that there is only mind.
Neither existent nor non-existent phenomena, free from all phenomena of existence and non-existence;
thus free from mental phenomena, I therefore speak of "mind-only.
Suchness, emptiness, the limit of reality, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm—
Because of the mind, body, and mental factors, I teach that there is "mind-only.
Discrimination depends on habitual tendencies and bondage; the mind arises in dependence upon various objects.
Sentient beings perceive external objects; therefore, I teach that there is "mind-only."
"It can be seen that external phenomena do not exist; when the mind is exhausted, one sees things in this way.
Because of the body, the means of livelihood, and the dwelling place, I therefore say 'Mind-Only.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has said:
‘As I have taught, you and all bodhisattvas must not become attached to the meanings of sounds and words.’”
"World-Honored One!
How does a bodhisattva not become attached to the meaning of words?
World-Honored One!"
"What constitutes speech?
What constitutes meaning?
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!”
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "What is sound?"

This refers to the conceptualization of various phenomena through speech, which arises based on the habitual tendencies of beginningless linguistic conventions and the combination of names and words; it issues forth due to the movement and coordination of the throat, nose, teeth, cheeks, lips, and tongue, and is thus called "sound."
Mahāmati! What is meant by "meaning"?

It is when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, relying on the power of noble wisdom derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation, sits alone in a secluded place and contemplates: "What is nirvāṇa? What is the path leading to nirvāṇa? He observes the sphere of practice within his own body and the superior characteristics of practice at each stage and in every place, thereby transforming the causes of beginningless habitual perfuming.
Mahāmati! This is called the Bodhisattva’s skillful understanding of the characteristics of meaning.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
What is meant by a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful understanding of the meaning of speech? Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva perceives that the meaning of the sound of speech is neither identical nor different; he perceives that the meaning and the sound of speech are neither identical nor different.
Mahāmati!
If one were to say that speech is separate from meaning, then meaning should not exist because of the sound of that speech; yet, meaning is discerned in dependence upon that speech.
Mahāmati! Just as one discerns various forms by relying on a lamp, Mahāmati!
For example, Mahāmati, it is like a person who lights a lamp to examine various precious jewels, [observing] that they are such-and-such in this place and such-and-such in that place.
Mahāmati!
The Bodhisattva relies on the sound of language to realize that which is beyond language, because he enters the meaning of practice within his own internal body.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; their self-nature is fundamentally in a state of nirvāṇa. The three vehicles, the one vehicle, the five dharmas, the mind, and the essence of all dharmas are identical. The meaning of the sound of language arises from grasping at signs based on various conditions; it falls into the views of existence and non-existence and slanders all dharmas. One perceives the essence of dharmas as abiding in distinct characteristics and discriminates these distinct characteristics. Having made such discriminations, one sees the various marks of phenomena as being like illusions, and sees various forms of discrimination.
"Mahāmati!
For example, the various and diverse discriminations of a magical illusion do not refer to the noble ones; they are the vision of ordinary worldlings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"Distinguishing the sounds of speech, one establishes various dharmas;
because of that establishment, one falls into the evil realms.
Within the five aggregates there is no self, and within the self there are no five aggregates."
It is not like those false appearances, nor is it non-existent.
Ordinary beings engage in false discrimination and see all phenomena as truly existent;
if things were as they are seen, everyone should perceive the truth.
If all phenomena were non-existent, then defilement and purity would also be non-existent;
yet their perception is not like that, nor is it a mere nothingness.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:

I shall now explain for you the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness; you and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should skillfully understand those characteristics of wisdom and consciousness so that, by practicing according to reality regarding the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, you may swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Mahāmati! There are three kinds of knowledge.
What are the three?
First, mundane wisdom;
second, supramundane wisdom;
third, the supreme supramundane wisdom.
Mahāmati! Consciousness has the characteristic of arising and ceasing; wisdom has the characteristic of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Those who possess consciousness fall into the notions of "with marks" and "without marks," and thus fall into the various causal marks of existence and non-existence.

Mahāmati! The characteristic of wisdom is that which is far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence, as well as the causal marks of being and non-being; this is called the characteristic of wisdom.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The accumulation of all phenomena is called the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*); the non-accumulation of all phenomena is called the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna*). Mahāmati!
Wisdom is of three kinds.
What are these three?
First, the observation of specific and general characteristics;
Second, observing the characteristics of arising and ceasing;
third, observing the characteristic of neither arising nor ceasing.
Mahāmati!
What is mundane knowledge?
When various non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings cling to the existence or non-existence of all phenomena, this is called the characteristic of mundane knowledge.
Mahāmati! What is supramundane wisdom?
It refers to the false discrimination of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas regarding particular and universal characteristics; this is called supramundane wisdom.
Mahāmati! What is the supramundane, most excellent wisdom?

It refers to the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who contemplate all phenomena as quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing; who attain the realization of selflessness in the stage of a Tathāgata, and who are free from the dualistic views of the factions of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
That which is called "wisdom" (jñāna) has the characteristic of being unobstructed; that which is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) cognizes the characteristics of those various objects.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

The conjunction of consciousnesses arising as that which acts and that which is acted upon is called the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*); the association with unimpeded dharmas is called the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the characteristic of non-apprehension is called wisdom; because it is the realm of practice realized by noble wisdom through personal internal realization, one enters and emerges from all dharmas like the moon in water—this is called the characteristic of wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Consciousness can accumulate all karmas; Wisdom can discern and differentiate;
Insight can attain the signless And the realm of wondrous adornment."
Consciousness is bound by its objects, while wisdom clearly discerns all realms;
signlessness and the supreme realm are the dwelling place of insight.
When the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness are far removed from all signs, [one attains liberation].
The Śrāvakas differentiate phenomena; they are not true disciples.
With the supreme progress of tranquil patience, they possess the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom;
born from this most excellent wisdom, they remain far removed from all conditioned activities.
I possess three kinds of wisdom, by which I attain the name of "Noble One";
through the conceptualization of those [objects], one is able to hear of existence and non-existence.
Departing from the practices of the two vehicles, this wisdom is free from objective realms.
Grasping at the notions of existence and non-existence arises from the various śrāvakas.
To be able to enter into the realization that this is merely mind is the stainless characteristic of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
The various non-Buddhists hold nine kinds of views regarding transformation. What are these nine?
The first is transformation of form and appearance;
Second, transformation of characteristics;
third, transformation of causes;
fourth, transformation of association.
Fifth, the transformation of perception;
sixth, the transformation of objects;
seventh, the transformation of the discernment of conditions.
Eighth, the transformation of the discernment of mental constructions;
ninth, the transformation of birth. Mahāmati!
This is called the view of ninefold transformation.
Based on this view of ninefold transformation, all non-Buddhists (tīrthika) assert that transformation arises from existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati!
What is the transformation of form and characteristics among the non-Buddhists? Mahāmati!

It is like using gold to fashion ornaments such as rings, bracelets, and necklaces; though their forms and characteristics differ in various ways, the essence of the gold remains unchanged. In the same way, the transformation of the forms and characteristics of all phenomena as conceptualized by all non-Buddhists is also like this.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who discriminate that all phenomena arise through the transformation of causes. Mahāmati!
Furthermore, those dharmas are neither thus nor not thus, because they depend upon conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Mahāmati, all such transformations are likewise to be understood as follows:

just as milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth undergo individual transformations through ripening, so too do the transformations of all externalists' conceptual constructions. Yet, there is no real dharma that can be transformed, for one perceives existence and non-existence within one's own mind, grasping at them and conceptually constructing existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! All ordinary beings are likewise; by relying on the discrimination of their own minds, they give rise to all phenomena. Mahāmati!
There is no dharma that arises, and there is no dharma that evolves, just as one sees various forms and phenomena within a dream or an illusion.
Mahāmati! It is like seeing all manner of things, or the birth and death of the son of a barren woman, within a dream.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The transformation of temporal forms and characteristics, The four great elements and the various sense-faculties,
The intermediate state and the various appropriations— Such appropriations are not wisdom.”
“The world arises from causes and conditions; the Buddha does not teach it otherwise.
Causes and conditions are themselves the world, like a city of the Gandharvas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will skillfully explain the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas; we pray that the Sugata will explain the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas, so that I and the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas may thoroughly understand the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas.
Having understood them through skillful means, we shall not fall into attachment to the characteristics of the continuity or non-continuity of all dharmas.”
Having transcended all conceptualizations of words and letters regarding the continuity or non-continuity of all phenomena,
they attain mastery over powers and supernatural faculties, traveling for the sake of transformation among the great assemblies in all Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
they are sealed by the excellent seal of the *dhāraṇī* gates and are turned by the excellent turning of the ten points of exhaustion, manifesting various transformations.
The radiance shines forth, like the four great luminaries—the sun, the moon, and the *maṇi* jewel—moving spontaneously.
Sentient beings enjoy it while remaining detached from all stages (*bhūmi*), perceiving only the marks of conceptualization within their own minds.
It demonstrates that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, and shows entry into the ground of reliance upon the Buddhas, according to the realm of sentient beings.
He preaches the Dharma as is appropriate, gathering beings and causing them to abide in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams;
he leads them away from the partisan extremes of existence and non-existence, and from the conceptual proliferation of birth, cessation, and false imaginings regarding the meaning of words.
Thus, they attain mastery over their rebirths and proceed to be born in superior realms.
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Very well, we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Regarding the characteristics of the continuity and non-continuity of all dharmas:

this refers to the continuity of attachment to meanings as held by the śrāvakas; the continuity of attachment to signs; the continuity of attachment to conditions; the continuity of attachment to existence and non-existence; the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of arising and non-arising; the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of cessation and non-cessation; the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of vehicles and non-vehicles; the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of the conditioned and the unconditioned; the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of the characteristics of the stages; the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of self-discrimination; and the continuity of attachment to the discrimination of existence and non-existence that leads one to join the factions of external paths."
Mahāmati!

In this way, foolish ordinary people possess a continuous succession of countless diverse mental discriminations. Relying on this succession, they engage in ignorant discrimination like a silkworm spinning its cocoon; relying on the threads of discrimination produced by the perceptions of their own minds, they delight in conjunction, binding themselves and others, and they cling to the continuity of the conjunction of existence and non-existence.
"Mahāmati!
However, there is neither continuity nor the characteristic of continuity, because one perceives that all dharmas are quiescent.
Mahāmati!"
Because all Bodhisattvas perceive all phenomena as being without the characteristic of discrimination, it is therefore called "the gate of the quiescent dharma of all Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

One is able to know all external phenomena as they truly are, free from existence and non-existence; one awakens to the appearances seen by one's own mind as they truly are, because one has entered the signless nature of one's own mind.
Mahāmati! Because one perceives the existence and non-existence of phenomena through discrimination, it is called "continuity";
because one perceives that all phenomena are quiescent, it is called "non-continuity," which is the absence of the characteristic of continuity.
Mahāmati, there is no characteristic of dharmas that involve continuity;
there is neither bondage nor liberation. It is by falling into dualistic views that one’s own mind discriminates between bondage and liberation. Why is this so?
Because they are unable to know whether phenomena exist or do not exist.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are three kinds of continuity for foolish ordinary beings.
What are these three?
They are greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the arising of craving and delight; because of this continuity, there is future birth. Mahāmati!
"Continuity" refers to the continuity of sentient beings as they are born within the five destinies. Mahāmati!
To sever continuity means there is no continuity and no characteristic of continuity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Because of clinging to the continuity of causes and conditions, one is born into the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). Since the various consciousnesses continue to evolve in succession without interruption, one perceives the three gates of liberation. By transforming and extinguishing the consciousness that clings to the causes of the three realms of existence, this is called "severing the continuity."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Unreal and false discrimination Is called the characteristic of continuity;
If one can know it as it truly is, The net of continuity will then be severed.”
"If one grasps at sound as real, it is like a silkworm cocooning itself;
bound by the delusive imaginings of their own minds, ordinary people do not understand this.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the Blessed One has said: 'By whatever various conceptualizing minds one conceptualizes whatever various phenomena, those respective phenomena lack such and such intrinsic natures and characteristics; they are merely the conceptualizations of one's own mind.'"
World-Honored One!
If it is only the discrimination of one's own mind and not the characteristic of those dharmas, then as the World-Honored One has taught, all dharmas should be neither defiled nor pure. Why is this?
"The Tathāgata has said that all dharmas are seen through false discrimination and lack any substantial reality.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "So it is, so it is!"
"It is as you have said, Mahāmati!
Yet all foolish ordinary beings discriminate among phenomena; however, those phenomena do not possess such characteristics, for they falsely discriminate them as being truly existent."
Mahāmati! Those are the false conceptualizations of ordinary beings regarding the essential characteristics of all phenomena; they are false cognitions and not seeing things as they truly are.
Mahāmati!

Just as the Noble Ones know the intrinsic nature and characteristics of all phenomena, by relying on the wisdom of the Noble Ones, by relying on the vision of the Noble Ones, and by relying on the eye of noble insight, they know the intrinsic nature of all phenomena exactly as it is.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said:
"World-Honored One!

Just as the various noble ones rely on noble wisdom, rely on noble vision, and rely on the noble eye of insight—rather than the fleshly eye or the divine eye—they realize that the essence and characteristics of all dharmas do not possess such characteristics, unlike the false conceptualizations of ordinary beings."
“World-Honored One!
How do foolish ordinary beings revolve within the marks of falsehood?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"One who can realize the realm of the noble ones as it truly is transforms deluded consciousness.
"World-Honored One!
Those ignorant ordinary people possess neither inverted views nor non-inverted views."

"Why is this? Because they are unable to see the reality of the dharmas within the realm of the sages as it truly is, and because they perceive the marks of existence and non-existence through transformation.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

Even all noble ones possess discrimination, yet all various phenomena do not possess such characteristics, because they are perceived as objective appearances through the manifestation of one's own mind.”
World-Honored One!

Those noble ones perceive the existence of the essence of phenomena and differentiate their characteristics, because the World-Honored One has neither stated that there is a cause nor stated that there is no cause. Why is this so?
Because one has fallen into the conceptualization of the characteristics of existence, other people perceive objects in a manner different from this perception.
World-Honored One!
To speak in such a way would entail the fault of infinite regress.
Why is this? Because they do not realize that the characteristics of all phenomena lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
World-Honored One!
"World-Honored One, it is not because of the existence of the intrinsic nature and characteristics of dharmas through conceptual discrimination that all dharmas exist. How, then,
does one conceptually discriminate?"
Is it not as they have conceptualized?
Should it be as they have conceptualized?
World-Honored One!
"World-Honored One, there are the characteristics of conceptual differentiation and the characteristics of intrinsic nature;
these two types of causes are not similar, for the characteristics of the entities of those various differentiated phenomena are distinct."
How do ordinary people make such conceptual distinctions?
These causes are not established in the manner they are perceived.
Thus the Blessed One said:

"I have made this statement in order to sever the deluded discriminative minds of all sentient beings; according to the deluded discrimination of those ordinary worldlings, such dharmas do not exist."
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do you prohibit sentient beings from holding views of existence and non-existence regarding phenomena,
yet cause them to cling to real dharmas as the realm of noble wisdom?"
World-Honored One!
You would further cause all sentient beings to fall into the state of non-viewing. Why is this?
"It is because all phenomena are described as quiescent and signless, for the essence of the Dharma realized by noble wisdom is likewise signless.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"I do not say that all phenomena are quiescent and signless; nor do I say that all phenomena are non-existent. I do not cause one to fall into the view of nihilism, nor do I cause one to become attached to such a state as the realm of the noble ones."

Why is this? It is because I wish for sentient beings to leave behind places of fear and terror. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have clung to the notion that all phenomena possess a real, intrinsic nature and characteristics; therefore, I say that while the noble ones know the nature and characteristics of phenomena to be truly existent, I also say that all phenomena are quiescent and signless.
Mahāmati!

I do not speak of the existence or non-existence of the essence of dharmas; rather, I speak of the dharma realized within my own person as it truly is. By hearing my teaching and practicing the tranquility of all signless dharmas, one attains the vision of the signless realm of suchness, enters the vision of dharmas within one's own mind, and remains far removed from the views of the existence or non-existence of external dharmas. Having attained the three gates of liberation, one uses the seal of reality to properly seal all dharmas, and through the observation of wisdom realized within one's own person, one becomes free from the views of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
a bodhisattva should not establish that all dharmas are unarisen. Why is this?
Because the establishment of dharmas is identical to the existence of all dharmas; were it otherwise, it would be identical to the non-existence of all dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, because one establishes that all dharmas exist, one speaks of "all dharmas"; within this establishment of dharmas, they are identical.
Why is this? Because that establishment is not the same as the non-arising of all phenomena; therefore, the establishment that asserts "all phenomena [arise]" is self-contradictory.

Why is this? Because within the establishment there is no such establishment; if it were otherwise, that establishment would not arise either, since it shares the same characteristic of non-differentiation as all phenomena. Therefore, the non-arising of the establishment of all phenomena is called "self-annulment."
Because those three dharmas and five dharmas exist through their mutual conjunction, there is no arising apart from the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! That conceptual construction enters into all phenomena because one does not perceive the existence or non-existence [of phenomena] therein.
Mahāmati!
If one establishes that all dharmas are unarisen and says,
"All dharmas are unarisen," [this is a mere conceptual construction].
"Mahāmati! Such a teaching establishes [a position] only to have it subverted. Why is this?"
Because it is free from conceptual construction, and because the characteristics of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.
Mahāmati! Therefore, one should not construct the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen.
Mahāmati!
Because that establishment is identical to the essence of all non-arising dharmas, one should not establish the non-arising of all dharmas, for there would be many faults.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, one should not establish that all phenomena are non-arising. Why is this?
Because the causes for each of those three and five dharmas are different,
Mahāmati! Furthermore,
one should not establish that all dharmas are non-arising.
Why is this? Because those three dharmas and five dharmas constitute conditioned phenomena and impermanence; therefore, one should not establish that all dharmas are non-arising.
Mahāmati!
In this way, one should not establish that all dharmas are empty, nor that all dharmas lack a substantial intrinsic nature.
Mahāmati!

Furthermore, bodhisattvas teach all phenomena to sentient beings as being like illusions and like dreams, because they perceive the characteristics of both the seen and the unseen, and because the characteristics of phenomena delude both vision and cognition. Therefore, they should speak of them as being like illusions and like dreams, in order to exclude and prevent all foolish ordinary people from falling into a state of alarm and fear.
Mahāmati!

Because ordinary beings fall into the false views of existence and non-existence, and because ordinary beings give rise to fear and terror upon hearing that things are like illusions and dreams, they abandon the Mahāyāna once they have become terrified by such teachings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“No intrinsic nature, no consciousness, No ālayavijñāna;
Fools engage in false conceptualization, Their wrong views are like a corpse.”
All phenomena are unborn; other views cannot establish them.
All phenomena are ultimately unborn; causes and conditions cannot bring them into being.
Since all phenomena are unborn, do not construct such dharmas.
Since identity and difference cannot be established, the very foundation of existence collapses.
Just as one with cataracts in the eyes falsely perceives floating hairs,
so do ordinary beings falsely perceive existence and non-existence through their conceptual constructions.
The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to phenomena.
Grasping at these provisional names as real, ordinary beings give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Characteristics, things, and provisional names are what the mind and consciousness experience and employ.
The Son of the Buddha is able to remain far removed, dwelling in the practice of the realm of tranquility.
Like deer with deluded and false minds perceiving water where there is no water,
ordinary people see phenomena in this way, whereas the noble ones do not.
The Sage perceives purity, giving rise to the three liberations and samādhis;
Far removed from arising and ceasing, he attains unobstructed tranquility.
In his practice, there is nothing that exists, nor does he perceive even non-existence.
The equality of existence and non-existence—therefore, the fruits of the noble ones arise.
What is meant by existence and non-existence?
How is their equality established?
"Because the mind cannot see, internal and external phenomena are impermanent;
if one can extinguish those phenomena, seeing the mind will become equanimity.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

As the World-Honored One has taught, when one observes with wisdom and cannot perceive any phenomena in the external realm, at that time one rightly knows that these are merely the internal mind. One realizes, as it truly is, the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness; there is no object to be grasped and no subject that grasps. Therefore, wisdom itself cannot differentiate or grasp anything.”
World-Honored One!

If it is said that wisdom cannot apprehend, is it because one perceives the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena—the various distinct characteristics and diverse natures of different phenomena—and thus wisdom cannot know them;
or is it because one perceives that the various natures and characteristics of all phenomena are not different, and thus wisdom cannot know them?
Because it is obstructed by mountains, ravines, rocky walls, curtains, groves, trees, grasses, and shrubs, as well as by earth, water, fire, and wind, wisdom cannot know it;
because it is at an extremely distant or extremely near location, wisdom cannot know it;
and because of being old or young, or being blind, dark-sighted, or lacking in sensory faculties, wisdom cannot know it.
World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are distinct, and the characteristics of dharmas are distinct—because the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the essence of dharmas are variously different—then wisdom would be unable to know them.
World-Honored One!
If that is so, then that wisdom is not wisdom. Why is this?
"Because one cannot know the actual reality of the preceding objects,
World-Honored One!

If the various essential natures and characteristics of all dharmas— whether their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)— are not seen as distinct, and thus wisdom cannot know them, then such wisdom could not be called 'wisdom'."
For what reason?
Because they are unable to know objects that truly exist.
World-Honored One!
To be able to see an existing object as it truly is is called wisdom (*jñāna*);

if, however, one is unable to know or see it due to mountains, cliffs, stone walls, curtains, trees, forests, grasses, or shrubs; or due to being too far or too near; or due to being old, young, blind, or having impaired faculties, then that wisdom is no wisdom, because although the real object exists, it is not known.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"As for what you have said regarding those who lack wisdom, that meaning is not so. Why is this?"
Because there is true wisdom, Mahāmati,

I do not rely on such a statement of yours as that "objects do not exist and are merely the vision of one's own mind"; rather, I teach that they are not perceived because they are merely one's own mind.

Seeing external objects as being either existent or non-existent, wisdom does not perceive such objective realms. When wisdom does not perceive them, they do not function within the mind; therefore, I say that even the wisdom that enters the three gates of liberation does not perceive them.

Yet, because ordinary beings have engaged in false discrimination since beginningless time, their minds are perfumed by the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and thus they discriminate in this way, seeing the forms and characteristics of external objects as existent or non-existent.

To free them from such deluded minds, I teach that all phenomena are merely the perceptions of one’s own mind; however, because they cling to "self" and "what belongs to self," they are unable to realize that these are nothing but their own mind.

To falsely discriminate between what is cognition and what is its object, and because of this discrimination between cognition and its object, one observes external phenomena and fails to see their existence or non-existence, thereby falling into the view of nihilism.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“There are various objective phenomena That wisdom cannot perceive;
They are neither ignorance nor wisdom— So say those who see falsely.”
To say that all phenomena are immeasurable, such that this wisdom cannot know them;
or that they are obstructed, distant, or near—this is deluded wisdom, not true wisdom.
Those who are old or young, whose faculties are dull, cannot give rise to wisdom.
Yet, if there were actually existing objects, that wisdom would not be true wisdom.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary beings, relying on the afflictions of beginningless conceptual proliferation regarding the body, establish their own dharmas upon a body that is like a phantom dancer. They cling to external objects as seen by their own minds, and they cling to names, phrases, and verbal expressions; thus they are unable to know how to establish the True Dharma, do not cultivate right practice, and remain far removed from the pure dharma that transcends the four propositions.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said: “So it is, so it is, World-Honored One!

Just as the World-Honored One has spoken, may the World-Honored One explain to me the established characteristics of the teachings he has proclaimed, so that I and all other bodhisattvas may, in future ages, skillfully understand the characteristics of establishing the teachings and not be deluded by the false views of externalists, nor by the incorrect views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are two kinds of teachings expounded by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present."
What are these two?
First, the establishment of the characteristics of the teaching;
second, the establishment of the characteristics of reality as it is.
Mahāmati! What is the establishment of the characteristics of preaching the Dharma?
It refers to various merits, sūtras, and upadeśas, wherein one preaches the Dharma according to the faith and inclinations of sentient beings.
Mahāmati! This is called the establishment of the characteristics of preaching the Dharma. Mahāmati!
What is the establishment of the characteristics of phenomena as they truly are (*yathābhūta-dharmalakṣaṇa*)?

It refers to practicing the correct conduct based upon certain phenomena, thereby remaining far removed from the false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) of all phenomena within one's own mind; not falling into the factions of those who hold to positions of identity, difference, both, or neither;
and transcending the mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) to personally realize (*pratyātma-adhigata*) the sphere of activity of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
It is free from views associated with the conjunction of causes and conditions;
it is free from all the false views of external paths;
and it is free from all the views of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Free from the partisan views of existence and non-existence,
Mahāmati! This is called the establishment of the characteristics of dharmas as they truly are.
"Mahāmati! You and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"I establish two dharmas: I teach the Dharma according to reality;
I teach the Dharma by means of names for the sake of those who practice in accordance with reality.
— *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Five: Lokāyata (6). Chapter Five: Lokāyata.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
At one time the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha spoke thus:"

“World-Honored One, if one associates with and makes offerings to those who engage in the various dialectical arguments of the Lokāyata, they will partake of the food of desire and not the food of the Dharma.
World-Honored One!
"Why is it said that the various eloquent discourses of the Lokāyata, which are cultivated, honored, and embraced for the sake of sensory food rather than the food of the Dharma?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The various rhetorical skills of the Lokāyata employ clever phrases to delude the world; they do not speak in accordance with the Dharma, nor do they speak in accordance with the meaning."

However, because they follow the inclinations of ignorant, ordinary worldlings, they speak of conventional matters; though their phrasing and literary expressions are elegant and beautiful, they have lost the correct meaning.
Mahāmati! This is called the fault of the various forms of eloquence and fondness for speech characteristic of the Lokāyata. Mahāmati!

The Lokāyata possesses such eloquence as this, yet it merely attracts worldly, ignorant, and ordinary people; it does not enter into the teaching of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Because they themselves do not realize that all phenomena [are but mind], they fall into the collection of false views of the two extremes. Having lost the right path themselves, they cause others to lose it as well; therefore, they cannot escape the various realms of existence (*gati*).

Because they fail to see that [all is] nothing but their own mind, they conceptually discriminate and cling to external phenomena as having real characteristics; for this reason, they do not transcend false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Mahāmati!

For this reason, I say that although the Lokāyatikas possess various kinds of skillful eloquence and delight in expounding all phenomena, because they have lost the correct principle, they cannot achieve liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress—the entire mass of suffering. This is because, by relying on various names, phrases, and syllables, they use skillful metaphors to delude and mislead people.
"Mahāmati!

Śakra Devendra, who has extensively mastered all treatises and composed his own work on phonology, had a disciple of the Lokāyata school who had attained worldly supernatural powers. This disciple went to the palace of Śakra and, establishing his system of debate, spoke these words: 'Kauśika!'"

"I shall debate with you; if I am defeated, I shall submit to your authority so that all devas and humans may witness it. Let us make this pact: if I defeat you, I shall strike you with my thousand-spoked wheel until you are shattered to pieces; if I am defeated, I shall have my body dismembered limb by limb from head to foot as reparation for you."

Having made this vow, a disciple of the Lokāyata appeared in the form of a dragon and engaged in debate with Śakra Devendra. By means of his own dialectical methods, he was able to defeat him; Śakra Devendra compelled him to submit, whereupon [the disciple] smashed his thousand-spoked wheel chariot in the heavens until it was like fine dust, and then descended to the human realm.
Mahāmati!
The Lokāyata brāhmaṇas employ various such analogies, even manifesting the bodies of animals under various names, to delude the world of devas, humans, and asuras.
Because all sentient beings in the world cling to phenomena that arise and perish—how much more so in the case of humans!

For this reason, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from the Lokāyata Brahmins, for their teachings give rise to a mass of suffering. Therefore, one should not associate with, make offerings to, revere, or seek instruction from the Lokāyata Brahmins.
Mahāmati!

The Dharma taught by the Lokāyata Brahmins merely concerns the objects of perception within the realm of present bodily and mental consciousness; they propound various false doctrines based on worldly designations.
Mahāmati!

The treatise composed by the Lokāyata brāhmaṇa consists of one hundred thousand verses; in future ages and at the end of time, it will be divided into many sections with various different names, because it is produced based on the causal views of one's own mind.
Mahāmati! Among the Lokāyata brahmins, there was no disciple capable of receiving their doctrine; therefore, in later generations, it split into many schools with various different names.
Mahāmati!

Because the various non-Buddhists lack internal realization of reality as it truly is, they rely on various causes and various divergent interpretations; following the fabrications of their own minds, they speak to others while clinging to such things as the cause of Īśvara.
"Mahāmati!

Among the treatises composed by all the non-Buddhists, there is no such teaching; rather, they are merely Lokāyatikas who, through various causal gateways, expound hundreds of thousands of millions of doctrines, yet they do not realize that these are merely Lokāyata."
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If all non-Buddhists speak only of Lokāyata, relying on various worldly names, phrases, and metaphors to cling to [theories of] causes;”
“World-Honored One!

When the sentient beings, devas, and asuras of all lands in the ten directions gather at the place where the Tathāgata resides, the Tathāgata likewise preaches the Dharma using various worldly names, phrases, and parables, yet does not speak of the Dharma realized through the internal wisdom of his own self. If this is so, it is no different from what is taught by all the non-Buddhists.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I do not speak of Lokāyata, nor do I say that all phenomena neither come nor go,
Mahāmati."
I teach that all dharmas neither come nor go.
Mahāmati, what is meant by "coming"?
Mahāmati!
That which is called "coming" is termed "arising and aggregation," because it arises through combination. Mahāmati!
What is called "going"? Mahāmati!
That which is called "going" is termed "extinction."
Mahāmati!
That which I describe as neither going nor coming is called non-arising and non-ceasing.
Mahāmati!
I say that my teaching is not the same as the doctrines of those non-Buddhists. Why is this?
Because I do not cling to the existence or non-existence of external objects, but establish and teach that what is seen is but the manifestation of one's own mind.
Because they do not dwell in two places and do not engage in the conceptualization of the objective realm of various marks;
because they know the manifestations of their own minds as they truly are;
and because they do not give rise to the conceptualized views of their own minds.
Because one who does not discriminate any marks is able to enter the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they are called "liberated. Mahāmati!
I recall that in the past, while I was dwelling in a certain place, a great Brahmin Lokāyata came to where I was and addressed me, saying:
"Gautama!..."
"Is everything created? Mahāmati!
At that time, I replied:
“O Brāhmaṇa! This ‘all is caused by an agent’ is the first Lokāyata.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Gautama! Is everything uncreated?
At that time, I replied:
"O Brahmin! 'Nothing at all is created' is the second Lokāyata.
Likewise, there are those who hold that everything is eternal, everything is impermanent, everything arises, and everything does not arise."
At that time, I replied:
"Brahmin! This is the sixth Lokāyata."
"Mahāmati! Lokāyata further asked me: 'Gautama!'"
Are all things identical? Are all things distinct?
Are all things both? Are all things neither?
All phenomena arise in dependence upon causes, for one observes that they arise from various causes.
"Mahāmati! At that time, I replied: 'Brāhmaṇa!'"
"This is the eleventh Lokāyata. Mahāmati!
He then asked me again:
"Gautama! Are all things indeterminate, or are all things determinate?
Is there a self, or is there no self?"
Is there this world, or is there not this world?
Is there a future life, or is there no future life?
Is there liberation, or is there no liberation?
Is everything empty? Is everything non-empty? Is everything void?
Is it not through the cessation of conditions?
“Is it nirvana, Gautama?
Is it something created, or is it uncreated?”
"Is there an intermediate state (antarābhava), or is there no intermediate state? Mahāmati!
At that time, I replied:
“Brahmin! All such teachings as you have spoken are merely Lokāyata; they are not my teaching, nor is it the Dharma you proclaim, Brahmin.”

I teach that the three realms of existence arise due to the habitual perfuming of afflictions caused by beginningless conceptual proliferation and false discrimination; because one does not realize that these are merely the perceptions of one's own mind’s discrimination, they appear to exist, yet external objects do not exist as they are conceived in the systems of the non-Buddhists.
"Mahāmati! The non-Buddhists say:
'The self, the sense organs, and the objects—through the conjunction of these three—can produce cognition.'"
“O Brahmin! It is not so for me.

I do not speak of a cause, nor do I speak of no-cause. I speak only of the appearances of objects as grasped and grasper arising from the conceptualization of one’s own mind. I say that all phenomena arise through the gathering of conventional causes and conditions; this is not the case for you, O Brahmin, or for other realms, because you have fallen into the view of self.”

"Mahāmati! Nirvāṇa, space, and the cessation of conditions do not constitute three distinct categories; how much less can one speak of them as being created, or as having been created, or as not being created? Mahāmati!"
Furthermore, a Lokāyata Brahmin came and asked me:
"Gautama! Are these various worlds produced by the causes of ignorance, craving, and karma within the three realms of existence, or are they without cause?"
I then replied: "Brahmin!
These two dharmas of the Lokāyata are not my dharma."
The brahmin asked me again:
"Gautama! Do all phenomena fall under their own characteristics or under common characteristics?"
I then replied: "Brahmin!
This is Lokāyata; it is not my Dharma."
“O Brahmin!
Any attachment to external objects by means of mind (citta), intellect (manas), or consciousness (vijñāna) is entirely Lokāyata; it is not my Dharma.
Thus spoke Mahāmati.
The Lokāyata brāhmaṇa again asked me: "Gautama!
Is there perhaps any teaching that is not Lokāyata?"
"Gautama!
All the various names, phrases, causes, and analogies established by the non-Buddhists in their teachings are my own dharma.
At that time, I replied:

“Brahmin! There is a Dharma that is not your Dharma; yet it is not that this is not established, nor is it that various names, phrases, and syllables are not spoken, nor is it that it is not taught in accordance with the meaning and based upon the meaning; yet it is not a Dharma established by the Lokāyata.”

"O Brahmin! There are dharmas that are not of the Lokāyata; for all those dharmas, you and all other outsiders are unable to comprehend them, because you engage in conceptual proliferation through false attachment to external, unreal phenomena."

What is this? It refers to observing the existence and non-existence of the appearances of one's own mind by remaining free from conceptual thought, and thus awakening to them as they truly are. Consequently, no conceptualization arises; because one does not grasp at external objective phenomena, the conceptual mind subsides and abides in its own place within the realm of tranquility.
