This is called that which is not Lokāyata; it is the doctrine of my teaching, not yours.
“Brahmin! One who dwells in his own abode does not give rise to birth or extinction; one who does not give rise to birth or extinction does not give rise to a discriminating mind. Brahmin!”
This is called what is not *lokāyata*. O Brahmin!

To speak briefly, in whatever state consciousness does not function, does not grasp, does not recede, does not seek, does not arise, does not cling, does not delight, does not see, does not behold, does not dwell, and does not touch—this is called "abiding. The names differ, but the meaning is one.
"O Brahmin! To cling to various signs and to have self-identity and attachment toward the various causes—this is the Lokāyata doctrine of the Brahmins, not my teaching."

"Mahāmati! When the Lokāyata Brahmin came to me and asked about such a teaching, I answered that Brahmin as I have just described. At that time, the Brahmin departed in silence, without asking me to establish the true Dharma."
At that time, the Lokāyata brāhmaṇa thought to himself:

"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, is outside my own doctrine and is truly pitiable; he asserts that all phenomena are without cause, without condition, and without the characteristic of arising, claiming instead that one merely perceives phenomena through the conceptualization of one's own mind. If one can awaken to the fact that these are appearances perceived by one's own mind, then the conceptualizing mind will cease."
"Mahāmati! You have now asked me:

For what reason do the various eloquent expositions of the Lokāyata, and those who associate with, make offerings to, and revere such people, result in grasping only the flavor of desire and not the flavor of the Dharma?"
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by the meaning of the term ‘nutriment’?”
"What is meant by the meaning of the Dharma-words?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"Excellent!"
Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!
You are able, for the sake of future sentient beings, to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding these two meanings.
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Indeed, we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"What constitutes food?"

This refers to the taste of food, the taste of touch, the seeking of pleasure, the pursuit of skillful means, flattery, attachment to flavors, and clinging to external objects; such phenomena as these are termed "different in expression but one in meaning," because they do not allow entry into the dharma-gate of the non-dual realm.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, that which is called "nutriment" refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) and the factors of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) based on false views; it does not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. Craving gives rise to existence; such phenomena as these are called "nutriment."
Therefore, I and all the Buddhas declare that those who associate with and make offerings to Lokāyata Brahmins obtain the flavor of food, but do not obtain the flavor of the Dharma.
Mahāmati! What is the flavor of the Dharma?

It refers to being able to know the two kinds of selflessness as they truly are; by perceiving the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena, one does not give rise to the marks of discrimination, because one is able to know the progressively superior wisdom of the various stages as they truly are.

At that time, being able to transcend mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), one enters the stage of receiving the empowerment of the wisdom of all Buddhas. One grasps the ultimate limit of all phrases and, as it truly is, knows the sphere of mastery of all Buddhas; this is called the "flavor of the Dharma" (*dharmarasa*), which does not fall into any false views, conceptual proliferation, discrimination, or the two extremes.
Mahāmati!
The teachings of the non-Buddhists mostly cause sentient beings to fall into the two extremes, rather than causing the wise to fall into the two extremes. Why is this?
Mahāmati!

The various non-Buddhists mostly propound the views of annihilationism and eternalism; because they deny causality, they fall into the view of eternalism, and because they perceive the cessation of causes, they fall into the view of annihilationism.
“Mahāmati!
I teach that seeing things as they truly are is non-attachment to arising and ceasing; therefore, I call this the ‘flavor of the Dharma.
Mahāmati!”
This is what I call the dharma of the flavor of food and the flavor of the Dharma.
Mahāmati! You and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should study this dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“I gather in sentient beings; Relying on the precepts, I subdue all evils;
With wisdom, I extinguish false views, And cause the three gates of liberation to increase.”
The false teachings of the non-Buddhists are all merely worldly treatises;
with their perverted views on cause and effect, they establish doctrines lacking right view.
I establish the system of dharmas, free from the views of false causes.
For the sake of his disciples, he taught that one should transcend worldly dharmas;
that there is only mind and no external phenomena, by means of a mind free from the two extremes;
and that the grasping subject and the grasped object are free from the views of nihilism and eternalism.
Whatever the mind ranges over is entirely mundane discourse;
if one can contemplate one's own mind, one will not see any delusions.
That which comes is seen as arising from causes; that which goes is seen as the cessation of effects.
Knowing going and coming as they truly are, one does not discriminate the false.
Regarding permanence and impermanence, or action and non-action, and such dualistic things;
all such phenomena are merely conventional discourse.
6. Chapter on Nirvāṇa (6). *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Chapter Six: “Nirvāṇa. At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
Regarding what the Buddha has called "nirvāṇa, nirvāṇa," by what dharma is the name "nirvāṇa" established?
Yet, the various non-Buddhists each falsely conceptualize nirvāṇa according to their own views.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
I shall explain this for you:
the various non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize the characteristics of nirvāṇa; yet that which is conceptualized by those non-Buddhists is not true nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"There are certain non-Buddhists who, weary of all sensory objects, perceive the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), and the impermanence of all phenomena. They maintain that the mind and mental factors do not arise before them; because they do not recollect the objects of the past, future, or present pleasures, when the aggregates are exhausted—like the extinguishing of a lamp or the subsiding of various winds—they do not grasp at signs or engage in false conceptualization and discrimination. This is what they call *nirvāṇa*."
Mahāmati!
Those non-Buddhists perceive such phenomena and give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa; it is not because they perceive cessation that it is called nirvāṇa, Mahāmati.
There are some non-Buddhists who claim that moving from one direction to another is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who conceptualize all objects as being like the wind; because they engage in such conceptualization, they call it *nirvāṇa*.
Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who speak thus: "The non-extinction of the state where neither the seer nor the seen is perceived is called nirvāṇa.
Moreover, Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists who speak thus: "Not seeing discrimination, yet seeing the permanent and the impermanent, is called nirvāṇa.
Moreover, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say:

"Discriminative views of the various diverse characteristics are able to give rise to all suffering. Because one perceives within one's own mind the false discrimination of all characteristics and feels fear toward these characteristics, one comes to deeply love and delight in the signless (animitta), giving rise to the notion of nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who perceive all phenomena as having both specific and general characteristics that are neither arising nor ceasing; they conceptually discriminate that the phenomena of the past, future, and present exist, and they designate this as nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who perceive the self, the person, sentient beings, life-span, the life-principle, and all phenomena as being indestructible; they engage in false conceptualization and designate this as "nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who, due to a lack of wisdom, conceptually differentiate the self-nature of what is perceived; they maintain that the transformation of the life-principle (*puruṣa*) and the conceptual differentiation of transformation is called *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who speak thus: "When demerit is exhausted, merit is also exhausted; this is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, [there are others who say:]...
Other non-Buddhists say that because the afflictions are completely exhausted based upon wisdom, it is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, other non-Buddhists speak thus: they perceive that Maheśvara creates sentient beings, and this false discrimination is called nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other outsiders who say that all sentient beings arise through mutual causality and not from any other cause. Like those outsiders who are attached to their views, they lack knowledge and awakening; being deluded, dull-witted, and engaged in false discrimination, they designate this state as "nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
There are other non-Buddhists who claim that the false discrimination regarding the path to realizing the truths is itself called nirvana.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Other non-Buddhists speak thus: they maintain that there is an agent and an object of action which, through their mutual conjunction, are perceived as identical, different, both, or neither; this false discrimination is what they call nirvana.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say that all phenomena arise spontaneously, just as a magician produces various forms and images. Seeing various things such as jewels and thorns arising spontaneously, they engage in false discrimination and designate this state as "nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are other non-Buddhists who say that all phenomena are produced by time; they falsely discriminate that mere awareness of time is what is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,

there are other non-Buddhists who say that seeing things as existent, seeing things as non-existent, and seeing things as both existent and non-existent— such conceptual discrimination is called nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, other proponents of the wisdom of establishing dharmas say: "For one who sees according to reality, there is only what belongs to one's own mind;
one does not grasp at external objects, remains free from the four kinds of dharmas, and perceives all dharmas as they abide in their respective natures."

Not perceiving the marks of one's own mental discrimination, not falling into the two extremes, and not seeing the objective realms of the grasper and the grasped, one sees that all worldly establishments are unreal and delusive regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
By not grasping at any phenomena, this is termed "reality. Through the realization of the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) within one's own body, one knows things as they truly are.

The two kinds of selflessness, being free from the stains of the two kinds of afflictions, consist in the pure knowledge of the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*) as they truly are;

entering the stage of the Tathāgata and attaining the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), one becomes far removed from the conceptual discriminations of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Such a vision is called *nirvāṇa*.
Mahāmati!

Furthermore, there are various non-Buddhists who, with their false views and discursive thoughts, propound various treatises that do not accord with the true Dharma as it really is; these are shunned and censured by the wise.
Mahāmati!
Such non-Buddhists as these all fall into the false discrimination of the two extremes and lack true nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!
All non-Buddhists thus falsely discriminate regarding nirvana, yet no one dwells in the world and no one enters nirvana. Why is this?

Because all non-Buddhists rely on the treatises of their own minds and falsely discriminate, lacking knowledge as it truly is; just as there are no such dharmas according to the discriminations of those non-Buddhists' own minds, so too there is no such nirvana for these non-Buddhists, characterized by coming, going, or movement.
"Mahāmati!
You and all other bodhisattvas should remain far removed from the false nirvana of all non-Buddhists.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists arise from various conceptual discriminations;
they all originate from the manifestations of the mind and lack the skillful means for liberation.
Not being free from the bonds and that which binds, they remain far removed from all skillful means."
They conceive the notion of liberation for themselves, yet in reality there is no liberation.
The non-Buddhists establish their own doctrines, and each of their various wisdoms grasps them differently;
they all lack liberation, being merely the deluded conceptualizations of ignorance.
All deluded non-Buddhists falsely perceive agent and action;
therefore, they have no liberation, for they speak of existence and non-existence.
Ordinary people delight in conceptual proliferation and do not hear the wisdom of reality.
Language is the root of the three realms; through knowledge of reality as it is, suffering is extinguished.
Like an image in a mirror, though seen, it does not exist;
the mind, like a mirror, sees through habitual tendencies, yet ordinary beings speak of duality.
Not knowing that what is seen is but mind, one thus discriminates between two;
by knowing according to reality that it is only mind, discrimination does not arise.
Mind is called "the manifold," for it is free from both the seer and the seen.
In the appearance of what is seen, there is nothing to be seen; ordinary people engage in false discrimination.
The three realms of existence are merely deluded thoughts; external objects do not truly exist.
Through deluded thoughts they perceive various things, yet ordinary people cannot understand this.
The sūtras explain through various distinctions, Using manifold and diverse names;
Yet apart from the dharma that transcends speech, Nothing is taught, for nothing can be apprehended.
Chapter Seven: The Dharma-body (6) Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Seven: The Dharma-body At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, will expound the Dharma of internal realization personally attained by yourself. By what Dharma is the so-called Dharmakāya named?”
“I and all the bodhisattvas well understand the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; both ourselves and others have entered into it beyond doubt.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent!”
Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!
Whatever you have doubts about, ask as you wish; I shall analyze it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, conditioned or unconditioned?”
Is this the cause or the effect?
Is it the seer or the seen?
Is it the speaker or that which can be spoken?
"Is this wisdom itself, or is it that which is awakened by wisdom?
Regarding such phrases as these, is the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body different [from them], or is it not different?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“The characteristics of the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—such phrases as these—are neither conditioned phenomena nor unconditioned phenomena, neither cause nor fruit.”
Why is this? Because both extremes involve faults, Mahāmati!

If one says that the Tathāgata is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma), then he would be impermanent; if he were impermanent, then all conditioned phenomena would be the Tathāgata. Yet the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha does not permit this doctrine.
Mahāmati!
If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were not a product of conditioning, it would be bodiless; to say that there is the cultivation of immeasurable merit and all practices would then be false.
Mahāmati!
If it were not an agent, it would be equivalent to a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman, because it would lack the cause of action and would likewise lack a body.
Mahāmati!
If a phenomenon is neither cause nor effect, neither existent nor non-existent, yet its essential nature is free from these four characteristics,
Mahāmati, those four types of phenomena are termed worldly discourse.
Mahāmati!
If a dharma is devoid of these four kinds of dharmas, that dharma exists only as a name, like the son of a barren woman.
Mahāmati!

The "son of a barren woman" and such are merely names and phrases; they are said to be identical to the four propositions. If one falls into these four propositions, the wise do not accept them. The wise should understand that all such inquiries regarding the Tathāgata’s words are of this nature.
The Buddha again addressed Mahāmati:
"I have taught that all dharmas are without self; you should listen attentively to the meaning of 'no-self.
As for 'no-self,' it means that within the internal body there is no self; therefore, it is called 'no-self.'"
Mahāmati! All dharmas exist in their own nature but do not exist in the nature of others, just as it is with oxen and horses. Mahāmati!
For example, a cow's body is not a horse's body, and a horse is likewise not a cow; therefore, one cannot say it exists or does not exist, yet is its own nature not non-existent?

Mahāmati! All dharmas are likewise thus: they do not lack intrinsic characteristics, yet they possess no self-nature. Foolish ordinary beings do not understand that all dharmas lack a self-nature; this is due to their discriminative minds, not because of non-discriminative minds.
Mahāmati!
Just as all phenomena are empty and all phenomena are unarisen, so too are all phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics.
Mahāmati!
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is likewise: within the five aggregates (skandhas), it is neither identical nor different. Mahāmati!
If the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata were identical with the five aggregates, it would be impermanent, because the five aggregates are conditioned phenomena.
Mahāmati!

If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were different from the five aggregates (skandhas), there would be two distinct dharmas with dissimilar essential natures and characteristics. It would be like the two horns of an ox, which are similar and not different, yet appear to have separate entities and seem different in their length.
Mahāmati!

If it were as you say, then all these dharmas would have no distinguishing marks, yet they do possess distinguishing marks. For example, the left horn of an ox is different from the right horn, and the right horn is different from the left; likewise, long and short are distinct in their mutual dependence, just as the various colors and forms differ from one another.

Mahāmati! Thus, the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body cannot be said to be identical to or different from the five aggregates; it cannot be said to be identical to or different from liberation; and it cannot be said to be identical to or different from nirvāṇa. It is by depending upon such liberation that it is designated as the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Mahāmati!

If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were different from liberation, it would be like material form and thus impermanent. If the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body were not different from liberation, there would be no distinction between the realizer and the realized.
Mahāmati! However, the practitioner perceives both the means of realization and that which is realized; therefore, they are not one. Mahāmati!
Thus one knows that the knowable object is neither identical nor different [from the knower]. Mahāmati!

If a dharma is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither cause nor effect, neither conditioned nor unconditioned, neither awakened nor non-awakened, neither the seer nor the seen, neither apart from the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana) nor identical with the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; if it is neither name nor object, neither one nor different, neither both nor not both, neither continuous nor non-continuous, transcending all dharmas—if, by transcending all dharmas, there is only its name, and if that dharma does not arise because it is merely a name, then because it does not arise, that dharma does not cease; and because it does not cease, that dharma is equal to space.
Mahāmati!
Space is neither cause nor effect. If a dharma is neither cause nor effect, that dharma is beyond investigation.
That which is beyond investigation transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
That which transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, this is the characteristic of the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, because it transcends the spheres of all the sense faculties.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Detached from all phenomena and the sense faculties, Neither fruit nor cause;
Already detached from the awakening and the awakened, Detached from the seer and the seen."
Regarding all conditions and the five aggregates, the Buddha has no dharma to be seen;
if there is no dharma to be seen, how can one make distinctions?
It is neither created nor uncreated, neither cause nor effect.
Neither the aggregates nor apart from the aggregates, nor does it exist elsewhere.
What kind of mind could conceptualize it?
Conceptualization cannot perceive it.
Those phenomena are not non-existent; the nature of all phenomena is simply thus.
One speaks of "non-existence" because they previously existed, and one speaks of "existence" because they previously did not exist.
Therefore, one does not say they are non-existent, nor can one say they are existent.
Deluded by self and non-self, they cling merely to sounds;
falling into these two extremes, they falsely speak of destroying the world.
Free from all faults, one is then able to see my Dharma.
"This is called right view; it does not slander the Buddhas.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me; I pray that the Sugata will explain this for me: how it is that the Tathāgata has stated in various places that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.
The World-Honored One further said that "neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body; therefore, it is called neither arising nor ceasing.
"World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata speaks of 'neither arising nor ceasing,' does he mean that because there is no dharma, it is called neither arising nor ceasing?"
Is it that "neither arising nor ceasing" is an alternative name for the Tathāgata?
For the Buddha, the Tathāgata, has constantly taught that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing, because they are free from the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence.
World-Honored One!

If all dharmas are non-arising, then one cannot speak of "all dharmas," because all dharmas are non-arising. If there is some other dharma upon which this name depends, World-Honored One, you should explain it to me.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a non-entity, nor is it the case that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing. One cannot say it exists by depending on causes and conditions, nor is it a false teaching to say it is neither arising nor ceasing."
Mahāmati!

I have always said that what is called "neither arising nor ceasing" refers to the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*). Because the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not within the realm of non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas, it is likewise not within the realm of bodhisattvas dwelling on the [first] seven stages.
"Mahāmati!
What I call 'neither arising nor ceasing' is simply another name for the Tathāgata,
Mahāmati!"

For example, Śakra Devānām Indra, King Śakra, Purandara, hand-claws, body, earth, *bumi*, space, and non-obstruction—such various names differ in designation but are one in meaning. One does not rely on these many names to claim that there are multiple entities such as Śakra and so forth.
Mahāmati! I am also like this:
within the Sahā world, there are three hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya names; although ordinary people speak of them, they do not know that these are alternative names for the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati! There are some sentient beings who know the Tathāgata as such; some know him as the Sovereign (Īśvara); some know him as the Omniscient One (Sarvajña);
some know him as the Savior of the World; some know him as the Guide; and some know him as the General.
Some know him as the Victorious One; some know him as the Sublime One; some know him as the World-Honored One;
some know him as the Buddha; some know him as the Bull-King; some know him as the Lion; some know him as the Rishi;
some know him as Brahmā; some know him as Nārāyaṇa; some know him as the Conqueror; and some...
Among those who know Kapila, there are some who know the Ultimate, some who know Ariṣṭanemi,
some who know the Moon, some who know the Sun, some who know Varuṇa, some who know Vyāsa,
some who know Śakra, some who know Bala, and some who know the Ocean.
There are those who know non-arising; there are those who know non-extinction; there are those who know emptiness; there are those who know *tathatā*;
there are those who know the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); there are those who know *nirvāṇa*; there are those who know the *dharmadhātu*;
there are those who know the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); there are those who know permanence; and there are those who know equality. There are...
Regarding the knowledge of non-duality: there is the knowledge of signlessness, the knowledge of conditions, the knowledge of the Buddha-body,
the knowledge of causes, the knowledge of liberation, the knowledge of the Path, the knowledge of the true truths,
the knowledge of omniscience, and the knowledge of the mind-made body.
Mahāmati! Such various names as these—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—are designated by the Tathāgatas in the Sahā world and in other worlds;
among these three hundred thousand asaṃkhyeya names, there is neither increase nor decrease.
All beings know this: like the moon in water, it neither enters nor exits;

yet ordinary people do not perceive or understand it, thereby falling into the continuity of the two extremes. Nevertheless, they all revere and make offerings to me, yet they do not skillfully comprehend the meaning of names and phrases;
grasping at marks of differentiation, they are unable to know themselves and remain attached.
Because of names, there is false conceptualization; that which is neither born nor extinguished is called "non-existent.

Yet they do not know that these are the distinct designations for the Tathāgata—just as with Indra, Śakra, King, or Purandara—and because they cannot determine the relationship between names and reality, they merely follow along with those names.
The grasping of dharmas through sounds is likewise so.
Mahāmati, in future ages foolish ordinary people will say such things as: "As is the name, so is the meaning," being unable to understand that different names may have the same meaning.
Why is this? Because meaning has no essential nature or characteristics.
Furthermore, it is said that meaning does not differ from names and sounds; names and sounds are themselves the meaning.
Why is this? Because they do not understand the essential nature and characteristics of names. Mahāmati!
Those deluded people do not understand that sounds arise and perish immediately, whereas their meaning does not arise or perish. Mahāmati!

The nature of sound falls within the realm of names and designations, but meaning does not fall within the realm of names and designations, because it is free from existence and non-existence, and because it is without arising and without essence.
Mahāmati!
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he speaks based on his own voice; because he does not perceive that syllables exist as either being or non-being, he does not cling to names and words.
Mahāmati!
If a person speaks while clinging to names and words, that person is not called one who skillfully teaches the Dharma.
Why is this? Because the Dharma is devoid of names.
Mahāmati!
For this reason, I have stated in my sūtras that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not utter so much as a single syllable nor indicate a single name. Why is this?
All dharmas are without letters; they rely on meaning and are not expressed through speech, for they are spoken of only by means of conceptual discrimination. Mahāmati!
If one were not to teach the Dharma, the wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas would be severed and extinguished.
When the Wheel of Dharma has ceased, there are likewise no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas;
and if there are no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas, for what kind of person, what kind of dharma, or for what purpose would one preach?
Mahāmati!
For this reason, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not become attached to words and names.
Mahāmati!

Because names, phrases, and sentences are not fixed dharmas, they are spoken in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach all dharmas according to the faith of sentient beings in order to cause them to distance themselves from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). They do not speak of establishing dharmas through their own internal realization of noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), for they are able to know all dharmas as they truly are—namely, their quiescent nature. Seeing only the dharmas known by the awakening of one's own mind, and being free from the marks of dualistic mental discrimination, they do not speak in such a manner.
Mahāmati!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the meaning and not on the words. If good sons or good daughters follow the literal expression of the text, they fall into false views; they ruin themselves by losing sight of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), and they likewise ruin others by preventing them from realizing it.
Mahāmati!
The various non-Buddhists each rely on their own treatises to express divergent views. Mahāmati!
You should thoroughly understand the characteristics of all stages (*bhūmi*), and thoroughly understand eloquence in speech, literary style, and phrasing;

having thoroughly understood the characteristics of all stages, you should advance to acquire the eloquence of names and phrases, and thoroughly understand the characteristics of the correspondence between the meanings of all phenomena.
At that time, one’s own person experiences the feeling of bliss within the joy of the signless dharma, abiding in the Great Vehicle so as to cause sentient beings to know it.
Mahāmati! To take up the Great Vehicle is precisely to embrace all Buddhas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas.
To embrace the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of all buddhas is to embrace all sentient beings;
to embrace all sentient beings is to embrace the sublime treasury of the Dharma;
and to embrace the treasury of the Dharma is to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed.
"To not sever the lineage of the Buddhas" means not severing all superior and sublime places of birth;

because Bodhisattvas and others vow to be born in those superior places, they establish all sentient beings within the Mahāyāna Dharma, and through the ten powers of mastery, they are able to manifest in accordance with the forms, colors, and dispositions of sentient beings to preach the Dharma as it truly is.
Mahāmati! What is the dharma as it truly is?
The dharma as it truly is is that which is neither different nor distinct, neither grasped nor abandoned, and free from all conceptual proliferation; this is called the dharma as it truly is.
“Mahāmati!
Sons and daughters of good family must not cling to words or sounds, because all dharmas are devoid of words.
Mahāmati!”

It is like a person who, in order to point out an object to someone else, uses a finger to indicate it; yet that foolish person clings to the finger itself and does not grasp the object indicated by the finger.

Mahāmati! Foolish ordinary beings are just like this: having heard sounds, they cling to the finger of names and words; thus, until the end of their lives, they are unable to abandon the finger of letters to grasp the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Mahāmati! It is like grain, which is called the food of ordinary people; it cannot be eaten unless it has been pounded and winnowed. If there were someone who had not prepared it as food, they would be called insane; it must necessarily undergo a sequence of steps until it is winnowed and cooked before it can become edible.
Mahāmati!
Non-arising and non-ceasing are likewise so; those who do not cultivate skillful wisdom and expedient means will not attain the fully adorned Dharma-body.
Mahāmati!

Those who cling to names and words, claiming to have attained the meaning, are like those foolish people who do not know how to husk or grind; they consume the grain of mere words but fail to obtain the nourishment of the meaning. For this reason, you should study the meaning and not be attached to the words.
Mahāmati!

That which is called "meaning" (artha) is named nirvāṇa; that which is called "names" (nāman) refers to the conceptualization of marks (lakṣaṇa-vikalpa) that binds one to birth and gives rise to worldly understanding. Mahāmati!
Meaning is obtained from those who have heard much. Mahāmati,
that which is called "having heard much" refers to skill in the means of meaning, not skill in the means of sound.
Mahāmati!

As for the skillful means regarding meaning, it is free from all the heterodox teachings of external paths and is not mixed with them. One who speaks in this manner does not fall into the heterodox dharmas themselves, nor do they cause others to fall into the dharmas of external paths.
Mahāmati! This is called the expedient means of the learned that possesses meaning. Mahāmati!

Those who wish to attain the true meaning should draw near to those who are learned and wise, honoring and revering them; those who are attached to mere names should distance themselves from such people and not draw near to them.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, empowered by the Buddhas, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
It is not considered extraordinary for the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, to teach that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished."
Why is this? All non-Buddhists also teach that all causes are neither produced nor extinguished;
likewise, the Tathāgata also teaches that space, cessation not through deliberation, and the realm of nirvāṇa are neither produced nor extinguished.
World-Honored One!
The various non-Buddhists also say that all sentient beings arise based on causes and conditions;
the Tathāgata likewise says that the various worlds arise from the causes and conditions of ignorance, craving, karma, and discrimination.

If that were so, the Tathāgata also speaks of the names and characteristics of causes and conditions as being distinct, asserting that all phenomena arise based on external causes and conditions; yet non-Buddhists also assert that all phenomena arise based on external causes and conditions. Therefore, there would be no difference between the Tathāgata’s teaching and that of the non-Buddhists.
“World-Honored One!

The non-Buddhists, based on atoms, the Primal Lord (Iśvara), Maheśvara, Brahmā, and so forth—relying on these nine external causes and conditions—proclaim that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished.

The Tathāgata also says that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended; this is because the four great elements do not perish, and their own characteristics are neither born nor extinguished.”

Although the Buddha-Tathāgata provides various different explanations, they do not diverge from what is taught by the non-Buddhists; for the non-Buddhists also maintain that the great elements do not exist apart from the essence of the great elements.
World-Honored One!
The various non-Buddhists differentiate the great elements; the Tathāgata likewise differentiates the great elements.
World-Honored One!

For this reason, that which the Tathāgata has taught does not differ from that of the non-Buddhists; if it were different, the Tathāgata should have explained the characteristics of their difference, and if there were such differing characteristics, one would know that it differs from what the non-Buddhists teach.
World-Honored One!

If the Buddha-Tathāgata did not proclaim the marks of excellence within his own Dharma, then the various non-Buddhist outsiders would also be Buddhas, for they too speak of all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing. Yet the Tathāgata has always said that it is impossible for multiple Buddhas to appear simultaneously within a single world-system.
As previously stated, there ought to be many Buddhas in a single world-system.
Why is this? Because the causes for their existence and non-existence have been explained as being without distinction.
"What the Buddha has spoken is without falsehood; why then, World-Honored One, do you not explain the superior characteristics within your own Dharma?
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati, saying: "Mahāmati!"

The teaching I have expounded regarding non-arising and non-ceasing is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the non-Buddhists, nor is it the same as their doctrine of non-arising impermanence. Why is this?
Mahāmati!

The various non-Buddhists claim that there is a real existence with an intrinsic nature that is unarisen and immutable; I do not fall into such partisan positions regarding existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati!

I teach that which is free from existence and non-existence, free from the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent; one perceives all various forms and images as being like illusions and dreams, and for this reason, one cannot speak of them as being either existent or non-existent.
Mahāmati! Why can it not be said that they are non-existent?
It is because the essential nature and characteristics of form are subject to being seen or not seen, and being grasped or not grasped.
Mahāmati!
For this reason, I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent.
Mahāmati!

Because they do not realize that these are merely views arising from the discrimination of one's own mind, and that all phenomena in the world are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, ordinary people give rise to such discriminations; is this not the case for the noble ones?
Mahāmati!

Those whose minds are deluded and who discriminate unreal objects are like ordinary people who see a city of Gandharvas or various illusory persons, elephants, and horses created by a magician; seeing them entering and exiting, they falsely discriminate and say, "They enter in such and such a way, and they exit in such and such a way."

Mahāmati! Yet in that true state, there is no one who enters or exits; it is merely the delusive discrimination of what is seen by one's own mind. The same applies to the phenomena of arising and non-arising.
Mahāmati!
Yet in that reality, these conditioned and unconditioned phenomena do not exist; they are like the illusory feats produced by a magician, while the magician himself neither arises nor ceases.
Mahāmati!

The existence or non-existence of all phenomena is likewise purposeless, for they are free from arising and ceasing. It is only ordinary beings who, fallen into perverted minds, discriminate between arising and ceasing; this is not said of the noble ones.

Mahāmati! As for inversion, it is like the mind’s discrimination that thinks of a phenomenon as being "thus and thus" while that phenomenon is not actually "thus and thus. Furthermore, inverted discrimination is not merely the attachment to phenomena as being either existent or non-existent; rather, it is because one does not see tranquility. Those who do not see tranquility cannot distance themselves from false conceptualization.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
Seeing tranquility is called the supreme characteristic; seeing various characteristics is not called the supreme characteristic, because it cannot sever the characteristics that cause birth.
Mahāmati!
That which is called "signlessness" is the distancing from all conceptualizing minds; that which is without arising and without signs is what I have taught as nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!

What is called *nirvāṇa* refers to seeing all dharmas as they truly abide; it is the distancing from the mind and mental factors of discrimination, practicing according to reality through successive stages, and that which is realized within one's own inner body by noble wisdom. It is this that I call *nirvāṇa*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"To block the arising of all phenomena, I establish the dharma of non-arising;
I teach that dharmas have no cause, Yet ordinary people cannot know it."
I teach that phenomena are without cause, yet ordinary beings do not understand.
All phenomena are unarisen, nor can it be said that they are non-existent;
like gandharvas’ cities, illusions, and dreams, all phenomena exist without a cause.
All phenomena are empty and signless; how could I explain them to you?
Apart from all conditions of combination, wisdom cannot perceive them.
Because emptiness is fundamentally unarisen, it is therefore said to have no intrinsic nature.
When each and every condition is assembled, the object seen cannot be found.
This is not what is perceived by non-Buddhists;
even when conditions assemble, nothing can be apprehended—like a dream, an illusion, the hair-tufts of a person with ophthalmia, a gandharva-city, or a mirage.
To see falsely without cause—mundane affairs are likewise so;
by subduing the doctrine of no-cause, one can establish the meaning of non-arising.
One who can establish non-arising ensures that my Dharma shall not perish or be destroyed.
When the treatises on the absence of causes are taught, the non-Buddhists give rise to alarm and fear.
How? By what means? Who? For what reason? And where?
The arising of all phenomena is without cause; it is neither caused nor uncaused.
If the wise can see this, they can leave behind the views of arising and ceasing.
Since there is no phenomenon that arises or does not arise, this is the characteristic of being without causal conditions.
If you speak of the names of dharmas for me as being without meaning,
then neither do dharmas arise from existence or non-existence, nor do they depend upon causes and conditions.
It is not that a dharma exists prior to its name, nor is it called "not empty" merely by way of designation.
This is not the domain of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths.
Abiding in the seventh stage, where the characteristic of arising is absent,
one transcends all dharmas of causes and conditions in order to negate those very causes and conditions.
I teach the establishment of Mind-only; I call this "non-arising.
All phenomena lack causes and conditions, being free from conceptualization and the conceptualized.
Free from the factions of existence and non-existence, I call this "non-arising."
The mind is detached from the phenomena of views, And detached from the essence of the two dharmas.
The transformation of the body and its support, along with their characteristics— I call this "non-arising.
Externally, there is neither reality nor unreality, Nor is it anything grasped by the mind.
Like an illusion, a dream, or the optical illusion of falling hairs;
like a gandharva-city or a mirage—being free from all views is called the characteristic of non-arising.
One should understand that such dharmas as emptiness are expressed through these various phrases.
There is neither arising nor emptiness of emptiness, yet there is no absence of the emptiness of arising.
Through the conjunction of various causes and conditions, there is arising and there is ceasing;
apart from all causes and conditions, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Apart from causes and conditions there are no phenomena; apart from their conjunction nothing is obtained.
The non-Buddhists engage in false discrimination, seeing things as either identical or different.
Phenomena are neither born from existence nor non-existence; neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended.
It is only through the conjunction of all dharmas that birth and cessation are perceived.
There are merely names, which form a continuous chain;
apart from that causal chain, the phenomenon of birth cannot be found.
Arising phenomena do not see arising; thus one is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists.
I speak of the chain of dependent origination, which ordinary people do not understand.
Apart from this chain of dependent origination, there is no other distinct phenomenon.
This would mean there is no cause or condition, and it would destroy the meaning of the chain of dependent origination.
Just as a lamp reveals various forms, so too does the chain of links give rise to things;
yet if this were so, there would be the arising of phenomena independently of the chain of links.
The dharmas that arise have no inherent substance; their self-nature is like empty space.
To seek dharmas apart from the chain of causes and conditions—such fools have no true knowledge.
Furthermore, there is another aspect of non-arising: the dharma attained by the sages.
That which arises is non-arising; this is the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
If one sees all worlds, one sees them as a chain of links;
since everything is a chain of links, the mind thereby attains concentration.
Ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth—these constitute the internal chain;
the axle, the clay lump, and the wheel are the great chain of seeds.
If there were any other phenomena that arose from causes and conditions, [they too would be included therein].
Those who are devoid of the meaning of the chain of dependent origination do not abide in the holy teaching.
If the produced phenomena were non-existent, for whom would there be a chain?
Because they arise in mutual succession, this is called the meaning of causal conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Ordinary beings give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the phenomena of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion;
yet apart from these fetters, no other phenomenon exists. Therefore, it is said that they have no intrinsic nature.
Just as a physician treats various illnesses by prescribing remedies according to the specific disease, so too does the Buddha teach the Dharma.
Yet the teaching is without distinction; because illnesses differ, the remedies vary.
I contemplate all sentient beings, who are defiled by the faults of afflictions;
knowing the differences in their faculties and strengths, I preach according to what they are able to receive.
My Dharma is without differentiation; it is taught according to the differences in faculties and ailments.
My vehicle is the Single Vehicle of the Buddha; it is the purity of the Eightfold Noble Path.
— *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: On Impermanence (7). Chapter Eight: On Impermanence.
At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
regarding what the World-Honored One calls 'impermanence,' all non-Buddhists also speak of impermanence."
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, relying upon names, words, and phrases, has spoken these words: ‘All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing.
World-Honored One!”
"Is this dharma real, or is it false?
World-Honored One!"
"Furthermore, how many kinds of impermanence are there?
The Buddha addressed the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!
All the non-Buddhists, through their false conceptualizations, speak of eight kinds of impermanence.
What are the eight?
First, to initiate an action and yet not perform it is called impermanence.
What is meant by "initiating"?
First, that which is called the arising of phenomena and non-arising phenomena, and of permanent phenomena and impermanent phenomena, is termed "arising impermanence";
second, the cessation of form and characteristics is termed "impermanence";
third, form and so forth are themselves impermanent.

Fourth, because form undergoes transformation, there is the impermanence of diversity; all phenomena continue in succession and cease spontaneously, like the transformation of milk into curd. Since one perceives neither their transformation nor their cessation within all phenomena, this is called impermanence.
Fifth, there are further non-Buddhists who, because things do not exist, call it impermanence.

Sixth, both existent and non-existent phenomena are entirely impermanent; because all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, they are called impermanent, and because impermanent factors are conjoined therein, they are therefore impermanent.

Seventh, there are yet other non-Buddhists who claim that "non-eternal" means that what was originally non-existent later comes to exist; they say that because the characteristics produced by the great elements perish, and because one does not perceive their arising apart from a continuous substance, it is called "non-eternal.

Eighth, there is "non-arising non-eternality," which means it is non-eternal because it is not permanent; they observe that all phenomena have neither arising nor non-arising, and even when examining them down to the subtlest atom, no arising of phenomena is perceived, hence they speak of "non-arising," for all phenomena do not arise.

Mahāmati! This is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence. However, the various non-Buddhists do not understand why those dharmas do not arise; therefore, they conceptually construct that all dharmas are unarisen and thus speak of impermanence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

The non-Buddhists discriminate regarding the dharma of impermanence, asserting that things exist. Those non-Buddhists, through the false discrimination of their own minds, conceive of impermanence as both permanent and impermanent, because they maintain that things exist.
Why is this? Because its own essence is not extinguished. That which is "not extinguished in its own essence" means that the essence of impermanence is eternally non-extinguished. Mahāmati!
If impermanent phenomena were substantial entities, they would give rise to all phenomena, because that impermanence could act as their cause. Mahāmati!
If all phenomena are not apart from impermanence, then the existence and non-existence of all phenomena should be perceived [simultaneously].

Why is this? Just as a staff, wood, tiles, or stones can destroy whatever is destructible and thus completely shatter them, because one perceives those various and diverse characteristics, impermanence is therefore not a cause for any phenomenon among all dharmas; it is neither a cause nor a result.
Mahāmati! Furthermore, there are other faults: because that cause and effect would be indistinguishable;
yet one could not say "this is impermanent" while "that is the effect," because cause and effect must be distinguishable.
One must not say that all phenomena are eternal, because all phenomena are without cause. Mahāmati!
All phenomena do have causes, yet ordinary people neither perceive nor understand this, for a dissimilar cause cannot produce a dissimilar effect.

Mahāmati! If a different cause could produce a different effect, then from the difference of the cause, all phenomena (*dharmas*) should be produced. If that were so, there would be yet another fault: one would perceive a distinction [in the effects] even when the causes are not distinct.
Mahāmati! If impermanence were a substantial entity, it would be identical to the effect produced by its cause;

furthermore, there would be another fault: within a single dharma, all dharmas would be fully present, because they would be identical to all effects, as there would be no distinction between the characteristics of cause, effect, and karma.
Furthermore, there is another fault: impermanence itself would possess the nature of impermanence, because impermanence has the essence of impermanence.
Furthermore, there is another fault: all phenomena would have to be permanent because they are impermanent.
Furthermore, there is another fault: if impermanence were identical to all phenomena, it would fall under the category of phenomena belonging to the three periods of time.
Mahāmati! Because past form is identical to impermanence, it has already ceased; because future dharmas have not yet arisen and are identical to the impermanence of form, they do not arise;

and because present existing dharmas are not separate from form—since form possesses the characteristics of those great elements (*mahābhūta*) and depends upon the five great elements and their objects—they do not cease, for they are mutually inseparable.

Mahāmati! All non-Buddhists do not admit the cessation of the great elements; they maintain that the three realms depend upon the great elements or upon atoms and the like. Therefore, based on those doctrines, they speak of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Mahāmati! Apart from these dharmas, there are no other dharmas such as the four great elements or the sense-objects. Because those non-Buddhists falsely discriminate that there is impermanence existing apart from all dharmas, they claim that the great elements are neither produced nor destroyed, asserting that their intrinsic nature and characteristics are eternally indestructible. Therefore, they define impermanence as the non-occurrence of the activity of origination during the interval between [origination and destruction].

The primary elements further give rise to the primary elements; there is no arising or ceasing of those various specific and general characteristics, because one perceives that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and thus gives rise to the wisdom of impermanence regarding them.
Mahāmati! What is called the impermanence of the cessation of form?

It refers to the forms of the primary elements and their derivatives; seeing these forms as distinct from one another—like long and short—and perceiving the transformation of the forms of the great elements even though the great elements themselves do not perish, such a person falls into the system of the Sāṃkhyas.

Mahāmati! Furthermore, regarding the impermanence of form and appearance: there are those who claim that it is "form" itself that is called impermanent; such people perceive only the impermanence of form and appearance, yet they do not recognize that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are themselves impermanent phenomena.
If the great elements were impermanent, then nothing in all the worlds could be discussed or described in terms of worldly affairs.

If one discusses worldly affairs, one falls into the faction of the Lokāyata heresy, for while asserting that all phenomena are merely names, one nevertheless perceives the self-nature and characteristics of those phenomena.

Mahāmati! As for impermanence as transformation, it refers to seeing the various different characteristics of all forms; it is not that the great elements themselves undergo transformation. For example, when gold is fashioned into ornaments, although the form changes, the essence of the gold does not differ; the transformation of other phenomena is likewise.
Mahāmati!

In this way, the false discrimination of the non-Buddhists views phenomena as impermanent; yet they hold that fire does not burn the primary elements, nor does it burn their own essence, because those primary elements possess distinct essential natures.
“Mahāmati!
The various non-Buddhists say that if fire were able to burn the great elements, then those great elements would be annihilated;
therefore, they do not burn them. Mahāmati!”
I teach that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their objects are neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? Because I do not say that external objects exist;

rather, I teach that the three realms are nothing but one's own mind. I do not say that various marks (*nimitta*) exist as such. Therefore, I speak of them as neither arising nor ceasing, being merely the conjunction of the causes and conditions of the four great elements. Neither the great elements nor their objects are real dharmas. Through a deluded mind, one discriminates between the two kinds of dharmas—the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). By truly knowing these two kinds of discrimination, one departs from the views of existence and non-existence regarding external objects. It is only the activity of one's own mind's discrimination that is called "arising," yet this activity does not arise, because one has departed from the discriminating mind of existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati! Why is it neither eternal nor non-eternal?
Because there exist mundane and supramundane dharmas of the highest order, it cannot be said that they are eternal.
Why is it not impermanent?
Because one is able to realize that these are merely the perceptions of one's own mind’s conceptualization, it is therefore not impermanent.

Yet, the various non-Buddhists fall into false views by clinging to the two extremes; they do not understand that these are the deluded conceptualizations of their own minds, nor do they realize that for the noble ones, there is no such conceptualization of impermanence.
Mahāmati! All dharmas are comprised of three kinds. What are these three?

First, the characteristics of worldly dharmas; second, the characteristics of supramundane dharmas; and third, the characteristics of the most excellent supramundane dharmas. These are taught through various verbal expressions, yet ordinary people do not perceive or understand them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Avoiding the notion of initial creation, As well as the distinction of forms;
To call impermanence a 'real entity'— This is the false discrimination of the non-Buddhists."
All phenomena have no cessation; the great elements abide in their own nature.
Falling into various views, the non-Buddhists proclaim impermanence.
Those non-Buddhists also claim that all phenomena are neither born nor do they cease.
If the great elements were eternal by nature, what dharma could be impermanent?
All worlds are but mind, yet the mind perceives two objects:
the grasped and the grasper; the dharmas of "I" and "mine" do not exist.
"The phenomena of the three realms, whether superior or inferior, I declare to be all mind;
apart from these mental phenomena, nothing else exists that can be apprehended.
Chapter Nine: Entering the Way (7) The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Nine: Entering the Way At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

We pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the sequential characteristics of how all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas enter the samādhi of cessation. If I and all other bodhisattvas can skillfully understand the sequential characteristics of entering the samādhi of cessation, we shall not fall into the bliss of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha samādhis and samāpattis of cessation, nor shall we fall into the delusive dharmas of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists.”
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively!
Listen attentively!
"I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"So be it; we shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"From the first stage up to the sixth stage, Bodhisattvas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas likewise enter the meditative absorption of cessation."
Mahāmati!

All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, throughout the seven stages, enter the samādhi of cessation in every thought-moment, because all Bodhisattvas are fully able to remain far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas.

Mahāmati! Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are unable to enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) at every moment of thought. This is because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas enter the meditative absorption of cessation by relying on conditioned activities (saṃskṛta-karma), thereby falling into the sphere of the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka). For this reason, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation at every moment of thought within the seventh stage; they give rise to thoughts of terror, fearing that they might fall into the state where all phenomena lack distinct characteristics.

They enter the meditative absorption of cessation by perceiving the various distinct characteristics of phenomena—such as existence and non-existence, wholesome and unwholesome, and common and specific characteristics—and because they lack the wisdom of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya-jñāna), śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation at every moment of thought within the seventh stage.
Mahāmati!
At the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva transforms and extinguishes the mind, manas, and mental consciousness of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Mahāmati!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first through the sixth stages perceive that the triple world is nothing but their own mind—its *citta*, *manas*, and *manovijñāna*—and is free from the phenomena of "self" and "what belongs to self. It is merely the discrimination of one's own mind; they do not fall into the various marks of external phenomena. Only the ignorant minds of ordinary people fall into the two extremes and perceive the phenomena of the grasped and the grasper. Due to ignorance, they fail to realize that all phenomena arise from the habitual perfuming of the delusions, afflictions, and conceptual proliferations of body, speech, and mind throughout beginningless time.
Mahāmati!
Within the eighth stage, all bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas conceive the notion that they have entered nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!

All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, by virtue of their own minds’ power of samādhi and the power of the Buddhas, do not enter the gate of the bliss of samādhi to abide in nirvāṇa, because they have not yet fulfilled the stage of a Tathāgata. If those Bodhisattvas were to abide in the state of samādhi alone, they would cease the liberation of all sentient beings, sever the lineage of the Tathāgatas, and extinguish the family of the Tathāgatas; therefore, in order to manifest the inconceivable realms of the Tathāgatas, they do not enter nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the gate of the dharma of the bliss of samādhi; for this reason, śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati!

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). They observe the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); they remain far removed from the grasping at signs of "self" and "what belongs to self"; they observe the emptiness of self (*ātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); they observe common characteristics and distinct characteristics; they skillfully understand the meaning of the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) and skillful means; and they enter the stages (*bhūmi*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) with mastery and in proper sequence.
“Mahāmati!

If I did not explain the dharmas of the common and distinct characteristics of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all bodhisattvas would fail to know the sequence of the stages as they truly are. Fearing that they might fall into the dharmas of external paths, false views, and the like, I have explained the characteristics of the stages in their proper order.”
Mahāmati!

If a person enters the stages (*bhūmi*) in succession, they do not fall into other paths. When I speak of the sequential characteristics of the stages, it is merely the manifestation of one's own mind regarding the sequence of the stages and the various modes of activity within the triple world (*tridhātu*). Yet, ordinary beings neither perceive nor understand this. Because ordinary beings do not perceive or understand it, I and all the Buddhas speak of the sequential characteristics of the stages and establish the various modes of activity within the triple world.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, while in the eighth Bodhisattva stage, become intoxicated by their attachment to the gate of the bliss of *samādhi* in cessation (*śamatha*), they are unable to properly understand that [all things] are but the manifestations of one’s own mind. Due to falling into the obstacles of the habitual tendencies of specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa-vāsanā*), and due to falling into the views regarding the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), they take the conceptualizing mind itself to be *nirvāṇa*, yet they are unable to know the quiescence of all phenomena.

Mahāmati! Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas perceive the gateway to the bliss of the samādhi of tranquility, they recollect their original vows and, with great compassion, deliver all sentient beings; furthermore, they know the wisdom that realizes the ten inexhaustible realities as they truly are. For these reasons, they do not immediately enter nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati! When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas remain far removed from the mind of false discrimination and remain far removed from the realms of the grasper and the grasped, this is called entering nirvāṇa. By means of suchness-wisdom (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), they know that all dharmas are merely their own mind; therefore, they do not give rise to a discriminating mind. Consequently, these Bodhisattvas do not grasp at the mind, the intellect, or the mental consciousness, nor do they cling to the characteristics of external phenomena as being truly existent. Yet, it is not that they do not practice the Buddha-dharma; rather, relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), they practice progressively in order to seek for themselves the realization-ground wisdom of a Buddha-Tathāgata.
Mahāmati!

It is like a person who, while dreaming, crosses a great ocean; employing great skillful means, he desires to carry himself across, but before he has finished crossing, he suddenly awakens and reflects:
"Is this real?"
"Is this illusory?
He further reflects:

"Such signs are neither real nor unreal; they are merely the unreal objects of my own fundamental false discrimination. Due to the cause of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), various forms are seen; their shapes and characteristics are inverted, not departing from existence and non-existence, just as one sees things in a dream through the perfuming of the mental consciousness."

"Mahāmati! It is the same for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: within the eighth stage, he perceives the discriminating mind; from the first to the seventh stages, all dharmas share the same characteristic, being equal and without difference—like a dream or a magical illusion. Having transcended all functional efforts and the discriminating mind of grasped object and grasping subject, he perceives the mind and its mental factors. For the sake of enabling those who have not yet attained the supreme Buddha-dharmas to attain them, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the sublime dharma, which is called Nirvāṇa; it is not the extinction of all dharmas that is called Nirvāṇa."

Because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are far removed from the conceptual characteristics of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), they attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Mahāmati! Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no succession, nor is there sequential practice; all phenomena are quiescent, just like space.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
the World-Honored One has said:..."
"The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas enter the gate of the bliss of extinction in the eighth Bodhisattva stage.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said:

"The Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know that [all things] are merely the conceptual differentiation of their own minds," and he has also said: "All Śrāvakas attain the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya), but they do not attain the emptiness of the selflessness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya)."
“If it is as you say, even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not yet able to realize the dharmas of the first stage, let alone the gate of the bliss of cessation of the eighth stage.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“I shall now explain this to you in detail for you.”

Mahāmati! There are three kinds of śrāvakas. Regarding those said to enter the gate of quiescence in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), these are practitioners who previously cultivated the bodhisattva path but fell into the stage of the śrāvaka; they return to rely upon their original mind to cultivate the bodhisattva path and thus likewise enter the gate of the bliss of quiescence in the eighth stage. They are not śrāvakas of quiescence characterized by overweening pride (*adhimāna*), for the latter cannot enter the bodhisattva practice. This is because they have never realized that the triple world is mind-only, have never practiced the various dharmas of a bodhisattva, and have never practiced the perfections (*pāramitā*) or the conduct of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Therefore, the śrāvakas of definitive quiescence cannot realize that gate of the bliss of quiescence practiced by the bodhisattvas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Mind-only exists; there are no phenomena, nor the stages of Buddhahood.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present—throughout the three times—they have taught thus."
The seventh stage is the ground of mind; the eighth stage is that of non-existence.
The second stage is called the ground of practice; the remaining stages are called the ground of self.
Realization within one's own body and purity—this is what is called the ground of self.
In the sovereign and most excellent place, the Akaniṣṭha Heaven,
he shines like a blazing fire, emitting wondrous rays of light;
with various beauties and delights, he manifests transformations throughout the triple world.
Manifesting the forms of the three realms, or manifesting within light;
there they teach the various vehicles—this is my stage of mastery.
The tenth ground is the first ground, and the first ground is the eighth.
The ninth stage becomes the seventh, and the seventh stage becomes the eighth.
The second stage becomes the third, and the fourth stage becomes the fifth;
the third stage becomes the sixth—when all is quiescent extinction, what sequence can there be?
Those who are fixed as śrāvakas do not practice the conduct of a bodhisattva;
those who enter together into the eighth stage—this is the original bodhisattva conduct.
Chapter Ten: Inquiry into Whether the Tathāgata is Permanent or Impermanent (7) At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, eternal or is he impermanent?
The Buddha addressed the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying:
“Mahāmati! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this?
Because both extremes entail faults. Mahāmati,
the two extremes of existence and non-existence must necessarily involve errors.
Mahāmati!
If one says that the Tathāgata is a permanent phenomenon, then he would be identical to a permanent cause.
Mahāmati!
Because the various non-Buddhists assert that atoms and other such causes are eternal and therefore not produced by conditions,
Mahāmati, one cannot say that the Tathāgata is eternal on the grounds that he is eternal while being something not produced by conditions.

Mahāmati! Furthermore, one must not say that the Tathāgata is impermanent; to say he is impermanent is to equate him with conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Since the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—both the visible and the seeing—are non-existent, and because the five aggregates cease, if [the Tathāgata were impermanent], the Buddhas and Tathāgatas would likewise be subject to cessation. Yet, the Buddha-Tathāgata is not a phenomenon characterized by annihilation.
Mahāmati! All things that are produced through effort are impermanent. For example, jars, garments, carts, houses, and cotton mats are all produced through effort; therefore, they are impermanent.
Mahāmati!

If one were to say that all things are impermanent, then all-knowledge, the Omniscient One, and all his merits would also be impermanent, because they share the same characteristics as all conditioned phenomena.

Furthermore, there is another fault: if one were to say that all things are impermanent, then the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, would be conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Yet the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are not conditioned phenomena, because there is no further superior cause to be explained. Therefore, I say that the Tathāgata is neither permanent nor impermanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the Tathāgata is not eternal. Why is this?
The nature of space likewise lacks the cultivation of any meritorious qualities. Mahāmati!
For example, space is neither permanent nor impermanent.

Why is this? Because it is free from permanence and impermanence; because it does not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence; or permanence, impermanence, neither permanent nor impermanent. Therefore, being free from all faults, it cannot be described in words.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
one must not say that the Tathāgata is eternal. Why is this?

If one says that [the Tathāgata] is permanent, he would be identical to the horns of rabbits, horses, camels, donkeys, tortoises, snakes, flies, fish, and so forth; therefore, one cannot say that the Tathāgata is permanent.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Furthermore, one must not say that the Tathāgata is eternal, for fear of falling into the [wrong] view of an unproduced eternity; therefore, one cannot say that the World-Honored Tathāgata is eternal.
Moreover, Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are other dharmas; by relying upon those dharmas, one may say that the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is eternal. Why is this?
Because he relies on internally realized wisdom to realize the eternal dharma, it can therefore be said that the Tathāgata is eternal.
Mahāmati!
The Dharma of the internally realized wisdom of all Buddha-Tathāgatas is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging. Mahāmati!

Whether the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is constant; likewise, the essence of phenomena is constant, and the laws of phenomena are constant. Thus, by means of that nature of phenomena, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others have neither heard nor seen it. This essence of phenomena does not exist within empty space, yet the ordinary worldlings of the "hair-path" (mūḍha-bāla) neither awaken to nor know it.
Mahāmati!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, derive their name from that wisdom of internal realization. Mahāmati!

One is named a Buddha by virtue of practicing in accordance with wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); it is not by virtue of being perfumed by mind, intellect, mental consciousness, ignorance, or the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Mahāmati!
All that exists within the triple world is designated by means of unreal conceptualization, discrimination, and frivolous discourse. Mahāmati!

The unreal conceptualization of two kinds of phenomena is what is termed "permanence" and "impermanence. Yet the Buddha-Tathāgata does not fall into these two phenomena, nor does he fall into the two extremes of the grasper and the grasped, because for the Tathāgata, who is quiescent, these two phenomena do not arise.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas cannot be said to be either permanent or impermanent.
Mahāmati!

Regarding all speech, one may speak of permanence and impermanence; yet for one who has distanced themselves from and exhausted all conceptual discrimination, it cannot be said that they grasp at the dharmas of permanence or impermanence. Therefore, I prohibit all ordinary beings from discriminating between permanence and impermanence; for those who have attained the truly quiescent Dharma exhaust all discrimination and do not give rise to further discrimination.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Free from permanence and impermanence, Neither permanent nor impermanent;
Whoever perceives the Buddha in this way Shall not fall into the evil realms.”
If one speaks of permanence or impermanence, all virtues are rendered false;
it is the ignorant who make such distinctions. To refute the claims of permanence and impermanence, [it is said]:
