"All those who establish doctrines possess various faults."
"If one can perceive that there is only mind, One will not fall into any faults.
Chapter Eleven: Buddha-nature (7) The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Eleven: Buddha-nature At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again requested the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will explain to me, and that the Sugata will explain to me, the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
"Bhagavān!
If there is no self, who is it that arises and who is it that ceases?
Bhagavān!"
"All ordinary beings dwell in dependence upon arising and ceasing; they do not see the exhaustion of suffering, and for this reason they do not know the characteristic of nirvana.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent! Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.”
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"Because the Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, it can act as the causal condition for birth and death within the six realms of existence. It is like an actor who performs various roles; because sentient beings rely upon the Tathāgatagarbha, they undergo birth and death within the five destinies."
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgatagarbha is free from "I" and "mine," yet the various non-Buddhists neither know nor realize this; therefore, the causes and conditions for birth and death within the triple world remain uninterrupted.
Mahāmati!

Because the various non-Buddhists falsely conceptualize a self, they are unable to see the Tathāgatagarbha as it truly is; this is because, since beginningless time, those non-Buddhists have been habituated by the false attachments to various kinds of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).

Mahāmati! The ālayavijñāna is called the Tathāgatagarbha; it coexists with the seven consciousnesses and ignorance, like the waves of the great ocean that are constantly uninterrupted because they arise simultaneously with the body.
Thus, it is free from the fault of impermanence and free from the notion of a self.

Beyond the self-nature of purity, the remaining seven consciousnesses—namely, the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—do not abide from moment to moment;

they are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. These seven consciousnesses arise from those false causes and are unable to discern all phenomena as they truly are, because they perceive characteristics such as high and low, long and short, and because they cling to names and appearances.
Because it causes one’s own mind to perceive the appearance of forms; because it enables the experience of suffering and pleasure; because it serves as the cause for detachment and liberation;
because it gives rise to secondary afflictions such as craving based on the perception of signs; because the various sense faculties perish due to that causal mindfulness;
because [the faculties] do not arise sequentially; and because other mental constructions of one's own do not give rise to the sensations of suffering or pleasure.
Therefore, those who enter the minor meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the *samāpattis*, the four dhyānas,
and the liberation through the realization of the true truths, give rise to the notion of liberation because they do not understand how to transform and extinguish false appearances.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna does not reside within the ālayavijñāna; therefore, while the seven kinds of consciousness arise and cease, the Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna is neither born nor extinguished.

Why is this? Those seven kinds of consciousness arise based on various objects through recollection and observation; these objects of the seven consciousnesses cannot be awakened to by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or practitioners of external paths, because they do not know the selflessness of persons as it truly is, because they grasp at dharmas characterized by common and specific marks, and because they perceive the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and other such phenomena.
Mahāmati!

Because they see the Tathāgatagarbha as it truly is—the five dharmas, their essential characteristics, and the selflessness of phenomena—it does not arise. Because they know the successive stages of the bodhisattva grounds as they truly are, through their progressive integration, other heterodox practitioners with incorrect views are unable to perceive it.

Mahāmati! When a Bodhisattva dwells in the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*), at that time they attain ten kinds of samādhi-gates as their primary focus, and acquire immeasurable and boundless samādhis. Relying on the empowerment of the Buddhas through these samādhis, and by virtue of observing the inconceivable dharmas of all Buddhas as well as the power of their own original vows, they shield and protect the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within the gates of samādhi. Having so shielded them, they enter the true realm of the dharma realized through the noble wisdom of their own internal body. This is not the same as the realms observed through the practices of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or outsiders; at that time, having transcended those ten kinds of noble paths, they enter the Tathāgata’s mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*), because they are free from the mental states of samādhi involving effortful application.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who wish to realize the supreme dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna should practice so as to bring them to purity.

Mahāmati! If the Tathāgatagarbha, the Ālayavijñāna, were called "non-existent," then apart from the Ālayavijñāna there would be neither arising nor ceasing. It is because they rely upon that Ālayavijñāna that all ordinary beings and noble ones experience birth and cessation. Because they rely upon the Ālayavijñāna, practitioners enter into the realization of the noble conduct within their own internal bodies, experiencing the blissful practice of the present dharma without ceasing.
Mahāmati!
These realms of the Tathāgata-mind, the ālayavijñāna, and the tathāgatagarbha cannot be discerned by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or followers of external paths.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgatagarbha is by nature pure, while adventitious afflictions defile it and render it impure. Mahāmati!

Based on this meaning, relying upon Queen Śrīmālā and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas of profound wisdom, I have taught the Tathāgatagarbha-Ālayavijñāna; together with the seven evolving consciousnesses, it is designated as the "characteristic of transformation and cessation. For the sake of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others, I have demonstrated the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya). Addressing Śrīmālā, I have said: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the domain of the Tathāgatas."
Mahāmati!

Regarding the realm of the Tathāgatagarbha and the Ālayavijñāna, I, you, and the other bodhisattvas who possess profound wisdom, are able to discern and distinguish these two kinds of dharmas; however, the other śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who are attached to mere names cannot understand these two dharmas.
"Mahāmati! Therefore, you and all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should study this Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
“The profound Tathāgatagarbha arises together with the seven consciousnesses;
when one grasps at two dharmas, birth occurs, but knowing them as they truly are, there is no birth.
Like reflections appearing in a mirror, the mind is perfumed by beginningless habitual tendencies.”
For one who observes according to reality, all objects are entirely empty and non-existent.
Like a fool who, when shown the moon by a finger, looks at the finger and not the moon;
so too, those who are attached to names and words do not see my true nature.
The mind is like a skilled actor; the intellect is like a cunning deceiver.
The mental consciousness and the five sensory consciousnesses falsely grasp at objects;
like a troupe of actors in union, they delude and deceive ordinary people.
Chapter Twelve: The Five Dharmas (7). The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Twelve: The Five Dharmas. At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

I pray that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will explain this for me; may the Sugata explain it for me: the essential characteristics of the five dharmas and the distinct modes of the two kinds of selflessness. If I and all other bodhisattvas can thoroughly understand the essential characteristics of the five dharmas and the distinct characteristics of the two kinds of selflessness, we shall practice these dharmas and enter the stages (bhūmis) in their proper sequence. By practicing these dharmas, one is able to enter into all the Buddha-dharmas; having entered the Buddha-dharmas, one may even enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s own internally realized wisdom.
The Buddha addressed the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I shall explain to you the essential characteristics of the five dharmas and the distinct modes of the two kinds of selflessness.
Mahāmati! What are these five dharmas?"
First is name, second is appearance, third is discrimination, fourth is correct wisdom, and fifth is suchness.

Those who internally cultivate the practice to realize the wisdom of the noble ones and depart from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, manifesting practice according to reality, do so by entering the gateway of practice consisting of the bliss of samādhi and samāpatti.
Mahāmati!

All ordinary beings do not awaken to or understand the essential characteristics of the five dharmas and the two kinds of selflessness; they perceive external objects solely through their own minds, and thus give rise to a mind of discrimination, which is not the way of the sages.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Why is it that ordinary people give rise to discriminative thoughts, whereas noble ones do not?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“All ordinary beings cling to names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) and follow along with the arising of phenomena.

Having followed along with the arising of phenomena, they perceive various marks (*nimitta*) and fall into the minds of false views regarding ‘self’ and ‘what belongs to self,’ clinging to all phenomena as being fully existent.”
Regarding signs (*nimitta*), having become attached, they enter into the dark enclosure of ignorance; having entered that enclosure, they give rise to a mind of craving;
having given rise to a mind of craving, they are able to perform the karma of greed, hatred, and delusion;
having performed these karmic actions, they cannot stop themselves, like a silkworm making a cocoon that entangles its own body with a discriminating mind, thus falling into [samsara].
The great ocean of the six realms of existence is a perilous difficulty, revolving like a waterwheel without one’s own awareness; because of a lack of wisdom,
one does not know that all phenomena are like illusions, nor does one know that there is no self or what belongs to a self,
and that all phenomena are not real but arise from false conceptualization and discrimination, nor does one know how to transcend the seen and the seer.
They understand that things are devoid of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, yet they do not realize that these arise from the delusions of their own minds;
instead, they claim to know that [phenomena] arise in accordance with Īśvara, time, atoms, or a self.
Mahāmati! What is meant by "name"?

It refers to the perception of the characteristics of external phenomena, such as forms, by the visual consciousness, as well as the characteristics of sounds, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body.
Mahāmati! Such characteristics as these, I call "name-characteristics" (nāma-lakṣaṇa). Mahāmati!
What is discrimination (*vikalpa*)?

It is that which, based on certain phenomena, is called "grasping at signs" (*nimittodgraha*); it is the discernment (*vijñapti*) of these phenomena as being "thus and thus," ultimately without variation—namely, the discrimination of various signs such as elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, people, and so forth. This is called discrimination.
Mahāmati! What is right knowledge?

It is the observation of names and marks; having observed them, one does not perceive real dharmas because they are seen to arise from mutual causality. When those things that arise mutually do not give rise to further consciousnesses, the characteristics of the discriminating consciousness are neither annihilated nor eternal. Therefore, one does not fall into the stages of any externalists, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas.
Mahāmati! This is called right knowledge.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

The Bodhisattva-mahāsattva, relying on correct wisdom, does not grasp at dharmas of names and marks as being existent, nor does he grasp at the non-perception of marks as being non-existent. Why is this?

Because it is free from the false views of existence and non-existence, and because one does not perceive names and marks as having the meaning of correct wisdom, I therefore call it *tathatā* (suchness), Mahāmati.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in the reality (*tathatā*) of phenomena, they enter the signless and tranquil realm; having entered it, they enter the first stage of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). When a Bodhisattva attains the Stage of Joy, they realize one hundred gateways of the luminosity of the adamantine samādhi (*vajra-samādhi*), abandon all karmic fruits of the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*), and transcend the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Abiding in the realm of *tathatā* within the family of the Tathāgatas, they practice according to reality, knowing that the five dharmas and their characteristics are like illusions and dreams. They observe all phenomena as they truly are and initiate the practice of the noble wisdom realized within their own bodies. In this manner, they progressively distance themselves from the realms of worldly conceptualization and discursive thought, proceeding step by step until reaching the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).

Having entered the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), one next enters the stage of the Tathāgata, which is adorned with various flowers through the mastery of samādhis, powers, and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).

Having entered the stage of the Tathāgata, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, one manifests various radiances and a body adorned according to circumstances, like the moon reflected in water. Relying on inexhaustible phrases, one skillfully binds those who are bound, preaching the Dharma to sentient beings according to their faith, because of being free from the body of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna-kāya*).
"Mahāmati!
Having entered into suchness, the bodhisattva attains within the stage of Buddhahood such and such immeasurable and boundless dharmas.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Does the World-Honored One intend for the five dharmas to enter into the three dharmas,
or for the three dharmas to enter into the five dharmas?”
"Are they distinct from one another in terms of their essential nature and characteristics?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The three natures are included within the five dharmas."
Mahāmati!
It is not only that the three dharmas enter into the five dharmas; the eight kinds of consciousness and the two kinds of selflessness also enter into the five dharmas, Mahāmati!
How do the three dharmas enter into the five dharmas?
Mahāmati! Name and appearance are termed the dharma-characteristic of discrimination.
Mahāmati!

Based on those two dharmas, the mind and its mental factors arise through discrimination; they occur simultaneously, not sequentially, just as the sun and its radiance exist simultaneously, yet there is a discrimination of various characteristics.
Mahāmati! These are called the three characteristics, because they arise through the power of causes and conditions. Mahāmati!
Correct wisdom and suchness are called the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), because they rely upon the dharma that is non-extinguished.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are eight kinds of differentiation in the phenomena of conceptual construction based on the views of one's own mind; because one regards these various characteristics as real, one becomes detached from the dharmas of arising and ceasing characterized by "I" and "mine," and at that time, one realizes the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Mahāmati!

The five dharmas are the gateway through which one enters the stages of all Buddhas; the characteristics of the dharmas of those stages also enter within the gateway of the five dharmas. All the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas likewise enter within the gateway of the five dharmas, and even the dharmas of the noble wisdom realized within the Tathāgata’s own body also enter within the gateway of the five dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five dharmas:
characteristics, names, discrimination, suchness, and correct gnosis. Mahāmati!
What is called "mark" (lakṣaṇa)?
A mark refers to seeing the forms, shapes, appearances, and qualities—whether superior or inferior—of material objects; this is what is called a mark. Mahāmati!

Based on those dharmic characteristics, one gives rise to conceptualized characteristics, thinking, "This is a jar," or "These are a cow, a horse, or a sheep," and so forth; that dharma is thus and not otherwise.
Mahāmati!
This is called "name. Mahāmati! Based on those dharmas, names are established;
they distinguish and manifest their characteristics. Therefore, various names such as "ox," "cow," "horse," and so forth are established; this is called the discrimination of mind and mental factors.
Mahāmati!

When one examines names and characteristics down to the finest atom, one never perceives the characteristic of even a single dharma; all dharmas are unreal, for they are discriminated by the deluded mind.

Mahāmati! That which is called *tathatā* (suchness) is named "the non-false. It is the definitive, ultimate exhaustion of the self-nature and self-essence; it is the true vision of the characteristics of *tathatā*. I, as well as all bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, declare that while the names are different, the meaning is one.

Mahāmati! Such [realizations] accord with right gnosis; they are neither annihilated nor eternal; they are beyond the sphere of non-conceptualization and conceptualization; they accord with the noble wisdom realized within one's own body, and they remain apart from all the heterodox views, factions, and incorrect gnoses of outsiders, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.
Mahāmati!
Regarding the five dharmas, the characteristics of the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—all the Buddha-dharmas are subsumed within the five dharmas.
Mahāmati! You and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study in order to seek supreme wisdom. Mahāmati!
"You know these five dharmas because you do not follow the teachings of others.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The self-nature and characteristics of the five dharmas, And the eight kinds of consciousness;
The two kinds of selflessness encompass all Mahāyāna teachings.
Name, appearance, and conceptualization are the three factors that constitute the characteristic of self-nature;
correct cognition and suchness are the characteristic of the ultimate truth.
Chapter Thirteen: The Ganges Sands (7) The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Thirteen: The Ganges Sands At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Just as the World-Honored One has spoken of past, future, and present Buddhas by way of names, saying they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River—
World-Honored One,
when the Buddha speaks thus, should I accept it in accordance with what has been uttered from the mouth of the Tathāgata?"
"Is there another meaning?
I pray that you will explain it to me.
The Buddha addressed the noble Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying:
“Mahāmati! Do not grasp at the names and phrases as I have spoken them in this way.
Mahāmati!”
The Buddhas of the three periods of time are not merely as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Why is this?
The analogies spoken of that transcend the world are not like ordinary metaphors.
Why is this? Because there are similarities and dissimilarities. Mahāmati!
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not definitively state whether the worldly metaphors they employ are similar or dissimilar [to the reality they illustrate]. Why is this?
Mahāmati!
I speak of parables only as partial illustrations. Mahāmati!
The parables spoken by myself and all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, express only a limited meaning.

Why is this? Because foolish ordinary people and various non-Buddhists are attached to the permanence of all phenomena, which increases their false views; they follow along with the world, revolving in the cycle of birth and death. To cause them to develop weariness toward that [cycle] and to hear [the truth] without fear, and so that upon hearing that there are Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they might conceive the thought that the unsurpassed holy path of the Tathāgata is easily attained and thus seek the supramundane Dharma.
"Mahāmati!
For this reason, I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. Why is that?"

In other sutras, I have said that the appearance of a Buddha in the world is as rare as the udumbara flower; having heard this, sentient beings say that the path of the Buddha is difficult to attain and fail to cultivate diligence. For this reason, I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
Mahāmati!

When I say that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is like the udumbara flower, it is based on the principle of those beings who are capable of being transformed; for this reason, I say that the Buddhas are like the udumbara flower.
Mahāmati, as for the udumbara flower, no one in the world has ever seen it, nor will anyone see it.
Mahāmati, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have been seen in the world, are being seen now, and will be seen in the future.
Mahāmati!
When I speak in this way, it is not based on a dharma attained by my own self; therefore, I say that just as the udumbara flower is rare, so too are the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati!

I teach the Dharma based on the realization of the internal body; therefore, I speak of metaphors that transcend the world, for ordinary people and beings lacking faith are unable to believe in the metaphors I have taught.

Why is this? Because the realm of noble wisdom within one's own body cannot be described through analogies; it is far removed from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), transcends all grounds of views, and the *tathatā*-dharma of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas is ineffable. Therefore, I employ various metaphors.
"Mahāmati!
When I say that the Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River, this is a partial analogy.
Mahāmati!"
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are equal and not unequal, because they do not engage in conceptualization through conceptualization. Mahāmati!

It is like all the sand in the river Ganges, which is trodden upon by fish, crocodiles, turtles, dragons, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, and various other beasts; yet that river sand does not give rise to conceptualization, nor does it feel aversion or resentment, nor does it form the thought, "They are disturbing me. Because it is free from conceptualization, it is pure and detached from all defilements.

Mahāmati! It is the same with the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas: having internally realized the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), they are fully endowed with powers, supernatural faculties, and sovereign merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. When the foolish fish and turtles of all the heterodox teachers and their proponents of false doctrines revile the Tathāgata with hearts of malice, the Tathāgata remains unmoved and gives rise to no discrimination. By the power of his original vows, in order to bestow upon sentient beings samādhis and samāpattis and to cause them to be fulfilled in all forms of happiness, he does not discriminate while yet discriminating.
Mahāmati!

For this reason, I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River. "Equal" means they are equal and without any marks of difference, because they have abandoned the body of craving.
Mahāmati!
For example, the sands of the Ganges River do not depart from the nature of earth. Mahāmati!

When the great earth is consumed by fire, the fire is not distinct from the earth; thus, the fire does not burn the earth, because the great element of earth possesses a continuous substance that contains fire. Mahāmati!

Foolish ordinary beings fall into inverted cognition and, through the discrimination of their own minds, say that the earth is being burned; yet the earth is not burned, for apart from the earth, no other body of the four great elements consisting of fire can be found.
Mahāmati!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise thus; the essence of the Dharma-body of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is like the sands of the Ganges River, for it is neither extinguished nor lost.
Mahāmati!
For example, the sands of the Ganges River are immeasurable and boundless.
Mahāmati!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise thus: they appear in the world and emit immeasurable light that pervades all the great assemblies of Buddhas, in order to transform sentient beings and cause them to attain awakening.
Mahāmati!
Just as the sands of the Ganges River do not give rise to further marks of birth, so too do those atoms abide with the essential characteristics of atoms.
Mahāmati!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are likewise thus: they neither arise nor cease within the world, because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have severed the causes of existence.
Mahāmati!

Just as when the sands of the Ganges River emerge from the river they cannot be seen, and when they enter into the river they also cannot be seen, nor do they give rise to the thought, "I am entering or emerging from the river."
Mahāmati!
The power of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is likewise: in delivering sentient beings, it neither undergoes extinction nor does it increase. Why is this?
"Because all dharmas are bodiless, Mahāmati!
All that possess a body are impermanent and subject to destruction; they are not bodiless dharmas, for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess only the Dharma-body."
Mahāmati!
It is like a person who, desiring to obtain ghee or oil, presses the sands of the Ganges River; they will never obtain it because there is no ghee or oil therein.
Mahāmati!

For the sake of the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings, the Tathāgatas do not give way to anger; they do not abandon the characteristics of their own Dharma-realm, nor do they abandon the characteristics of the flavor of their own Dharma, nor do they abandon their original vows to bestow happiness upon sentient beings. Having attained the perfection of great loving-kindness and great compassion, [they resolve]: "If I do not cause all sentient beings to enter Nirvāṇa, my own body shall likewise not enter Nirvāṇa."
Mahāmati!
Just as the sands of the Ganges River flow along with the water and never flow upstream,
so it is, Mahāmati!
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, likewise teach the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; they accord with *nirvāṇa* and do not flow against the current.
Mahāmati, for this reason I say that the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are like the sands of the Ganges River.
Mahāmati!

When it is said that the sands of the Ganges follow the flow of the river, this does not mean they have gone away. If the Buddha-Tathāgata possessed the sense of "going," then all Buddha-Tathāgatas would be subject to impermanence and cessation.
Mahāmati!
Since even the original limit of the world cannot be known, how could I rely on that which is unknowable to explain the meaning of "going"?
Therefore, the Tathāgata does not hold to the meaning of "going."
“Mahāmati!
The meaning of ‘departure’ is the meaning of ‘cessation,’ yet ignorant ordinary beings neither perceive nor understand this.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If sentient beings are in the cycle of saṃsāra within this world, and their past and future limits are unknowable, how is it that the Tathāgata has attained liberation and further enables sentient beings to attain liberation?”
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati, saying: “Mahāmati!

What is called ‘liberation’ is so named because it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), afflictions, and the discriminative mind conditioned by beginningless habituation; because one knows, in accordance with reality, that what is seen is merely one’s own mind; and because the mind turns away from the external objects that are discriminated. For these reasons, I declare it to be liberation.”
Mahāmati!
That which is called liberation is not the extinction of dharmas; therefore, your current question—asking how one can attain liberation if the original limit (pūrvakoṭi) is unknown—is invalid.
Mahāmati! What is called the "primordial limit" (pūrvakoṭi) is merely another name for the single essence of the discriminating mind. Mahāmati!
Apart from the discriminating mind, there are no sentient beings; it is this very discrimination that is called "sentient beings. Mahāmati!
True wisdom contemplates internal and external phenomena because there is neither an object to be known nor a subject that knows.
Mahāmati! Because all dharmas have been quiescent from the very beginning. Mahāmati!

Failing to know, as it truly is, that what is seen is merely one's own mind and is false discrimination, one gives rise to a discriminating mind; one who knows it as it truly is does not give rise to discrimination.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Those who contemplate all Buddhas, As being like the sands of the Ganges—
Neither extinguished nor born— Such people are able to see the Buddha.”
Far removed from all dust and defilement, Like the sands of the Ganges River;
Flowing along without changing, The Dharma-body is also thus.
— *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter Fourteen: On Moments (Kṣaṇavarga). (8) Chapter Fourteen: On Moments.
At that time, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

I pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will explain for me; O Sugata, please explain for me the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all dharmas. How is it that the Tathāgata says all dharmas do not abide for even a single moment?"
The Buddha said to Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
“Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"All dharmas, all dharmas" refers to wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas; conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas; mundane dharmas and supramundane dharmas; tainted dharmas and untainted dharmas; internal dharmas and external dharmas.
Mahāmati!

Briefly stated, the phenomena of the five aggregates arise from the growth of the perfuming of mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Because all ordinary persons rely on the perfuming of mind, intellect, and mental consciousness, they discriminate between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Mahāmati!
The noble ones directly realize the blissful practice of the untainted wholesome dharmas of samādhi and samāpatti. Mahāmati!
These are called wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
what are called wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are the so-called eight consciousnesses.
What are the eight? First, the ālayavijñāna;
second, the manas;
Third, mental consciousness;
fourth, visual consciousness;
fifth, auditory consciousness;
Sixth, nose-consciousness;
seventh, tongue-consciousness;
eighth, body-consciousness.

Mahāmati! The five bodies of consciousness, together with the body of mental consciousness, continue in a succession of mutually distinct states through wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; yet their essence is without distinction. As these bodies arise in conformity with the arising of dharmas and, having arisen, cease again, they do not know that what they perceive are illusory objects of their own mind. Thus, at the very moment of cessation, they grasp the forms, characteristics, dimensions, and relative qualities of those perceived objects.

Mahāmati! The mental consciousness arises in conjunction with the five bodies of sensory consciousness; it does not abide for even a single moment. Therefore, I say that those dharmas do not abide for even a moment.

Mahāmati! That which is called a *kṣaṇika* (moment) is termed "empty. The *ālayavijñāna* is called the Tathāgatagarbha; it is termed "empty" because it lacks the perfuming of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) associated with the mind, but it is termed "not empty" because it is fully endowed with the dharmas of untainted perfuming.
Mahāmati!

Foolish ordinary beings, failing to perceive and failing to understand, cling to the notion that all phenomena do not abide for even a moment; they fall into false views and assert that even untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) do not abide for even a moment.
This is because they destroy true suchness (*tathatā*) and the Tathāgata-garbha.
Mahāmati!
The five bodies of consciousness do not arise in the six destinies, do not experience suffering or pleasure, and do not act as the cause for nirvāṇa. Mahāmati!

The Tathāgatagarbha does not experience suffering or pleasure and is not the cause of birth and death; other dharmas arise and perish together because they are intoxicated by the four kinds of perfuming. Thus, ordinary beings, failing to perceive or understand this, are permeated by false views and claim that all dharmas do not abide for even a single moment.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
The Vajra Tathāgatagarbha, the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata, is not momentary and does not cease to exist.
Mahāmati!
If the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata were not to abide for even a single moment, then all noble ones would not be noble persons.
Mahāmati, they are not non-noble persons, because they are indeed noble persons.
Mahāmati!
A vajra remains for one kalpa; its measure remains equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Mahāmati!

How is it that foolish ordinary beings discriminate among phenomena, claiming they do not abide for even a single moment, yet these ordinary beings fail to grasp my intention and remain unaware and ignorant that all internal and external phenomena do not abide from moment to moment?
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
the Tathāgata has often said that by fulfilling the dharma of the six pāramitās, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
World-Honored One!
What are the six pāramitās?
How are they fulfilled?
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying:
“Mahāmati, there are three distinctions among the pāramitās: namely, worldly pāramitās, supramundane pāramitās, and the most excellent supramundane pāramitās.”
Mahāmati!

What is called the worldly pāramitā refers to foolish ordinary people who, clinging to the dharmas of "self" and "what belongs to self," fall into the two extremes; they practice the pāramitās for the sake of various excellent and sublime objects, seeking the retributive fruits of objects such as form.
Mahāmati!

Foolish ordinary beings practice the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), even as far as being born in the Brahma heavens, seeking the mundane dharmas of the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
Mahāmati! These are called the worldly pāramitās.
Mahāmati!

Regarding what are called the supramundane pāramitās: this refers to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who, with the mind set on attaining the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, practice the pāramitās.
Mahāmati! Just as those foolish worldlings in the world practice the worldly pāramitās in order to seek the bliss of nirvāṇa for themselves;
so too do the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who likewise seek the bliss of nirvāṇa for their own sake and practice the supramundane pāramitās, yet they seek that which is not ultimate bliss.

Mahāmati! As for the supramundane, unsurpassed *pāramitā*, it is the ability to know, according to reality, that external objects are merely false discriminations of one’s own mind. At that time, one truly knows that the internal and external phenomena are seen only as one’s own mind; because one does not discriminate false discrimination and does not grasp at the forms and characteristics of the internal and external mind, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices the *dāna-pāramitā* by knowing all phenomena as they truly are, in order to cause all sentient beings to attain fearlessness and the bliss of peace. This is called the *dāna-pāramitā*.
"Mahāmati!
When a bodhisattva contemplates all those dharmas and does not give rise to discrimination, but instead accords with coolness, this is called the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā),
Mahāmati."

The bodhisattva’s patience that is free from conceptual discrimination consists in practicing according to reality and knowing that the spheres of the grasper and the grasped are not real; this is called the bodhisattva’s pāramitā of kṣānti.
Mahāmati!

How does a bodhisattva cultivate the practice of vigor? By constantly and diligently practicing during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, following the Dharma as it truly is to sever all conceptual discriminations—this is called the *vīryapāramitā*.
Mahāmati!

When a bodhisattva is free from the discriminating mind and does not follow the characteristics of the external objects of grasping and the grasper as held by the non-Buddhists, this is called the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Mahāmati! What is the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva?

It is when a bodhisattva observes the characteristics of the conceptualization of their own mind as they truly are; seeing no conceptualization, they do not fall into the two extremes. Relying on practice according to reality, they transform their basis; they see neither the arising of a single dharma nor the cessation of a single dharma. This internal realization within oneself through the practice of noble conduct is called the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva.
"Mahāmati!
When the meaning of the pāramitās is fulfilled in this manner, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Empty, impermanent, and momentary—thus do the foolish discriminate conditioned phenomena;
like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they are empty, impermanent, and momentary.
The meaning of 'moment' is thus discriminated, and the moment itself is likewise."
Momentary things do not arise; they are quiescent and free from activity.
That all phenomena do not arise—this is what I teach as the meaning of "moment.
That things perish as soon as they arise is not taught for the sake of ordinary beings.
The dharma of continuous succession is discriminated, and through false conceptualization,
one perceives the six realms; if ignorance is the cause that can give rise to all minds,
then until form has yet arisen, upon what does it depend in the interim?
As soon as it arises, it undergoes cessation; other minds arise following that [mind].
Since form does not abide for even a single moment, what dharma can one observe arising?
Upon what cause does a dharma arise?
The mind arises without a cause;
therefore, its arising is not established. How can one know the destruction of thought?
The practitioner realizes meditative concentration, which is like a vajra or a Buddha-relic.
The palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven are imperishable things within the world;
as they accord with the reality of the realized Dharma, so is the wisdom of the Tathāgata accomplished.
When a bhikṣu realizes equality, how could his mindfulness not abide?
Gandharvas and illusory forms—why do thoughts not abide?
If form is seen without the four great elements, what function do the four great elements perform?
Chapter 15: On Transformations (Aṣṭama) At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has bestowed the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the various Arhats;
so too has the Tathāgata further declared that all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not enter parinirvāṇa.”
Furthermore, it is said that from the night the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha realized great Bodhi until the night he entered Parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interval;
yet the Tathāgata further says that all Buddha-Tathāgatas constantly abide in the samādhi of non-thought, non-discursive thought, and non-discrimination;
and again, he speaks of performing various emanations and transformations to deliver all sentient beings.
The World-Honored One further taught that all consciousnesses arise and cease in every moment, never remaining still, and that Vajrapāṇi constantly follows and guards him;
he further taught that the original limit of the world is difficult to know;
and he further stated that sentient beings enter parinirvāṇa, yet if they were to enter nirvāṇa, there ought to be an original limit.
Furthermore, it is said that although all Buddhas have no enemies, they encounter various Māras;

and it is said that although the Tathāgata has severed all obstacles, he was seen to be slandered by Cañcāmāṇavikā, Viśvantarī, and others, and when the Buddha entered the village of Śālavana, he departed with an empty bowl, having received no food at all.
World-Honored One!
If this were so, the Tathāgata would possess immeasurable karmic offenses.
How could the Tathāgata, without being free from all sins, faults, and evils, attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and the knowledge of all modes?
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Excellent, Mahāmati!
Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon those śrāvakas who have previously practiced the bodhisattva path, based on their attainment of nirvana without remainder.
Mahāmati, my bestowing of predictions upon śrāvakas is for the purpose of generating a spirit of courage in those beings who are timid."
Mahāmati!

In this world and in other Buddha-fields, there are sentient beings who practice the bodhisattva path yet take pleasure in the practices of the śrāvakas. To cause them to turn toward the attainment of great enlightenment, the nirmāṇakāya buddha grants predictions of awakening to those nirmāṇakāya śrāvakas; it is not the saṃbhogakāya or dharmakāya buddha that bestows such predictions.
Mahāmati!
There is no difference between the nirvāṇa of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
Because there is no difference in the severing of afflictions, the severing of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) does not entail the severing of the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, by seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one severs the cognitive hindrances; by seeing the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), one severs the afflictive hindrances.
Mahāmati!

By the transformation of the manovijñāna, one cuts off the karmic obstacles and the obstacles of dharmas; by the transformation of the manas and the vāsanās of the ālayavijñāna, one attains ultimate purity. Mahāmati!

I always abide in accordance with the essence of the fundamental Dharma, giving rise to no further dharmas; relying on the original names, chapters, and phrases, I speak of all dharmas without conscious deliberation or thought.
Mahāmati!

The Tathāgata always possesses knowledge that accords with his will and never loses mindfulness; therefore, the Tathāgata is without vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). This is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, having transcended the four stages, are far removed from the two kinds of death, the two kinds of obstacles, and the two kinds of karma.
Mahāmati!

The seven consciousnesses—the mental consciousness, the intellect, and those of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—do not abide for even a single moment, because they are conditioned by false habitual tendencies and are devoid of all untainted wholesome dharmas.
Mahāmati! The Tathāgatagarbha is neither born nor dies in the world; it neither comes nor goes; it is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there exist the causes for worldly existence, nirvāṇa, suffering, and pleasure; yet ordinary beings, failing to perceive or understand this, fall into emptiness, falsehood, and inversion.
Mahāmati!

Vajrapāṇi constantly follows and attends to the manifested Tathāgata, surrounding him before and behind; he does not attend the dharma-buddhas, reward-buddhas, or the fundamental Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
Mahāmati!

The fundamental Tathāgata is far removed from all sensory faculties and the various measures of magnitude and minuteness; he is far removed from all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and the like.
Mahāmati!

Those who practice according to reality and attain the realm of the blissful practice of that True Suchness (tathatā) know the Fundamental Buddha; because they have attained the patience of the equality of dharmas (samatā-dharma-kṣānti), Vajrapāṇi accordingly manifests as a transformation Buddha.

Mahāmati! The emanation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha) has neither karma nor slander; yet, while the emanation Buddha is not different from the dharma-body Buddha (dharma-buddha), the reward-body Buddha (saṃbhoga-buddha), and the Tathāgata, it is also not identical to them. Just as a potter or salt performs various functions, the emanation Buddha performs the work of transforming sentient beings; it teaches the Dharma through diverse characteristics of reality, but does not teach the inner realized Dharma that is the realm of noble wisdom (āryajñāna).
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

All ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas perceive the cessation of the six consciousnesses and thereby fall into the view of annihilationism; failing to see the ālayavijñāna, they fall into the view of eternalism.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Because one does not perceive the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of the conceptualization of one's own mind, the world is said to be "without an original limit. Mahāmati!
To be far removed from the views of one's own mental discrimination is called liberation and the realization of nirvana. Mahāmati!
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are far removed from the four kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are therefore without fault.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The three vehicles and the non-vehicle, The immeasurable vehicles of all Buddhas;
All are recorded as the Buddha-ground, Explaining the severance of all afflictions.”
Having personally realized noble wisdom within and attained nirvana without remainder,
the Tathāgata conceals his teaching in order to encourage and lead those timid beings;
thus, having attained realized knowledge himself, he also speaks of that path to them.
Sentient beings rely on the entry into the Path; for those of the Two Vehicles, there is no Nirvana.
They perceive desire, form, and existence, as well as the four kinds of perfumed stages;
these are also produced by the mental consciousness, which is seen to dwell together with it.
"Seeing the mind, the eye, consciousness, and so forth, as permanent, impermanent, or subject to annihilation;
based on such views of permanence regarding the mind and other faculties, one gives rise to the view of nirvāṇa.

Chapter 16: Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat (8) The Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Sixteen: Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat. At that time, the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I observe that as sentient beings in the world transmigrate through birth and death, bound by knots of enmity and falling into the various evil realms, it is entirely due to eating meat and killing one another, which increases greed and hatred and prevents escape from suffering—this is truly a great misery.”
World-Honored One!
Those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion; those who cultivate the Noble Path should not consume it.
World-Honored One!

The various non-Buddhists propound false views and the Lokāyata doctrines that fall into worldly discourse; they all prohibit the eating of meat, neither consuming it themselves nor permitting others to do so. Why, then, within the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma, do you not restrain yourself from eating meat or allow others to eat it while practicing the Brahma-faring life?
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, regards all sentient beings with equal compassion; why then do you permit the eating of meat?
How excellent, World-Honored One!

Out of pity for the world, we pray that you will explain for us the faults of eating meat and the merits of not eating it. Having heard this, I and all the Bodhisattvas shall practice in accordance with reality and propagate it widely, so that all sentient beings of the present and future may fully understand it.
The Buddha said to the noble Mahāmati Bodhisattva:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Excellent, Mahāmati!
Out of great compassion and pity for sentient beings, you are able to inquire about this meaning. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:

“Now, there are immeasurable faults in eating meat; Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who cultivate great compassion must not eat it. I shall speak briefly of the merits of abstaining from meat and the transgressions of eating it; listen attentively now.”
“Mahāmati!

I observe that sentient beings, due to the habit of eating meat since beginningless time, become greedily attached to its flavor and kill one another; they remain far removed from the noble ones and undergo the suffering of birth and death.

Those who renounce the taste of meat will hear the taste of the True Dharma; by practicing according to reality on the bodhisattva stages, they will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, they cause other sentient beings to enter the place of rest belonging to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and once they have rested there, lead them into the stage of the Tathāgata.”
Mahāmati!
Such benefits as these have compassion as their root. Since those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion, how could they ever attain such great benefits?
Therefore, Mahāmati!

I observe sentient beings circling through the six realms of existence, all dwelling together in birth and death, mutually giving birth to one another, and alternating as fathers, mothers, brothers, sisters, sons, daughters, paternal relatives, maternal relatives, and the six classes of kinsmen. Whether in other realms, whether in good or evil paths, they are constantly kin to one another. For this reason, I observe that among sentient beings who devour one another’s flesh, there is none who is not a relative. Driven by greed for the taste of flesh, they devour each other in turn; constantly harboring harmful intent, they increase their karma of suffering and transmigrate through birth and death, unable to attain liberation.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, all the evil rākṣasas, hearing what the Buddha taught, completely abandoned their malevolent intentions and ceased eating meat. They exhorted one another to give rise to a mind of compassion, protecting the lives of sentient beings even more than they protected their own bodies. Renouncing all kinds of meat, they vowed not to eat it, and weeping with tears streaming down, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I have heard the Buddha teach that one should contemplate the six realms of existence with discernment; I realize that the flesh I eat has all been my own kin. Thus I know that for sentient beings who eat meat, it constitutes a great enmity that severs the seed of great compassion, fosters unwholesome karma, and serves as the root of great suffering.
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I shall renounce and abstain from eating meat, and I shall not permit even my own retinue to eat it.
If there are disciples of the Tathāgata who do not eat meat, I shall personally attend to and protect them day and night; if there are those who eat meat, I shall bring them great harm.”
The Buddha said, “Mahāmati!

Even rākṣasas and evil spirits who constantly eat flesh, upon hearing what I have taught, will give rise to a mind of compassion and renounce eating meat; how much more so should my disciples who practice the wholesome Dharma refrain from eating it? If one eats meat, you should know that such a person is a great enemy of sentient beings and severs my holy lineage.”
Mahāmati!
If my disciples, having heard what I have taught, eat meat without careful reflection, you should know that they are of the Caṇḍāla caste; they are not my disciples, nor am I their teacher.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
If you wish to become my followers, you must not eat any kind of meat whatsoever.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva should contemplate that all meat is derived from the impure body produced by the union of the mother’s blood and the father’s semen; therefore, a bodhisattva contemplates the impurity of meat and should not eat it.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

When sentient beings smell the odor of those who eat meat, they all become terrified and flee far away. Therefore, a Bodhisattva practicing according to reality should not eat meat for the sake of transforming sentient beings."
Mahāmati! It is like this: wherever there are outcasts, hunters, butchers, or those who catch fish and birds, sentient beings see them from afar and think to themselves:

"I am now certain to die; for these approaching ones are great evildoers who do not recognize sin or merit, but take the lives of living beings. Seeking immediate profit, they have come here now to seek us out. Since our bodies are all covered with flesh, they have come today and we are certain to die."
"Mahāmati! Because people eat meat, it causes all sentient beings who see them to give rise to such fear and alarm.
Mahāmati!"
All sentient beings throughout the void and the earth, upon seeing one who eats meat, become terrified and give rise to this doubt:
"Am I now dead or alive?"

Such evil persons do not cultivate a mind of loving-kindness; they wander through the world like jackals and wolves constantly seeking meat to eat. Like oxen devouring grass or dung beetles chasing after filth, they know no satisfaction. My body is flesh and is precisely their food; I should not be encountered by them.
"Immediately they would abandon it and flee far away, no different from a person who fears a *rākṣasa*.

Mahāmati! Those who eat meat cause all sentient beings who see them to give rise to such terror; you should know that meat-eaters are great enemies to sentient beings. Therefore, a Bodhisattva practicing compassion, in order to gather in sentient beings, should not eat it. It is not a flavor consumed by those of noble wisdom; its evil reputation spreads, and it is censured by the sages."
Therefore, Mahāmati,
a bodhisattva, for the sake of gathering in all sentient beings, should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
A bodhisattva, in order to protect the faith of sentient beings, should not eat meat.
Why is this? Mahāmati!

When people speak of a bodhisattva, all sentient beings know that this is a seed of the compassionate mind of the Buddha-Tathāgata, capable of serving as a place of refuge for sentient beings. Upon hearing this, they naturally give rise to no doubt or fear, but instead conceive of them as a kinsman, a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), and one who inspires fearlessness. They say, "I have found a place of refuge, I have found a place of peace and stability, and I have found a good guide."
Mahāmati!

By not eating meat, one can generate such faith in sentient beings; however, if one eats meat, sentient beings will lose all their faith, saying that there is no one in the world who can be trusted, thereby severing the root of faith.
Therefore, Mahāmati,
for the sake of protecting the faith of sentient beings, a bodhisattva should not eat any kind of meat whatsoever.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
My disciples, in order to protect the world from slandering the Triple Gem, should not eat meat. Why is this?
Because there are people in the world who, seeing one eat meat, slander and revile the Triple Gem, saying these words:
"Within the Buddha-dharma, where could there truly be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas practicing the holy life?

Having abandoned what is the natural food of the sages, they eat the flesh of sentient beings; like rākṣasas whose bellies are filled with meat, they sleep unmoving in a state of intoxication. Relying on the power and influence of worldly, ordinary people, they seek out and devour meat, like the king of rākṣasas who terrifies sentient beings."
Therefore, in various places they cry out these words:
"Where can there be true śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who practice pure conduct?

Where there is no Dharma, no śramaṇas, no Vinaya, and no practitioners of purity, such immeasurable and boundless evil and unwholesome thoughts arise; they sever my Wheel of Dharma and extinguish the lineage of the noble ones—all of this is due to the fault of those who eat meat.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
My disciples, in order to protect against evil persons who slander the Triple Gem, should not even give rise to the thought of meat, let alone eat it.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

A bodhisattva seeking to purify a buddha-field and to transform sentient beings should not eat meat. One should regard all meats as a human corpse—something one does not wish to see with the eyes and does not wish to smell; how much less should one inhale its odor or place it within the mouth? All meats are likewise thus."
Mahāmati!
Just as the foul odor of a burning corpse is no different from the stench of burning other meats, how could there be any distinction therein between what is edible and what is inedible?
Therefore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva seeking to purify a buddha-field and to transform sentient beings should not eat meat.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"

A bodhisattva, seeking liberation from birth and death, should single-mindedly contemplate the practice of compassion; possessing few desires and being content, they should grow weary of worldly suffering and swiftly seek deliverance. They should abandon clamor and bustle to resort to secluded places, dwelling in charnel grounds, forest hermitages, among graves, or beneath trees, sitting alone in contemplation. They observe that there is not a single thing in all the worlds worth delighting in: they regard wives, children, and kinsmen as shackles and fetters; palaces and towers as prisons; all precious jewels as heaps of excrement; and all food and drink as pus and blood. When receiving food and drink, they treat it like an ointment applied to a festering sore, accepting only what is necessary to sustain life while fixing their minds on the Noble Path rather than for the sake of craving flavors. They completely renounce and abstain from alcohol, meat, onions, leeks, garlic, and scallions, as well as all foul-smelling things.
Mahāmati! If one acts in this manner, that is true practice, and such a person is worthy of receiving offerings from all devas and humans;

however, if one does not develop weary detachment toward the world, but instead greedily clings to flavors and eats meat, wine, and pungent vegetables whenever the opportunity arises, they should not accept the faithful offerings of the world.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati! There are sentient beings who, having cultivated immeasurable causes and conditions in the past, possess subtle roots of goodness and thus hear my Dharma. With faith, they leave the household life and enter into my teaching. Yet, because they previously belonged to the retinue of rākṣasas or were born among tigers, wolves, lions, cats, and wildcats, they retain the residual habits of eating meat. Although they are within my Dharma, they take pleasure in seeing those who eat meat, approaching them with joy; they enter cities, villages, stupas, and monasteries, drinking alcohol and eating meat as their delight. The devas look down upon them and see that they are no different from rākṣasas vying to devour corpses. Unaware that they have already lost their place in my assembly and become part of the rākṣasa retinue, though they wear the *kāṣāya* robes and have shaved their hair and beards, living beings who see them feel terror in their hearts, as if fearing a rākṣasa."
Therefore, Mahāmati,
those who take me as their teacher should not eat any kind of meat whatsoever.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:

If even those worldly practitioners of heterodox mantras and sorcery fail to achieve their incantations when they eat meat—and yet they refrain from eating meat even for the sake of accomplishing such heterodox arts—how much more so for my disciples who seek the unsurpassed, noble path of the Tathāgata and the supramundane liberation? They cultivate great compassion and diligently practice asceticism, yet still fear they may not attain it; how could such liberation ever be obtained by those deluded people who eat meat?
Therefore, Mahāmati,
my disciples, seeking the bliss of supramundane liberation, should not eat meat.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:

Eating meat can increase physical strength and complexion, yet people are often greedily attached to its flavor; one should contemplate this carefully: among all those in the world who possess body and life, each cherishes themselves and fears the suffering of death. There is no difference between humans and animals in their protection and attachment to body and life; would one rather joyfully preserve the body of a scabby jackal than give up life to receive the pleasures of the devas?
For what reason?
Because they fear the suffering of death, Mahāmati!
Observing in this way that death is a great suffering and a source of dread, how could one who fears death for oneself eat the flesh of others?
Therefore, Mahāmati!
"Those who wish to eat meat should first reflect upon their own bodies and then consider other sentient beings; they ought not to eat meat.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who eat meat are shunned by the devas, let alone by the sages. Therefore, a bodhisattva, desiring to be seen by the sages, should cultivate compassion and must not eat meat."

Mahāmati! For one who eats meat, sleep is painful and waking is also painful. If they see various evils in their dreams, they become terrified and their hair stands on end; their minds are constantly unsettled because, lacking a heart of compassion, they are deficient in all wholesome powers. If they dwell alone in secluded places, non-human beings often watch for an opportunity to harm them, and tigers, wolves, and lions also come to seek and desire to eat their flesh; their minds are constantly filled with alarm and fear, finding no peace or security.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati! Those who eat meat find it difficult to satisfy their greedy minds;

they do not know moderation in eating and cannot digest what they consume. This increases the impurities of the four great elements, making their breath rank and fishy. Within their bellies there are countless evil worms, and their bodies are riddled with sores, scabs, leprosy, and various other impurities. Such things are unpleasant even for ordinary people to hear or see in the present, let alone the possibility of attaining a future human body that is free from disease, fragrant, and pure."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, I say that even when ordinary people eat pure food for the sake of seeking a pure livelihood, they should still give rise to the thought that it is like the flesh of their own son; how much more so should this be the case regarding the eating of food that is not fit for noble ones?

The Sage who has transcended the world [declares] that because meat can give rise to immeasurable faults and cause one to lose all supramundane merits, how could he say, "I permit my disciples to eat various impure flavors such as meat and blood"?
To say, "I have permitted this," is to slander me. Mahāmati!

When I said my disciples eat the food appropriate for the noble ones, I did not mean the food that the noble ones avoid; rather, the food of the noble ones can produce immeasurable merit and distance one from all faults.
Mahāmati!

Regarding the food consumed by the noble ones of the past and present, this refers to non-glutinous rice, large and small wheat, various beans, diverse kinds of oils and honey, sugarcane and sugarcane juice, khaṇḍa, mṛdvīkā, and so forth; whatever is obtained according to the season is permitted as pure food for consumption.
“Mahāmati!

In future ages there will be foolish people who, speaking of various disciplinary codes (vinaya), claim that it is permissible to eat meat. Because they have been habituated to eating meat in the past and are attached to its flavor, they speak thus according to their own mental views; it was not the Buddhas or the Noble Ones who declared meat to be a choice food.”
Mahāmati!

Those who do not eat meat must have, in the past, made offerings to the Buddhas and planted various roots of goodness; they are able to believe the Buddha’s words, firmly abide by the Vinaya, and trust in cause and effect. Reaching the point where they can exercise self-restraint in body and speech, they do not crave worldly flavors, and upon seeing those who eat meat, they are able to give rise to a mind of compassion.
"Mahāmati!

I recall that in the past there was a king named Siṃhadāsa who ate various kinds of meat and became addicted to their flavors. Gradually, he even came to eat human flesh. Because of eating human flesh, his parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen all abandoned him; the ministers, the kingdom, and the villages then conspired together and took his life."
Because those who eat meat have such faults as these, one should not eat any kind of meat.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Sovereign Lord of Heaven transformed himself into a pigeon, and Śakra Devendra, the Lord of the Gods, due to the habitual tendencies of having eaten meat in the past, transformed himself into a hawk and pursued this pigeon. The pigeon came to take refuge with me; at that time, I was King Śibi. Out of compassion for sentient beings who devour one another, I offered my own flesh to the hawk in exchange for the pigeon. When the flesh I cut was insufficient, I remained upon the scale and underwent great suffering.
Mahāmati!

Such are the faults that exist within one's own body and the bodies of others due to the habitual conditioning of eating meat throughout immeasurable lifetimes; how much more so for those who, devoid of shame, constantly consume meat.

Mahāmati! Furthermore, there was another king who did not eat meat. While riding a horse for recreation, he was startled by the animal and dragged into a deep mountain. Having lost his attendants and being unaware of the way back home, because he did not eat meat, lions, tigers, and wolves felt no intent to harm him. He engaged in sexual intercourse with a female lion and eventually fathered sons, such as King Citrāṅga. Due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from eating meat in past lives, even while acting as a human king he continued to eat meat. Living in a village of seven families, he took great pleasure in eating meat; through excessive meat-eating, he eventually began to eat human flesh, and all the sons and daughters born to him became *rākṣasas*.

Mahāmati! Beings who eat meat, due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of eating meat from past lives, are mostly reborn among rākṣasas, lions, tigers, wolves, jackals, leopards, cats, wildcats, owls, crows, eagles, vultures, hawks, and falcons. Among the various classes of living beings, each protects its own body and does not allow itself to be preyed upon; yet, suffering from hunger, they constantly harbor evil thoughts of eating the flesh of others. When their lives end, they fall again into the evil realms (*durgati*). It is difficult for them to obtain a human birth, let alone attain the path to nirvāṇa.
“Mahāmati, you should know that those who eat meat have such immeasurable faults as these; those who do not eat meat are, however, a collection of immeasurable merits.”
Mahāmati! Ordinary worldlings do not understand such faults of eating meat nor the merit of abstaining from it; therefore, I shall now briefly explain why the eating of meat is forbidden.
Mahāmati!

If all people did not eat meat, there would likewise be no one who kills sentient beings. Because people eat meat, if there is nothing available to eat, they seek it out everywhere and purchase it; those motivated by profit kill for the sake of sale, and those who buy cause the killing. Therefore, the buyer is no different from the killer. For this reason, eating meat can obstruct the Noble Path.

Mahāmati! Those who eat meat become attached to its flavor; eventually, when there are no more animals left, they will even eat human flesh—how much more so for deer, wild boar, pheasant, rabbit, goose, swan, pig, sheep, chicken, dog, camel, donkey, elephant, horse, dragon, snake, fish, and turtle? Having life as their nature, whether in water or on land, if one encounters them, one does not eat them [only out of compassion], yet because of attachment to the taste of meat, one employs various expedients to slaughter sentient beings. One creates all kinds of snares, nets, traps, and pitfalls; one sets nets upon mountains, spreads nets upon the ground, and dams rivers and seas. Everywhere across water and land, one places nets, traps, pit-falls, bows, swords, and poisoned arrows until there is no empty space between them. Sentient beings throughout the void, on land, in the air, and in the water are all slaughtered for the sake of eating meat.

Mahāmati! Hunters, butchers, and those who eat meat possess a firm and malicious intent that renders them incapable of compassion. Upon seeing sentient beings with plump bodies and well-nourished flesh, they give rise to a craving for the taste of raw meat; pointing to one another, they say, "This may be eaten," without conceiving even a single thought of revulsion. For this reason, I say that those who eat meat sever the seed of great compassion.

“Mahāmati! When I observe the world, there is no such thing as meat that does not come from a living being. It is impossible for there to be meat that one has not killed oneself, nor caused another to kill, nor approved of being killed by another, yet which has not originated from a living being.”
If there were such meat that did not originate from the command [of killing] and was a fine delicacy, for what reason would I not permit people to eat it?
Having searched throughout the world, no such meat exists; therefore, I declare that eating meat is a transgression. Because it cuts off the lineage of the Tathāgata, I do not permit its consumption.

“Mahāmati! After my parinirvāṇa, in a future age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be those among my disciples who have left the household life, having shaved off their hair and beards, claiming for themselves: ‘I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya. Clad in my kaṣāya robes, they will be as ignorant as small children. Claiming to be masters of the Vinaya, they will fall into the two extremes; with various false conceptualizations and discursive thoughts agitating their minds, they will be greedily attached to the taste of meat. Following their own subjective views, they will say within the Vinaya that it is permissible to eat meat. They will also slander me by saying that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, permit people to eat meat; they will say that meat-eating was permitted because of a specific prohibition; and they will even slander me by saying that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, himself ate meat.”
Mahāmati!

In all the sūtras, such as the *Gajapramardana*, the *Aṅgulimālīya*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Mahāmegha*, I have not permitted the eating of meat, nor have I taught that meat constitutes a flavor worthy of food.

Mahāmati! If I had permitted my śrāvaka disciples to eat meat, I would never have praised with my own mouth those who constantly practice great compassion and act in accordance with reality; nor would I have praised those who practice the dhūta austerities in the śmaśānas; nor would I have praised those who practice the Mahāyāna and abide in the Mahāyāna; nor would I have praised those who abstain from eating meat. I do not eat it myself, nor do I permit others to eat it; therefore, I encourage the cultivation of bodhisattva practices and praise the non-eating of meat, urging that one should regard all sentient beings as if they were one's only child. How then could I proclaim that I permit the eating of meat?

For the sake of my disciples who practice the three vehicles, so that they may swiftly attain the fruits [of their practice], I have prohibited all meat and forbidden its consumption entirely; how, then, can you say that within my Vinaya I permit people to eat meat?

Furthermore, as for the statement that in other sūtras the Tathāgata permitted people to eat three kinds of meat, one should know that such a person does not understand the sequential prohibitions of the Vinaya, and thus proclaims that eating is permissible.
Why is this? Mahāmati!
There are two kinds of meat: first, that which is killed by another; [the second is that which dies naturally].
Second, as for those that die of themselves:

because worldly people say that some meat may be eaten while other meat may not, [they claim] that the flesh of elephants, horses, dragons, snakes, humans, ghosts, monkeys, pigs, dogs, and oxen is forbidden to eat, while the rest may be eaten. Yet butchers do not distinguish between what may or may not be eaten; they slaughter them all and sell them everywhere. Sentient beings, having committed no fault, are thus slain without cause. For this reason, I have ordained that neither meat from animals killed by others nor meat from those that died of themselves may be eaten.
"Those involving seeing, hearing, or suspecting are what is called 'killed by another'; those not involving seeing, hearing, or suspecting are what is called 'died of natural causes.
Therefore, Mahāmati, in my Vinaya I proclaim these words:"

"Whatever meat there may be is an impure food for all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya; it defiles the pure life and obstructs the factors of the noble path. There is no expedient means by which it can be consumed."

"If there is someone who says that within the Buddha’s Vinaya, the three kinds of meat are taught as not being permitted for consumption and not being permitted for consumption, you should know that this person firmly abides in the Vinaya and does not slander me."
Mahāmati!
Now, within this Laṅkā Sūtra, at all times and in all circumstances, there is no means whatsoever by which any meat may be eaten.
Therefore, Mahāmati!
I do not prohibit the eating of meat for the sake of a single person; rather, it is forbidden for all beings in both the present and the future.

Therefore, Mahāmati, if those deluded people who call themselves Vinaya masters claim that the *Vinaya* permits the eating of meat, or even slander me by saying that the Tathāgata himself eats meat, those foolish people will create great karmic obstacles. For a long night they shall fall into places devoid of benefit, lacking holy ones, and where the Dharma is not heard; they shall not encounter the noble disciples of the present or the future, let alone the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Mahāmati!

Regarding the various grains, flours, oils, honey, sesame, and beans that śrāvakas should regularly consume to sustain a pure livelihood—yet which they might store improperly or acquire through improper means—I say that such impure food is not even permitted to be eaten; how much less, then, could the impurity of blood and flesh ever be permitted?
"Mahāmati!
My disciples—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas—feed upon the food of the Dharma, not upon the food of physical sustenance; how much more so, then, is this true for the Tathāgata?
Mahāmati!"

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, subsist on the Dharma and abide in the Dharma; they do not possess bodies sustained by food and drink, nor bodies that dwell upon any kind of nutriment. They are free from craving for the necessities of life and the pursuit of existence; they have distanced themselves from all afflictions and the faults of habitual tendencies. With excellent discernment, they know the mind, mental factors, wisdom, omniscience, and all-seeing vision, and they regard all sentient beings with impartial compassion.
Therefore, Mahāmati, I regard all sentient beings as my only child; how could I permit them to eat meat?
I do not even approve of it, much less eat it myself.
Mahāmati!

Just as all these—scallions, leeks, garlic, and shallots—are foul-smelling, impure, and capable of obstructing the noble path, and likewise obstruct the pure realms of worldly humans and devas, let alone the retributive fruits of the pure lands of the Buddhas;
so too is alcohol, for it can obstruct the noble path, diminish wholesome karma, and give rise to various transgressions.
"Therefore, Mahāmati,
those who seek the noble path should not consume any pungent flavors that leave a lingering scent, such as wine, meat, onions, leeks, garlic,
or scallions. At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked:
