"The Buddha declared that wine, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic are impure, and that none of these are permitted to be eaten."
Rākṣasas and the like devour them; these are not flavors consumed by the noble ones.
Those who eat them are rebuked by the noble ones, and an evil reputation spreads abroad.
We pray that the Buddha will explain in detail: what are the transgressions and blessings of eating and not eating?
"O Mahāmati! Listen attentively as I speak of the faults within food: wine, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic—these obstruct the factors conducive to the Noble Path."
I observe that within the three realms, among those who have attained the noble path,
and throughout the world since beginningless time, there is not one who has not been my relative through successive births.
How can it be that, in the midst of such kinship, some are eaten while others are not?
Contemplate the origin of flesh: its source is most impure;
it arises from a mixture of pus and blood, combined with urine, excrement, pus, and mucus.
A practitioner of purity should contemplate this and refrain from eating it.
Various kinds of meat and onions, as well as wine, must not be drunk;
various kinds of leeks and garlic—the practitioner should always keep far from these.
One should always stay far from sesame oil and never sleep on a bed with holes in it.
Because they fly about and kill other living beings,
and because eating meat increases physical strength; from strength arises wrong thought,
and from wrong thought arises craving— therefore, the eating of meat is not permitted.
From eating meat, craving arises; through craving, the mind becomes deluded and intoxicated.
This intoxication fosters desire, preventing liberation from birth and death.
For profit they kill sentient beings; for meat they pursue wealth.
Those two, due to their evil karma, will fall into the Raurava Hell after death.
The three kinds of pure meat—those not seen, heard, or suspected of being killed for oneself—do not exist in this world;
those who eat meat will be reborn among the flesh-eaters.
Foul and loathsome, one will constantly be born among the insane;
One will often be born into the families of caṇḍālas, Hunters, and butchers.
Or one may be born as a rākṣasī, Or in various places where meat is eaten.
Rākṣasas, cats, and wildcats— those who eat meat are born among them.
In the *Gaja-pāda*, the *Mahāmegha*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, I have not permitted the eating of meat.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas, all censure those who eat meat without shame or remorse;
such persons shall be constantly deranged in every birth.
Having first spoken of meat seen, heard, or suspected, all flesh-eating has already been forbidden.
Due to deluded thoughts and lack of awakening, one gives rise to the notion of eating meat.
Just as the fault of lust obstructs the noble liberation,
so too do wine, meat, scallions, leeks, and garlic all serve as obstacles to the Noble Path.
Sentient beings in future ages, out of ignorance regarding meat, will say:
"This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it.
One should regard pure food as medicine, just like eating the flesh of one's own son.
Contentment gives rise to disenchantment; practicing the way, one goes for alms.
For those who dwell securely in a mind of loving-kindness, I say they are always disenchanted;
even with lions, jackals, tigers, and wolves, they may constantly dwell and travel together.
The sight of one eating meat causes fear; how, then, can it be eaten?
Therefore, the practitioner, with a mind of loving-kindness, does not eat meat.
Eating meat severs the heart of compassion and distances one from nirvāṇa and liberation.
Furthermore, because it violates the teachings of the Sages, I do not permit the eating of meat.
Those of the Brahma-lineage who do not eat meat, as well as those practicing the Path,
attain wisdom and prosperity precisely by not eating meat.
17. Chapter on Dhāraṇīs (8). *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Chapter Seventeen: Dhāraṇīs. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the noble Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "Mahāmati!"

"You should listen attentively and receive and uphold this *dhāraṇī* of my *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. This *dhāraṇī* has been spoken, is being spoken, and will be spoken by all Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
Mahāmati!
I shall now also speak for the sake of those Dharma-preachers who uphold, receive, read, and recite the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra;
thus I utter this mantra: "Dhūti dhūti."
Cūdā-cūḍe sucūḍe sucūḍe kāṭe kāṭe.
Amale amati vimale vimale.
Nimi nimi khi mi khi mi bha mi bha mi.
Kali kali kara-kali ācāma āci.
Cai cai dou cai rang cai su fu cai.
Khaṭe khaṭe bhaṭe bhaṭe himi himi ḍimi ḍimi.
Rāṭi rāṭi, vāṭi vāṭi, vaṇḍe vaṇḍe.
A-ṭi-mi-ṭi-tu-ḍa-ri-du-ḍa-di-pa-ra-di.
E ě jì e ě jì zhuó jì zhuó jì lí lì ěr qǐ mēi.
Śrīṃ kṣiṃ kṣiṃ kṣiṃ kṣuḥ kṣuḥ kṣuḥ kṣuḥ!
Chou xu chou xu zhou zhou zhou zhou chu chu chu chu.
*Svāhā*. "Mahāmati!
These are the mantra phrases from the Great Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra.
Good men and good women, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās—"
Bhikṣuṇīs and others who are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain these phrases to others—
no one will be able to find fault in them, whether it be gods or goddesses, nāgas or nāga daughters, yakṣas or yakṣa daughters,
asuras or asura daughters, garuḍas or garuḍa daughters, or kinnaras...
Naras and Nārī-kinnaras, mahoragas and mahoraga-nāris, pūtanas and pūtana-nāris,
kumbhāṇḍas and kumbhāṇḍa-nāris, piśācas and piśāca-nāris, mūṣakas and mūṣaka-nāris,
apsarases and apsaras-nāris, rākṣasas and rākṣasa-nāris.
Te-ka-te-ka, daughter; U-chou-ho-lo, U-chou-ho-lo, daughter; Chia-t'a-pu-to-lo, Chia-t'a-pu-to-lo, daughter.
Whether they be humans or non-humans, whether they be human women or non-human women, none can find fault in them.
If there are evil spirits or ghosts who seek to harm people, [this mantra] shall cause them to quickly depart.
"Regarding those evil spirits who depart: if one recites this dhāraṇī mantra one hundred times, all those evil spirits will flee in terror, wailing and crying out as they run away.
The Buddha further addressed Mahāmati:
“Mahāmati! To protect these Dharma-preachers who uphold the Dharma, I shall further proclaim a dhāraṇī.
And he spoke this mantra:
“Pātumī pātumītebi heṇiheṇiheṇide jūri jūra jūre hūra hūre yūre yūra yūre pare para pare munci cchindai bhindai vandhai madai tichana kāli svāhā. “Mahāmati! [This is the mantra.]”
Regarding these dharani mantra phrases, if a good son or a good daughter receives,
maintains, reads, recites, and explains them to others, no one will be able to cause them harm— whether it be a deva or a devi,
a naga or a nagi, a yaksha or a yakshini, or an asura or an asuri.
Garuḍas and Garuḍa maidens, kiṃnaras and kiṃnara maidens,
mahoragas and mahoraga maidens, gandharvas and gandharva maidens, bhūtas and bhūta maidens,
kumbhāṇḍas and kumbhāṇḍa maidens, piśācas and piśāca maidens, and mātṛs.
Mūṭolā women, amātrā-amātrā women, rākṣasas and rākṣasa women, mūḍharas and mūḍhara women,
kāṭapūtanas and kāṭapūtana women— whether they be humans or non-humans,
whether they be human women or non-human women— all of them [shall not...].
One will be able to discern its faults. Mahāmati!

If there is anyone who can receive, uphold, read, and recite these mantra syllables, that person shall be said to have recited the entire Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra. For this reason, I have taught these dhāraṇī syllables to ward off all rākṣasas and to protect all good men and good women who uphold this sūtra.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter 18: General Summary (9–10), Part One of Eighteen At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate the profound meaning of this sutra, spoke these verses:
"Just as various birds and beasts in summer Are deluded by the waves they perceive in their minds;
Just as various birds and beasts crave water, yet that water has no substantial reality;
so too, the seed of consciousness perceives the movement of all objective realms.
All ignorant sentient beings are like those with cataracts who see illusory objects.
Contemplation and the object of contemplation, as well as the one who contemplates—when one sees the distinction of the true reality, one knows it and attains liberation.
These dharmas are not solid; they arise from false discrimination.
Empty is false conceptualization; based upon that emptiness, conceptualization arises.
The dharmas of the five aggregates, consciousness, and so forth, are like the reflection of a tree in water;
like seeing illusions, dreams, and the like—do not engage in conceptualization within consciousness.
Like illusions, zombies, or mechanical devices, And like dreams, lightning, or clouds—always thus;
By severing the continuity of the three marks, Sentient beings attain liberation.
Based on various dharmas of false conceptualization, Therefore, consciousness arises.
The eight or nine various consciousnesses are like the many waves upon the water;
Relying on the principle of perfumed seeds, they constantly and firmly bind the body.
The mind flows toward its objects, just as iron is drawn to a magnet.
Relying upon all sentient beings, the true nature is free from all conceptualizations;
it is remote from all conditioned activities and detached from both the knower and the known.
Practicing the illusion-like samādhi, one transcends the practices of the ten stages.
Observe the dharma of the mind-king, which is free from the characteristics of mind, objects, and consciousness.
When one knows that the mind is constantly shifting, one abides in that which is eternally unchanging;
dwelling in the palace of the lotus, it appears as an illusory realm.
Having dwelt in that supreme state, one attains all sovereign activities;
like a mani jewel manifesting colors, one performs the work of liberating sentient beings.
There is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned, as all conceptualizing minds are eliminated.
The ignorant grasp with a lack of wisdom, like a barren woman dreaming of a child.
Quiescence and non-arising, the five aggregates, and the continuity of the person;
the conditions of all objective realms—emptiness, existence, and non-existence.
I speak of various skillful means, yet there is no such real nature therein;
the ignorant grasp at it as truly existent, though there is neither a characteristic nor that which is characterized.
I have awakened to all phenomena, yet I do not awaken to anything at all.
I possess all-knowledge, yet I am without all-knowledge.
Fools and ordinary people discriminate, claiming themselves to be wise men of the world;
I have never awakened to anything, nor do I awaken sentient beings.
All phenomena are but mind; the aggregates are like the appearance of falling hairs.
Since the appearance of the wheel is ultimately non-existent, where could there be any discrimination?
From the beginning, there have been no produced things, nor are they found within any conditions.
The son of a barren woman and empty flowers— if one can thus perceive conditioned phenomena,
then at that time, seeing and the seen, and the delusion regarding dharmas,
will all cease; I shall not enter nirvana, nor shall I extinguish the karma of various marks.
The cessation of all conceptualizing consciousness—this is my nirvāṇa;
it is not the cessation of the characteristics of phenomena, which is the false conceptualization of the ignorant.
Just as when a torrential stream is exhausted, at that time no waves arise.
Just as various consciousnesses cease, having ceased they do not arise again.
Emptiness and the absence of the marks of consciousness are like illusions, fundamentally unarisen;
transcending existence and non-existence, these phenomena are like dreams.
I speak of the one true dharma, which is free from all conceptualization and reflection;
it is the sublime realm of the noble ones, devoid of the essential nature and characteristics of dualistic phenomena.
Just as one perceives the appearance of a firefly, which is manifold yet lacks reality; so too is this world.
The world perceives the four great elements, and all various things are likewise so.
Just as one displays various illusory forms based upon grass, wood, and stone,
yet those illusions possess no such reality, so too is the nature of all phenomena.
There is no grasping and nothing to be grasped; there is neither liberation nor bondage.
Like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like a dream, or like a film over the eye—when one sees thus in reality, one is free from the defilement of conceptual discrimination.
Abiding in suchness-concentration, they see me without doubt.
Herein there is no mind or consciousness; it is like space or a mirage.
Knowing all phenomena in this way, yet not knowing even a single phenomenon.
Detached from the conditions of existence and non-existence, all phenomena are unborn;
the mind is deluded within the three realms, and thus various views arise.
Dreams and worldly phenomena—these two are equal.
The visible and the means of subsistence, All tactile objects and their measurements;
The body is impermanent in this world, And various forms are likewise so.
Thus did the World-Honored One of the world Speak regarding these matters.
The mind is the seed of the three realms; through delusion, one perceives the present and the future.
Knowing that worldly distinctions have no such real dharmas, and seeing the world in this way, one is able to leave behind all birth and death.
Arising and non-arising are the views of the deluded and confused;
Non-arising and non-ceasing are what those who cultivate wisdom perceive.
The sublime realm of Akaniṣṭha is a place free from all unwholesome conduct.
Always acting without discrimination, detached from all mental factors;
having attained mastery over the powers and superknowledges, they reach the states of various samādhis.
Therein they achieve perfect enlightenment, while transformation buddhas achieve it here.
All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished; such is the essence of all phenomena.
Through immeasurable billions of emanations, he appears within that very essence;
when fools hear the Buddha’s Dharma, it is like an inconceivable echo.
Far removed from beginning, middle, and end, And free from existence and non-existence;
Universally unmoving and pure, Without characteristics, yet manifesting all characteristics.
The nature of consciousness veils the Dharmakāya, Yet it exists within all bodies.
Delusion is a phantom existence; the phantom is not the cause of delusion.
The mind has no dharma of delusion, nor is it that it does not exist at all;
bound by these two dharmas, the ālayavijñāna arises.
When the mind perceives in this way— that my Dharma is like a torrential stream—
and views the world thus, at that moment it transforms all mental states;
such a one is my true child, who has accomplished the practice of the true Dharma.
Heat, moisture, solidity, and motion—thus do the ignorant discriminate among phenomena.
They do not truly exist through focused mindfulness; there is neither the characteristic nor that which is characterized.
These eight kinds of substances constitute a single body: the physical form and the various sense faculties.
The fool discriminates among various forms, Deluded by the net of the body;
Through the conjunction of various causes and conditions, Ignorance gives rise to discrimination.
Not knowing such dharmas, One wanders through the three realms.
All phenomena and language are the conceptual constructions of sentient beings;
yet all phenomena are non-existent, like illusions and like dreams.
Observing all phenomena in this way, one dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa.
The mind contains manifold seeds; the objective realm of the mind is directly perceived.
From the discernment of what is seen, delusion delights in dualistic dharmas.
Ignorance, craving, and karma are the causes of this mind and its mental factors.
Dependent on the phenomena of other-power they arise; therefore, they are called phenomena of other-power.
Based on the phenomena of dependent origination, the mind is deluded regarding its objects;
thus, they do not constitute [true] discrimination, but are rather deluded and false discrimination.
The mind is bound by causes and conditions; therefore, various bodies are born.
If one is free from all causes and conditions, I say that no phenomena are perceived.
Free from all phenomena of causes and conditions, one is free from the marks of all phenomena.
Not abiding within any phenomena, I speak of not perceiving objects.
Just as a king or a householder, having gathered various birds and beasts together in a house or a field, shows them to his children.
These various marks of mine are like diverse reflections;
with the wisdom of my inner body as my son, I teach the Dharma of the ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi).
Just as the waves of the great ocean arise from the conditions of the wind, [so does this wisdom arise].
It is able to arise and manifest before one, without any interruption.
The *ālaya-vijñāna* is constant; arising based on the realm of wind, the various waves of consciousness are able to dance forth, arising without end.
The characteristics of the grasper and the grasped—sentient beings perceive them thus;
yet the visible has no such characteristics—the ignorant see it in this way.
The *ālaya* fundamental consciousness, the manas, and the mental consciousness;
Free from the grasped and the grasper—such is the characteristic I have taught.
Within the five aggregates there is no self, nor person, nor sentient being;
when they arise, it is the various consciousnesses that arise; when they cease, it is the various consciousnesses that cease.
Just as the heights and depths in a painting are visible though they do not exist as such,
so too these various material bodies appear with characteristics that do not exist as such.
They are like a city of the Gandharvas, or the water seen by birds and beasts in their parched thirst.
Thus, what can be seen is seen; yet through the observation of wisdom, such [seeing] does not exist.
It is free from the measurable and from conceptualization; it is neither cause nor effect.
It is free from the grasper and the grasped; it is free from the seer and the seen.
Awakening occurs by depending on the aggregates as conditions; there is no seer and nothing seen.
If neither the seer nor the seen is perceived, how can one cultivate that Dharma?
Through conditions, causes, and analogies, one establishes the intent and the causal conditions.
Like a dream, a gandharva-city, a wheel, a mirage, the sun and moon,
a flame, an illusion, and other such metaphors, I negate the arising of all phenomena;
like a dream or a delusion, beings are empty conceptualizations.
Not relying on the three realms, with neither internal nor external existing;
seeing that all phenomena do not arise, one then attains the patience of non-arising.
One attains the illusion-like samādhi, as well as the body of sovereign power.
The various supernormal powers and masteries, The strengths, the mind, and its manifold phenomena— All dharmas are fundamentally unarisen;
In emptiness, they lack any intrinsic nature or characteristics.
Those people are deluded and do not realize this; They follow causes and conditions in arising and ceasing.
Just as the deluded discriminate, the mind perceives its own mind;
seeing various external appearances, yet in reality there is no dharma to be seen.
One sees the skeletal form of a Buddha-image and the dissolution of the great elements.
The well-awakened mind is able to know that which sustains the characteristics of the world;
the body sustains the necessities of life, and these are the three kinds of objects that can be grasped.
Consciousness grasps the realm of consciousness, and the mental consciousness is the third among the three types of discrimination.
Discrimination and the object of discrimination, as well as the realm of all words—these cannot reveal the true dharma; those whose awakening is deluded do not see it.
All dharmas lack intrinsic nature; this the wise are able to realize.
The practitioner then comes to rest, abiding in the state of signlessness.
Like a figure drawn in ink upon a rooster, the fool grasps it as "this is my rooster";
so too do the deluded worldlings grasp [the teachings], for the three vehicles are one and the same.
There are no śrāvakas, nor are there any pratyekabuddhas;
yet those who see the forms of śrāvakas, as well as those who see all the Tathāgatas,
are shown these transformation bodies by the great compassion of the bodhisattvas.
The three realms are mind alone, devoid of the two kinds of essence and characteristics.
The transformation of those various characteristics is itself suchness;
the characteristics of phenomena and persons blaze like the light of the sun and moon.
Just as great maṇi jewels perform their functions without discrimination,
so too are the dharmas of all Buddhas; like those with cataracts who perceive floating hairs,
the ignorant grasp at these dharmas through false conceptualization.
Free from arising, abiding, and ceasing, And free from permanence and impermanence,
The phenomena of defilement and purity that can be seen Are like the appearance of floating hairs in the sky;
Like a person under the influence of datura Who sees various forms upon the great earth.
All things appear as gold, yet there has never been any gold therein;
likewise, these deluded people are stained by the mental phenomena of the beginningless mind.
Existence arises like a phantom or a mirage, yet fools grasp it as real.
The one child and the childless: the great ocean is the one child, yet it is also the childless multitude; observe the seed of the mind.
When the one child is pure, it transforms into the seedless.
Equal and without discrimination, arising is itself birth-and-death;
it can produce all manner of seeds, and for this reason it is called the seed.
Phenomena are not produced by causes and conditions; phenomena do not cease by causes and conditions.
Phenomena arise solely through causes and conditions; the mind discriminates them in this way.
The three realms are merely provisional names; in reality, there is no substantial essence to phenomena.
Those with deluded awareness discriminate and grasp at these provisional names as being real.
When observing the substantial reality of all phenomena, I do not deny delusion;
since phenomena do not arise from substantial reality, observing this leads to liberation.
I do not perceive that illusions are non-existent, yet I speak of all phenomena as being existent.
Inversion is as swift as lightning; therefore, it is said to be like an illusion.
It is not born from its own nature, yet it appears as if born; all causes and conditions lack intrinsic substance.
There is no location nor any essence, for there is only verbal expression.
It does not obstruct dependent arising and ceasing, nor does it obstruct the conjunction of conditions;
it only obstructs the various views of the deluded who conceptualize that things arise from causes and conditions.
In reality, there is no dharma with a substantial essence of consciousness, nor is there any objective entity or fundamental consciousness.
Ignorance gives rise to conceptualization, like the evil perceptions of a corpse.
The triple world is but mind; the sons of the Buddhas are able to see this.
They immediately attain the body of the same nature, free from the conditioned phenomena of volitional construction.
Attaining power and mastery, as well as the associated dharmas;
manifesting all various forms, the mental dharmas arise in this way.
Yet there is neither mind nor form; it is the delusion of the beginningless mind.
At that time, the practitioner attains the vision of the signless (*animitta*).
Observing within wisdom, they do not perceive any sentient beings;
nor do they perceive signs, things, or conventional designations (*prajñapti*), for the mind grasps at all shifting phenomena.
My sons have transcended this; they practice without conceptual discrimination.
Like a city of gandharvas, a magical illusion, a mass of hair-tufts, or a mirage—though devoid of reality, they perceive it as real; such is the nature of all phenomena.
Just as the mind perceives all phenomena, they possess no such intrinsic nature or characteristics.
All phenomena are unarisen; one perceives only delusive dharmas.
Those of the hair-path (ordinary beings) are deluded by discrimination, for they abide in the duality of dharmas.
Initial consciousness gives rise to discrimination, And various seeds are perfumed;
Consciousness arises like a torrential stream— If that is severed, it will not arise again.
Various thoughts and contemplations of dharmas, If they arise solely within the mind;
Just as within empty space or a wall, why do [things] not arise?
If there were even the slightest perception of characteristics, the mind would arise from conditions;
if it arose from causes and conditions, one could not say it is "mind-only."
The mind grasps its own mind; there is no dharma and nothing born from causes.
The essence of the mind and its dharmas is pure; there is no perfuming within empty space.
Through false imagination, one grasps at one's own mind; therefore, the mind manifests as arising.
External phenomena have no visible existence; therefore, it is said that there is only mind.
The fundamental consciousness is simply mind, while the manas is able to contemplate objects.
Because it can grasp all objects, I say that there is only mind.
The mind is always of an indeterminate nature; the intellect grasps signs from both extremes.
Grasping present phenomena is consciousness, which is either wholesome or unwholesome.
To be free from these two types of conscious characteristics is the gateway to the ultimate truth.
The distinctions of the three vehicles are taught, yet in tranquility there are no such characteristics.
If the mind abides in tranquility and practices upon the Buddha-ground, this was taught by the Buddhas of the past;
it is likewise for those of the present and the future.
The first seven stages are the ground of mind; the eighth stage is the stage of tranquility.
The second stage is the sphere of practice; the remaining stages are my own Dharma.
When one’s inner body is purified, this is my stage of mastery.
In the ultimate state of mastery, Akaniṣṭha manifests;
like the flames of a fire, it emits various radiances;
with all manner of delightful minds, it transforms and creates the triple world.
There may be a prior transformation, which then manifests as the three realms of existence;
where those dharmas are taught, that is my own sovereign ground.
The stages have no temporal sequence, and the same applies to the transformation of the lands.
Transcending all states of mind, this is the fruit of abiding in tranquility.
That which is unreal is called real, yet various things are perceived;
the foolish grasp at these with inversion—this is the variety of inversions.
Just as non-conceptual wisdom does not correspond to objective phenomena, so too the mind is not of the nature of form; therefore, it is non-conceptual.
This applies to the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless samādhis.
All marks are ultimately extinguished; therefore, they do not exist within the mind.
The dharmas of the fruit of srotāpanna, the sakṛdāgāmin, and the anāgāmin, as well as the fruits of the arhat—all these are delusions of the mind.
Emptiness, impermanence, and momentariness—these are how the foolish conceptualize conditioned phenomena;
through the analogies of the river and the seed, they analyze the meaning of momentariness.
Momentariness is non-conceptual and free from all conditioned activities.
All phenomena are unborn; this is what I teach as the meaning of the momentary (*kṣaṇika*).
To speak of birth in terms of existence or non-existence is the false doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas and others;
that all phenomena are ineffable is likewise their claim.
There are four modes of answering: answering directly, answering with a counter-question, answering by distinguishing the particulars, and answering with silence to refute externalists.
According to conventional truth, all things exist; according to ultimate truth, they do not.
Yet the true substance is without marks; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
To perceive illusory phenomena is therefore called conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*);
arising from verbal expression, such a real substance does not exist.
Where there is no phenomenon, there are words; yet in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), these do not truly exist.
This is precisely a matter of inversion; even that which is visible is non-existent.
If phenomena were to exist through inversion, then ultimate tranquility would be utterly non-existent.
Based upon inverted objects, one perceives the arising of all phenomena;
yet these are ultimately and certainly non-existent, being devoid of intrinsic nature.
The various things that are perceived arise from the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
The mind perceives external delusions, manifesting as the grasping of objects before it;
both conceptualization and non-conceptualization are the true nature of emptiness.
Like illusory images and various forms, they are like the golden hue of tree leaves.
Those who can see perceive through the eyes; the mind is permeated by the habit-energy of ignorance.
The Sage does not see delusion, nor does he see reality in the interval between them.
Delusion itself is reality, for reality is precisely that interval.
To be free from all delusions, yet still give rise to various signs—
that itself is delusion, like the impurity of a cataract in the eye.
Just as one with a cataract sees floating hairs, so too do people grasp at phenomena based on their confusion.
Within all objective realms, the deluded grasp at these phenomena.
All dharmas are like falling hairs, like the illusion of water in a mirage;
the three realms are like dreams and illusions—by practicing thus, one attains liberation.
Discrimination and the object of discrimination, that which gives rise to discrimination;
the bound, the binder, and the cause—these six are the causes of liberation.
There are no stages or truths, no lands or emanations.
The Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—these are merely the mind’s discriminations.
The human body and the five aggregates, all conditions and atoms;
the Supreme Person (Puruṣa) and the Creator (Īśvara)—these are merely the mind’s discriminations.
The mind pervades all places; all places are the mind.
Because one does not contemplate the mind skillfully, the nature of the mind appears to possess various marks.
Within the five aggregates there is no self; within the self there are no five aggregates.
These phenomena do not exist through conceptual construction, yet those phenomena are not non-existent.
Just as the ignorant construct all phenomena as existing, so too,
if one were to see them as truly existent, then everything would have to be seen as truly existent.
If all phenomena were non-existent, there would be neither defilement nor purity;
such is the view of the deluded, yet those phenomena are not thus.
To conceptualize the appearance of delusion is the discrimination of the *paratantra* (dependent nature).
Whatever names belong to those characteristics, these are called the characteristic of conceptualization (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*).
Names and characteristics are conceptualization; they are the conjunction of causes, conditions, and things.
If that mind does not arise, this is the characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*).
The reality-body of the Buddha of Retribution, as well as the marks of the emanated Buddhas;
sentient beings and Bodhisattvas, together with the lands of the ten directions;
the Dharma-emanated Buddha of habitual tendencies, and those who act as emanated Buddhas.
All these are derived from the land of Amitābha;
they are the teachings spoken through emanations and transformations, as well as the teachings spoken by the Reward Buddha.
These are extensively explained in the sūtras; you should understand their underlying intent.

Gold, silver, red and white copper, alms bowls, and various vessels—
those who practice the pure life must not possess any of these;
garments made of *kauseya* silk— none of these may be worn.
Kambala robes, cow-dung, grass, fruit, and leaves;
dyed with green, red, or clay-based liquids to spoil their original white color;
made of stone, clay, or iron; or of conch-shell and lapis lazuli.
Such an almsbowl is permitted for possession, provided it is of the measure of a māṭhara.
For the sake of cutting cloth, the possession of a four-inch knife is permitted;
its blade should be curved like a half-moon. One must not learn worldly arts and crafts.
A practitioner who trains according to reality must not purchase requisites through trade;
for what is needed, they should request them from laypeople or various upāsakas.
They should constantly guard the sense faculties and understand the meaning of reality as it is.
Reciting and studying the Sūtras, as well as training in the various Vinayas;
not mingling with laypeople— such is the practice of those who cultivate the Way.
In empty places and among burial mounds, in caves and beneath forest trees.
In the grass of the śītavana cemetery, or even in the open air;
a practitioner who trains according to reality should dwell in such places.
The three robes should always accompany the body, and no other wealth or money should be stored.
For the sake of the body, one requires clothing; when others offer it, one may accept it.
When going out to beg for food, one likewise does not look to the left or right, but gazes six feet ahead on the ground, proceeding steadily and with composed dignity.
Just as a bee gathers from various flowers, so too is the begging for alms;
yet when bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are mingled among the crowds,
I declare to you, my disciples, that this is living by an evil livelihood.
One who practices according to reality shall not accept food at this place.
Whether it be a king, a minor ruler, a prince, a great minister, or a householder;
for the sake of seeking food and drink, one must not go to any of them.
The house of the deceased and the house of the living, the house of kinsmen and the house of those one loves;
a bhikṣu and his various associates—these practitioners do not eat from such places.
Where the smoke of the monastery never ceases and various kinds of food are constantly prepared;
Therefore, one should not eat what has been prepared for another person.
Free from the factions of existence and non-existence, and able to see the bonds of the seen and the seer;
the practitioner contemplates the world as being apart from the dharmas of arising and ceasing.
Through union with the power of samādhi, And mastery over the various supernormal faculties;
If one does not give rise to conceptual discrimination, One will before long attain the Dharma as it truly is.
From the most excellent of beings, who are like subtle atoms, Do not engage in discrimination regarding conditions.
Through the conjunction of various causes and conditions, the practitioner does not engage in conceptual discrimination.
One discriminates the various worlds as arising from diverse habitual perfumings;
yet when the practitioner contemplates according to reality, the three realms of existence are like illusions and dreams.
Do not discriminate among the three realms of existence—body, sustenance, and abode;
Be free from the slanders of existence and non-existence, and likewise free from views of existence and non-existence.
Regarding food and drink as if taking medicine, keep body and mind always upright.
With single-minded devotion and reverence,
one should know the characteristics of all the Vinayas and the various Sūtras,
as well as the characteristics of all dharmas, by practicing according to reality toward the Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas.
The five dharmas, their essence, and the mind— Practicing the signless nature of non-self;
The pure inner dharmakāya, The various stages and the stage of Buddhahood.
One who practices in this manner Abides upon the great lotus flower.
The Great Compassion of all Buddhas Strokes his head with hands that grant all wishes.
Transmigrating through the six realms, He conceives a sense of weariness toward all existence;
Arousing the practice of suchness, He proceeds to the śītavana forest.
The forms and characteristics of the sun and moon, as well as the characteristics of flower-groves;
the various [manifestations] of space and fire—these are the dharmas seen by the practitioner.
Seeing such various signs, they grasp at the teachings of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, following the path of the śrāvakas and the realm of the pratyekabuddhas—
having distanced himself from such things— he dwells in a place of tranquility;
at that time, the Buddha’s wondrous radiance proceeds to all lands.
He strokes the crown of that Bodhisattva’s head—this is the wondrous mark of stroking the crown;
by acceding to the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), at that moment one attains a sublime body.
The essence of dharmas is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
To slander the existence or non-existence of phenomena is to discriminate within the Middle Way.
To discriminate that there are no causes is the view of nihilism;
to perceive various external phenomena is for such a person to destroy the Middle Way.
Not abandoning the characteristics of all phenomena, for fear of the characteristic of annihilation;
existence and non-existence are slanders against the Dharma—thus one speaks of the Middle Way.
Awakening is merely the internal mind; it does not extinguish external phenomena.
The transformation of false discrimination is itself the Dharma of the Middle Way.
When there is only mind and nothing visible, and one does not give rise to [thoughts] apart from the mind—
this is the Dharma of the Middle Way, as taught by me and all the Buddhas.
Arising and non-arising, existence and non-existence are empty;
all phenomena lack intrinsic nature—do not discriminate between these two dharmas.
To discriminate that there are existent dharmas, and for the fool to discriminate liberation, [is delusion].
When the mind’s conceptualization is not perceived, one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings.
When one realizes that what is seen is but one's own mind, at that time one is free from the two views;
knowing reality as it is and remaining detached, one does not extinguish the characteristic of conceptualization.
One truly knows that the visible is mind; at that time, one knows that discrimination arises.
When no discriminations arise, this is True Suchness, free from mind.
It is free from the errors of all non-Buddhists; yet if one perceives the arising of various phenomena, [one remains bound].
The wise should grasp that which is nirvāṇa and not annihilation.
To know this dharma is to know the Buddha, as taught by me and other Buddhas;
to view all dharmas otherwise is the teaching of the outsiders.
Unborn yet appearing to be born, Non-retrogressive yet constantly appearing to retrogress;
Simultaneously like the moon in water, Seen in ten billion lands.
A single body and infinite bodies, Kindling fire and pouring down rain;
The essence of mind and mind are not different; therefore, it is said that there is only mind.
Within the mind there is only mind; the mind arises without a mind.
The various colors and forms perceived are nothing but mind.
The bodies of Buddhas and śrāvakas, as well as the bodies of pratyekabuddhas,
and furthermore various other forms— these are said to be merely the internal mind.
The formless realm is without form, as are the form realm and the hells.
Forms appear for the sake of sentient beings, But these are merely causes and conditions of the mind.
Through the dharmas of the illusion-like samādhi, The body is born according to one's will;
With mastery over the mind in the ten stages, The Bodhisattva transforms and attains them.
The conceptualization of names within one’s own mind is stirred by frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*);
based on what is seen and heard, knowledge arises, and the ignorant rely on characteristics (*nimitta*) for their cognition.
These characteristics are the substance of the other-power (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which relies upon names for its conceptualization.
Discrimination consists of various marks; it arises from dharmas of dependent origination.
When wisdom contemplates all dharmas, there is neither dependence on others nor marks;
since ultimately nothing is established, upon what could wisdom rely to discriminate?
"If there were a perfected phenomenon, it would be free from existence and non-existence;
being free from the nature of existence and non-existence, how could two natures exist?
If one discriminates between two kinds of natures, then those two natures ought to exist."
Discrimination perceives various things; purity is the realm of the sages.
Discrimination is manifold; discrimination is dependent on other-power (*paratantra*).
If one discriminates otherwise, one falls into the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Discrimination is discrimination; seeing is the characteristic of the causal essence.
Discriminating speech is discrimination; seeing is the arising of the causal characteristic.
To be free from these two types of discrimination is the very accomplishment of the Dharma.
The Buddha’s emanations in the lands consist of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles.
There is no nirvana whatsoever; emptiness is free from all arising.
Regarding the thirty distinctions of the Buddha, there are further ten types.
The vessels of all lands depend upon the minds of sentient beings;
according to how they conceptualize the characteristics of phenomena, various phenomena appear to their vision.
Those phenomena possess no such diversity; such is the nature of both phenomena and the Buddha-world.
The Dharma-Buddha is the true Buddha; all others are emanations based upon him.
Through their own seeds, sentient beings perceive the forms of all Buddhas;
relying on the deluded, revolving mind, they are able to give rise to conceptual discrimination.
Reality is not separate from conceptualization, nor is it separate from signs;
it is the substantial essence and the experience of bliss, manifesting again as further emanations.
The thirty-six assemblies of Buddhas are the substantial essence of all Buddhas.
Like blue, red, and salt; like conch, milk, and rock honey;
like fresh fruit and various flowers; like the moon and its various rays:
they are neither one nor different, just like the great waves upon the water.
In this way, the seven consciousnesses, together with the mind, are in harmony;
just as the great ocean undergoes transformations, so do its various waves.
The ālaya is likewise, and the so-called consciousnesses are also thus.
The mind (citta), the mental faculty (manas), and the consciousness (vijñāna) differentiate the meaning of external signs.
These eight lack any distinct characteristics; they are neither the seer nor the seen.
Like the waves upon the waters of the great ocean, they possess no differentiated characteristics.
The various consciousnesses within the mind cannot be found through transformation;
the mind is able to create all karma, the manas is that which discriminates,
the mental consciousness is able to cognize phenomena, and the five consciousnesses are false perceptions.
Blue, red, white, and various other forms—these are what the consciousness of sentient beings perceives.
The Muni has taught me that this is like the relationship between water and waves;
yet blue, red, white, and the various others do not exist within the water or the waves.
The deluded perceive various signs and say they revolve within the mind;
yet this essence does not exist within the mind, and apart from the mind, there is no external perception.
If there were an object to be grasped, there would necessarily be a grasper.
The body, the means of subsistence, and the environment—these are said to be like water and waves.
The manifestation of consciousness in sentient beings is similar to water and waves;
just as waves arise from the waters of the great ocean, they appear as a whirling dance.
The fundamental consciousness transforms in this manner; why then is it not perceived?
Due to ignorance and lack of wisdom, the fundamental consciousness is like the waves of the ocean.
Because the water and the waves transform in relation to one another, this analogy is thus taught.
Just as the sun appears in the world, It shines equally upon all sentient beings.
"Likewise, O World-Honored One, Lamp of the World, Why do you not preach the Dharma for the ignorant?
Abiding in the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā), For what reason do you not speak the truth?"
If one speaks of real dharmas, there are no real dharmas within the mind;
They are like waves upon the waters of the sea, Like a mirror and like a dream.
As with the objects of one's own mind, They are seen equally, without before or after.
There is no simultaneous objective realm; therefore, they arise in succession.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to cognize all phenomena, while the mind (*manas*) further discriminates them.
The five consciousnesses perceive phenomena directly; in their state of quiescence, there is no succession.
Just as a master painter and his apprentice,
I abide in the sublime Dharma and speak for the sake of those who practice according to reality.
Free from conceptualization and its objects, this is the internal wisdom of true reality.
I, the Son of the Buddhas, speak this not for the sake of the foolish.
Just as various illusions may be seen though they do not exist in that way, so too are the various [teachings] spoken; whether they are spoken thus or not thus.
He teaches the Dharma for one person, but not for others;
just as when illnesses differ, physicians prescribe different medicines.
So too do the Buddhas, for the sake of sentient beings, teach various dharmas according to their minds.
Based on the seeds of external phenomena, one discriminates and speaks of present phenomena.
When the mind grasps phenomena of dependent power, that which is grasped is discrimination;
relying on the seeds within the mind, one perceives and grasps external objects.
The two kinds of transformation are delusion; there is no third cause.
Since delusion does not arise, upon what dharma could it not arise?
The sixty and eighteen dharmas—therefore, it is said that they are but mind.
One’s own mind perceives external phenomena; perceiving them as distinct from the self, if one enters into the discrimination of the mind, one can leave behind the marks of all dharmas.
Relying upon the ālaya, the various consciousnesses are produced.
The ignorant enter into the internal bases, while the mind perceives the external bases;
they grasp at stars and the optical illusion of hair-tufts, like seeing forms in a dream.
Whether conditioned or unconditioned, permanence does not exist as such within conceptual discrimination.
The city of the gandharvas and illusions, like the water-craving of birds and beasts—such things do not exist, yet they appear to be so; the dharmas of other-power are likewise.
My faculties, forms, and characteristics—I speak of these as the three kinds of mind.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are devoid of their own essential nature;
mind, intellect, and consciousness are devoid of the essential nature of others.
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are without self and without dual nature.
The intrinsic nature and characteristics of the five dharmas are the realm of all Buddhas.
Regarding their characteristics, there are three kinds, which depend upon a single cause of perfuming;
just as with a single type of pigment, various forms are seen upon a wall.
The two kinds of mind of non-self, The characteristics of the manas and the various vijñānas;
The characteristics of the five kinds of dharmic entities— The nature of self is not like these.
Far removed from all mental characteristics, Consciousness is detached from the characteristics of the manas.
The essence of all phenomena is thus; this is my domain.
Apart from the essence of all phenomena lies the nature of all Tathāgatas.
Regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind, they do not perform wholesome dharmas.
The nature of the Tathāgata is pure, Transcending all conditioned practices;
Mastery over the purification of the superknowledges Is adorned by the power of samādhi.
The various mind-made bodies Are this pure nature of the Tathāgata.
The wisdom of the inner body is free from defilement, transcending all causal characteristics.
The eighth stage and the Buddha stage—these are the nature of all Tathāgatas;
as are the Dūraṃgamā, Sādhumatī, Dharmameghā, and Buddhābhūmi stages.
This is the nature of all Buddhas, yet it is interspersed with the three vehicles on the other stages;
distinguished according to the bodies of sentient beings, it also manifests as the characteristics of ignorance.
To explain the seven stages, the Buddha taught the "Mind-Ground" (Cittabhūmi).
The various obstacles of speech, body, and mind do not exist within the seventh stage.
In the eighth stage, the sublime body is like the appearance of a dream or a torrential waterfall;
in the eighth and fifth stages, one trains in various arts and crafts.
All the sons of the Buddhas act as kings within the three realms of existence;
regarding birth and non-birth, they do not distinguish between emptiness and non-emptiness.
As for reality and unreality, such distinctions do not exist within their minds.
"This is real, this is not real"—do not discriminate that this is real.
This was not spoken for the sake of the Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas, nor for the sons of the Buddha;
existence and non-existence are not real, nor is there even the mark of emptiness.
Designations and real dharmas—none of these exist within the mind;
Dharmas exist according to worldly convention, but in the ultimate sense, they are entirely non-existent.
The delusion regarding the absence of real dharmas constitutes all these worldly conventional dharmas.
All phenomena are non-existent phenomena; I speak of them as mere designations.
Language and its employment—fools perceive these as real;
yet from the perspective of linguistic phenomena, they appear as real objective domains.
Phenomena arise from language, yet when phenomena are seen, they are not thus;
Just as there is no painting apart from a wall, and just as a shadow is absent apart from its form, so too is the fundamentally pure consciousness: it does not manifest as waves upon water.
The mind is like an illusion, and the mental faculty is like a cunning deceiver.
Consciousness, together with the five [sense-faculties], discriminates and perceives like a painter;
this is said to be the practice of the true Dharma, wherein all that is accumulated is a transformation.
These are the fundamental Buddhas; all others are transformation Buddhas.
When the mind is deluded within the visible, the visible exists within the mind.
The body, the means of sustenance, and the environment are all manifestations of the ālayavijñāna.
Mind, mentation, and consciousness—these five dharmas are the true substance.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas have taught that the two kinds of selflessness are pure;
they are not the domain of false conceptualization, nor are they for the śrāvakas.
This is the realm of the internal body, as taught by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas;
long and short exist in mutual dependence, and this and that arise in reliance upon one another.
Existence can bring about non-existence, and non-existence can bring about existence.
When analyzing atoms, one does not analyze the substance of form.
To say that it is "only mind" is a false view that cannot be purified;
therein, one analyzes emptiness, and non-emptiness is likewise so.
Existence and non-existence are merely conceptual constructions; it can be said that they do not exist in such a way.
When the atoms of merit combine, the ignorant conceptually construct "form.
Since each individual atom is non-existent, the meaning of [inherent] existence does not hold.
The forms and appearances are seen by one's own mind, yet sentient beings perceive them as existing externally;
since there are no external phenomena to be perceived, this [notion of externality] has no basis in reality.
The mind is like the appearance of floating hairs, an illusion, a dream, or a city of the Gandharvas.
The fire-wheel and the deer’s craving are truly non-existent, yet people perceive them;
so too with permanence and impermanence, oneness, duality, and non-duality.
Bound by the faults of beginningless time, the ignorant are deluded by conceptual discrimination.
I do not speak of three vehicles, but speak only of the One Vehicle;
it is for the sake of gathering in sentient beings that I speak of the One Vehicle.
There are three kinds of liberation, and I also teach the selflessness of phenomena.
The afflictions of the wisdom of equality are distinguished based on liberation.
Just as a piece of wood in water is carried away by the waves,
so too do deluded śrāvakas drift and wander amidst various signs.
They have no ultimate destination, nor do they undergo rebirth again.
Having attained the samādhi of quiescence, they remain unaware for immeasurable eons;
this is the concentration of the śrāvakas, not that of us bodhisattvas.
Free from all secondary afflictions, yet bound by the habitual tendencies of the afflictions;
intoxicated by the state of the bliss of samādhi, they dwell in that untainted realm (anāsrava-dhātu).
Just as a person intoxicated in the world awakens only after the wine has worn off;
Only then can that person attain the body of my Buddha-dharma.
Like an elephant sunk in deep mud, its body tossing and moving to and fro;
so too it is with the śrāvakas who are intoxicated by samādhi and thus submerged.
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Nine;
Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Chapter 18, Part 2: Summary "Relying on the sustaining power of all Buddhas, The powers of their vows are purified;
Their empowerment, samādhis, Virtues, and the ten stages."
Space, the horns of a rabbit, and the son of a barren woman—such are the conceptualized phenomena;
they are non-existent, yet names are spoken for them.
Conditioned by the perfuming of seeds, the world exists in a state that is neither existent nor non-existent.
One who is able to see this attains liberation, understanding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The substantial entity is a conceptual designation; the other-nature arises from causes.
I declare this to be the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*); it is thus taught throughout the sūtras.
Regarding syllables, phrases, and the collection of names—these are superior dharmas within the collection of names;
yet ignorant people discriminate among them, like an elephant sinking into deep mud.
There is the Deva-yāna and the Brahma-yāna, as well as the Śrāvaka-yāna.
The Tathāgatas and the Pratyekabuddhas—these are the vehicles I have taught.
The various vehicles are inexhaustible, for as long as there is a mind, they arise in such a way.
When the mind ceases and is extinguished, there are neither vehicles nor those who ride them.
The mind (citta), discrimination (vikalpa), and consciousness (vijñāna); the intellect (manas) and the mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna);
the ālaya and the three realms of existence—these are synonyms for the thinking mind (cintā-citta).
Life-force (jīva), warmth (uṣman), and consciousness; the ālaya and the life-faculty (jīvita-indriya).
The mind (*manas*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are different names for the same discrimination.
The mind sustains the body; the mind-organ (*manas*) constantly cognizes all phenomena;
consciousness perceives the objects of its own mind, and together with the [mental] consciousness, it discriminates.
I say that craving is the mother, and ignorance is the father;
consciousness perceives all objects, and for this reason it is called the Buddha.
The latent tendencies are the enemies, and the collection of elements is the aggregates.
When there is no longer a continuity of personal existence, the severance of that [continuity] is called "immediate" (*ānantarya*).
Through the two types of selflessness regarding afflictions and the two types of selflessness regarding phenomena,
and through inconceivable transformation, one who is without birth and death is named a Buddha.
The nature of phenomena associated with the mind—this is my teaching regarding the internal body;
if one can see it thus, one does not follow deluded cognition.
In reality, there are no phenomena such as those discriminated by the ignorant.
Relying on unreal and non-existent dharmas, how can one attain liberation?
Bound by the conjunction of arising and ceasing, one perceives conditioned phenomena;
thus increasing the two views, yet not losing the law of causes and conditions.
Like a plantain tree, a dream, or an illusion—such is this world;
Only this one dharma is real: nirvāṇa, which transcends the functioning consciousness.
There is greed and there is hatred, And there is delusion, yet no person exists.
From craving arise the aggregates; the existence of these aggregates is like a dream.
On the night I realized the Dharma and on the night I entered parinirvāṇa—between these two moments, I have not uttered a single word.
Having personally realized the Dharma within my own body, I speak thus;
neither that Buddha nor I have any superior Dharma to proclaim.
If a real self-substance existed, the five aggregates would be devoid of its characteristics.
The substance of the aggregates is substantially existent, yet within those aggregates there is no self.
Through various perceptions and discriminations, one follows the secondary afflictions and the latent tendencies;
by attaining the world as one's own mind, one leaves suffering behind and achieves liberation.
Through various causes and conditions, the world arises in this way;
those who associate with these four dharmas do not abide in my teaching.
Phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent in their arising; apart from existence and non-existence, there is no arising.
How can the ignorant discriminate, based on causes and various conditions?
When one can see the world as free from the four extremes of existence and non-existence,
at that time the mind and consciousness are transformed, and one immediately attains the dharma of selflessness.
All phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; therefore, they arise through causes and conditions.
Those conditions themselves are the fruit, and within the fruit, existence arises.
Within the fruit, two kinds arise; thus, there should be two within the fruit.
In the two there is no fruit, and within the fruit no object is seen.
Apart from the observer and the observed, if one perceives conditioned phenomena;
apart from the mind, there is only mind—therefore I teach "Mind-Only."
The actual substance and form of valid cognition are devoid of the substance of conditions;
ultimately and supremely pure—this is what I call valid cognition.
Just as "self" is a mere conventional designation, no real dharma is to be perceived.
Thus, the aggregates and their essential nature are merely provisional designations and not real.
There are four kinds of equality: equality of characteristics, equality of causes, equality of arising, and equality of selflessness;
these are the dharmas for the four types of practitioners.
All views, as well as the subject and object of discrimination, are transformed;
because they are neither perceived nor produced, I teach that there is only mind.
There are no phenomena, yet it is not non-existent; it is free from the nature of both existence and non-existence.
Tathatā is free from the mind; therefore, I teach that there is only mind.
Tathatā, emptiness, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), Nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu);
The mind-made body (manomayakāya) and the mind— Therefore, I teach that there is only mind.
Based on the habitual tendencies of discrimination, various things arise from various [causes];
sentient beings perceive externals through their minds, therefore I teach that there is only mind.
There are no external objects to be seen; what is seen is the mind manifesting as various appearances.
Because of the body, the means of subsistence, and the sustaining environment, I say that all is but mind.
From the *kṣayajñāna* (knowledge of exhaustion) of the śrāvakas, the Tathāgatas are born;
from all the pratyekabuddhas, they are born without [external] conjunction.
There are no external forms or signs; it is one's own mind that perceives external phenomena.
When one realizes that these are but one's own mind, the ignorant still conceptualize conditioned things.
Fools do not know that what they perceive as external is but their own mind appearing in various ways.
Using analogies to restrain the foolish who cling to four kinds of dharmas—
those that are causeless and non-conceptual— and through the fivefold discourse on analogies regarding the essential nature and forms of one’s own mind, one who can understand this is truly wise.
Based on discrimination, distinctions can be made; this is the characteristic of discrimination.
Relying upon discrimination, discrimination manifests in the present life.
Each distinct combination is a single causal seed.
The two dharmas of the guest are dual; therefore, the human mind does not arise.
Discriminating between mind and mental factors, one dwells within the two realms;
though they manifest as all phenomena, their essence is illusory.
Because causes and conditions depend on present conjunction, there are thus the twelve bases (*āyatana*);
because one contemplates dependence and conjunction, I do not say that these are dharmas.
It is like seeing an image in a mirror, or seeing a net of hairs with cataracts in the eye.
Thus, based on the perfumed mind, the minds of the deluded perceive;
through the mutual differentiation of the distinguishable, conceptualization arises.
It is like the conceptualizations of non-Buddhists, for such external signs do not exist.
Just as a person who does not recognize a rope takes it to be a snake,
so too one who does not understand the meaning of one's own mind discriminates external phenomena. Yet,
by mounting the vehicle of the vehicle itself, one departs from the extremes of oneness, otherness, and the middle.
To differentiate between vehicles is the fault of one's own mind.
Based on what dharma or what essence could differentiation perceive?
One cannot say that they do not exist; such is the nature of all dharmas.
Based on existence, one speaks of non-existence; based on non-existence, one speaks of existence.
Therefore, one cannot say it is non-existent, nor can one say it is existent.
This is merely conceptualization upon conceptualization; this is not the true nature of phenomena.
How can one perceive the absence of intrinsic nature and yet give rise to conceptual discrimination?
The nature of form is not a physical body, like a jar or a cloth;
since that which is visible is a non-entity, how can there be conceptual discrimination?
"If conceptual differentiation is delusion, and conditioned phenomena are beginningless,
then what phenomenon causes sentient beings to be deluded?
O Muni, please explain this to me."
All phenomena lack the essence of a dharma; it is taught that they are merely mind.
Failing to perceive one’s own mind, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination.
If such discrimination were non-existent, it would be like the discrimination of a fool.
Those phenomena have no distinct essence, yet wisdom cannot perceive them.
If the Noble Ones possessed such phenomena, they would not be the false conceptualizations of ordinary beings;
if the Noble Ones falsely possessed them, there would be no distinction between the Noble and the ignorant.
The Sage is free from delusion, for he has attained a pure mind;
the fool lacks faith, and thus engages in conceptual discrimination upon discrimination.
It is as if a mother, for the sake of her children, were to bring fruits down from the sky.
"Take the fruit and do not weep; let the child take various fruits.
I, for the sake of all sentient beings, distinguish various fruits;
I cause them to desire various teachings so that they may leave behind the factions of existence and non-existence."
If there were no fundamental essence of phenomena, they would be neither causes nor derived from causes;
fundamentally unarisen yet arising for the first time, they likewise possess no body.
Being bodiless, they are not produced, and apart from causes and conditions, they have no locus.

By transforming the conceptualizing consciousness, one is liberated from change and cessation.
As with a rabbit’s horn or a mani-jewel, so it is said by those who have attained liberation.
Just as one relies on the conjunction of knots, so too is it with the reliance on phenomena;
relying on the conjunction of conjunctions, do not discriminate between them as different.
The karma and sensation of eye-consciousness, ignorance and right view;
the eye, forms, and the mind—the defilement of mental consciousness is thus.
The Buddha preached this sublime sutra for the noble and great wise one.
Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, the Great King Rāvaṇa,
Śukabaraṇa, the Piśāca Uṣṭra-karṇa and others,
devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras.
The assembly of devas and bhikṣus rejoiced greatly and practiced accordingly.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
